title: Build to Bond: The Full Story of How Bamboo Bikes Are Rebuilding Family Connections in Prison
tags: Bamboo Bikes, Build to Bond, Family Connection, HMP Lowdham Grange, Impact, Investec Beyond Business, James Timpson, OCN Level 2, Prison Rehabilitation, Social Enterprise
summary: Prison Rehabilitation | HMP Lowdham Grange | 2025–ongoing How a six-week bamboo bicycle building course is reconnecting incarcerated parents with their children — and earning national recognition from the Financial Times, the UK Prisons Minister, and the Investec Beyond Business award.
body: A Category B prison in Nottinghamshire. A 2,000 square foot workshop. Bamboo, hemp, and hand tools. And a waiting list — because no one wanted to miss it. Build to Bond is not a craft project. It is not a "keep prisoners busy" programme. It is a structured, accredited rehabilitation pathway in which incarcerated Makers learn sustainable manufacturing, earn a nationally recognised qualification, and build a bicycle with their own hands — often for the child waiting at home for them. The Financial Times covered it in September 2025. The UK Prisons Minister endorsed it publicly. And the 3,500+ people who have built bamboo bikes through Bamboo Bicycle Club — most of them free, most of them paying — are the proof that this approach works at scale. Why Bamboo? Bamboo has the tensile strength of steel. It can be cut and shaped with hand tools — no lathes, no CNC machines, no specialist equipment that cannot safely exist inside a Category B prison. It is a renewable material that grows back within three to five years. And it looks extraordinary when finished. That last point matters more than it sounds. When a Maker holds their finished frame, something shifts. The object in their hands is undeniable proof that they are capable of more than they knew. "For a lot of prisoners, the programmes offered are quite dull, but bamboo bikes have that cool factor that excites them. In the programme there is maths and English, but it is built into design, creativity and bike mechanics." — James Marr, Founder, Bamboo Bicycle Club (Inside Time, November 2025) Over 14 years and 4,000+ people trained across 36 countries, Bamboo Bicycle Club has refined what works when teaching non-engineers to build something durable, precise, and beautiful. Build to Bond takes that curriculum into the places it is needed most. How the Programme Works Each cohort runs for six weeks, four hours a day — eighteen hours of structured workshop time per week. Twelve Makers per cohort. They work through: Week 1–2: Foundation and materials science. Workshop safety, bamboo properties, frame geometry, technical drawing. The maths is real; it is embedded in measurement and design. Week 3–4: Frame construction. Cutting and preparing bamboo culms. Hemp-fibre and bio-resin joining at the nodes. Building the frame incrementally, checking geometry at every stage. Week 5: Mechanics and finishing. Wheel-building, component assembly, paint and finishing techniques. The bike becomes a complete, rideable object. Week 6: Enterprise and completion. Business basics. What sustainable manufacturing looks like as a career. Qualification assessment. And — for those who qualify — entry into Build to Bond itself. Three participants at HMP Lowdham Grange have been trained as peer instructors. They co-deliver elements of the programme alongside BBC staff. This is not a cost-saving measure — it is by design. Peer instruction is one of the most powerful learning mechanisms there is, and it transforms participants into leaders. "The bamboo bike course offers more than just technical training — it provides an avenue for creativity, teamwork, and self-expression." — Sally Allsopp, Industries Manager, HMP Lowdham Grange The Build to Bond Moment: Building a Bike for Your Child Build to Bond is the follow-up course for Makers who complete the foundation programme. In it, they build a children's bamboo balance bike — small, light, perfectly proportioned for a toddler — and gift it to their child, grandchild, nephew, or niece. The kit uses the same materials as the full-size frame: natural bamboo, hemp fibre, bio-resin, water-based paint. The build process mirrors the one the Maker has already mastered. But the purpose is entirely different. "When one Maker received a balance bike kit for his toddler, he was inspired and excited that he could create something — and suddenly all that communication developed with his daughter that he might never have had." — James Marr, describing a Build to Bond participant (

title: Hasan: Building a Bamboo Bike Changed How I Learn
tags: community, confidence, impact, learning, personal story, transformation
summary: Individual Transformation | London | 2020 Hasan came to BBC to build a gravel bike. What he left with was something he did not expect: a different way of understanding himself as a learner....
body: Hasan came to BBC to build a gravel bike. What he left with was something he did not expect: a different way of understanding himself as a learner. In his build review, he wrote: 'I don't think I'll ever forget this experience. It was instrumental in creating a shift in my life in terms of gaining confidence in myself and realising that there are different ways of learning and experiencing the world.' That is not a product review. That is a description of a change in identity — a person who came in uncertain leaving with evidence that they can do things they previously could not. Hasan's reflection represents something BBC encounters regularly but rarely documents: the confidence shift that comes from completing a bamboo frame. Participants arrive nervous. They leave with a bike and proof — physical, irrefutable — that they can do difficult things. Key Facts Builder: Hasan Year: 2020 Build type: Gravel bike Outcome: Significant confidence and learning identity shift "It was instrumental in creating a shift in my life in terms of gaining confidence in myself and realising that there are different ways of learning." — Hasan, BBC build review, 2020

title: BBC's Sustainability Story: From Science to Negative Carbon
tags: carbon, environment, green, impact, science, sustainability
summary: Environmental Impact | 2012–2025 BBC's first Facebook post in August 2012 led with a number: bamboo tensile strength is 28,000 newtons per square metre, compared with 23,000 for steel. BBC's sustainability case has always been ground...
body: BBC's first Facebook post in August 2012 led with a number: bamboo tensile strength is 28,000 newtons per square metre, compared with 23,000 for steel. BBC's sustainability case has always been grounded in science, not slogans. Over 13 years, that foundation has grown. BBC has published on bamboo's anti-bacterial properties, rapid growth cycle, carbon sequestration credentials, and workability with hand tools. In 2024, an independent analysis confirmed that a BBC bamboo bike has a negative CO2 footprint. The sustainability story runs through every product: workshop bikes use bio-resin and responsibly sourced Tonkin bamboo. Educational kits teach circular manufacturing — frames deconstructed at course end and materials reused. In 2022, BBC collaborated with Presca to produce carbon-neutral cycle jerseys. In 2025, BBC can say something very few cycling companies can: an independent expert confirmed our bikes have a negative carbon footprint. That statement, backed by independent analysis, is worth more than any amount of green marketing. Key Facts Tensile strength: 28,000 N (vs 23,000 N steel) Carbon footprint: Negative (independent, 2024) Manufacturing: Hand tools, bio-resin, no power machinery "His bamboo bike has a negative CO2 footprint." — Manish, sustainability professional, 2024

title: Taro: Ten Years on One Bamboo Bike
tags: community, durability, impact, Japan, member story, Taro
summary: Community Member Story | Japan/UK | 2015–2024 In 2015, Taro built a bamboo bicycle at BBC in London. Then he rode it from London to Paris. Then he took it back to Japan. Then he kept riding it — for ten years....
body: In 2015, Taro built a bamboo bicycle at BBC in London. Then he rode it from London to Paris. Then he took it back to Japan. Then he kept riding it — for ten years. In 2024, Taro's bike was still his bike. Still the frame he built in a Hackney workshop in 2015. Still the bamboo he selected, cut, mitred, joined, and finished with his own hands. Ten years of riding is the most powerful durability proof BBC has. Not a manufacturer's warranty or a materials test. A decade of daily use, documented by the person who built it. Taro's story is also about what building something does to your relationship with it. You do not discard a thing you made. You maintain it, adjust it, repair it — because you built it. The 10-year bike is the logical outcome of learning to make something properly. Key Facts Builder: Taro Built: 2015, BBC London Still riding: 2024 First route: London to Paris Location: Japan "Ten years on my hand-built bamboo bike — and still going." — Taro, 2024

title: 4,000+ People Trained Across 36+ Countries: 13 Years of Impact
summary: Scale of Impact | Global | 2012–2025 Since August 2012, Bamboo Bicycle Club has trained more than 4,000 people in bamboo bicycle construction across more than 36 countries. Over 3,500 bamboo frames have been completed. Every one of them ...
body: Since August 2012, Bamboo Bicycle Club has trained more than 4,000 people in bamboo bicycle construction across more than 36 countries. Over 3,500 bamboo frames have been completed. Every one of them is a different person's story. The 36+ countries figure is the cumulative result of 13 years of workshops in London, Munich, Amersfoort, and Toulouse; educational kits delivered to schools in the Netherlands, Germany, and the UK; charity expeditions to Norway, Singapore, and South America; corporate sessions in Zurich, Hampshire, and London; and community programmes in Kenya, Rwanda, and Ghana. Each of the 4,000+ people trained came with a different motivation. Some were cyclists. Some were makers. Some were sustainability professionals. Some were prisoners. Some were school students discovering they could do engineering. The number grows every week. But the more important figure is what lies behind it: 4,000 people who discovered that bamboo is a serious material, that making changes how you think, and that a bicycle you built is a different object from one you bought. Key Facts People trained: 4,000+ Countries: 36+ Frames completed: 3,500+ Years operating: 13 (2012–2025) "4,000+ people trained across 36+ countries. 3,500+ bikes built." — Bamboo Bicycle Club

title: Grand Palais Paris: BBC in a World-Class Exhibition
tags: cultural, exhibition, Grand Palais, impact, international, Paris
summary: Cultural Impact | Paris, France | November 2023 In November 2023, BBC's home build kit was selected for inclusion in an exhibition at the Grand Palais, Paris — one of the most prestigious cultural venues in the world. James Marr was invited to writ...
body: In November 2023, BBC's home build kit was selected for inclusion in an exhibition at the Grand Palais, Paris — one of the most prestigious cultural venues in the world. James Marr was invited to write for the exhibition catalogue on reimagining bicycle craftsmanship. James's essay argues that mass production has removed our agency over the objects we own — and that building your own bicycle is a direct act of reclaiming that agency. 'As humans we have engaged in the act of making for thousands of years,' he wrote. The Grand Palais placement positions BBC not as a cycling company but as a participant in wider discourse about craft, sustainability, and what it means to make things in a consumer-driven world. The appearance adds to BBC's cultural credibility alongside London Design Festival (2024), UK Bamboo Summit at Coventry University (2024), and The Engineering Club lecture (2025). Key Facts Venue: Grand Palais, Paris Date: November 2023 Contribution: Home build kit + catalogue essay by James Marr "I strongly believe in the importance of physically touching, crafting and tweaking a design, until you have a unique finished product." — James Marr, Grand Palais Paris catalogue, 2023

title: Corporate Build Donates Balance Bikes to Upcycle Brixton
tags: Brixton, charity, community, corporate, CSR, impact, Upcycle
summary: Corporate CSR + Community Impact | London | December 2024 In December 2024, a company completed a corporate team-building session at BBC. The session produced finished bamboo balance bikes. Those bikes were donated to Upcycle — a cycling charity in Brixton w...
body: In December 2024, a company completed a corporate team-building session at BBC. The session produced finished bamboo balance bikes. Those bikes were donated to Upcycle — a cycling charity in Brixton working to get more people on bikes in South London. This is BBC's social impact logic made tangible: a corporate team pays for a workshop, learns to build together, and the product of their work goes directly to a community that needs it. Corporate team gets a meaningful experience. Charity gets bikes. Children get access to cycling. Upcycle works to make cycling accessible in communities where cost, confidence, and culture are barriers. Bamboo balance bikes — lightweight, robust, hand-built — are exactly the kind of asset they can use. The Upcycle donation model is one BBC can repeat with every corporate session — instead of bikes staying with the company as ornaments, they circulate into the community as tools. Key Facts Output: Bamboo balance bikes Recipient: Upcycle, cycling charity, Brixton Date: December 2024 Model: Corporate learning → community asset → cycling access "The finished balance bikes will be donated to Upcycle, a charity in Brixton, to encourage cycling." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, December 2024

title: Article 25: Bamboo Bikes for Humanitarian Architecture
summary: Charity Partnership | London | 2019 In 2019, BBC worked with Article 25 — a humanitarian architecture charity that uses design to improve health, livelihoods, and resilience to disasters — bringing together two organisations who believe...
body: In 2019, BBC worked with Article 25 — a humanitarian architecture charity that uses design to improve health, livelihoods, and resilience to disasters — bringing together two organisations who believe design, craft, and making are tools for positive change. Article 25 works in some of the world's most challenging environments, designing buildings and infrastructure for communities recovering from disaster, conflict, and poverty. BBC's bamboo construction knowledge is directly applicable in bamboo-growing regions where other structural materials are expensive or scarce. The collaboration was a proof of concept for a deeper working relationship — demonstrating that BBC's expertise has relevance beyond recreational cycling, connecting to questions of sustainable construction and design for development. The Article 25 partnership reflects BBC's position as a genuine social impact organisation with multiple credible institutional relationships: Investec, Big Issue Invest, TNL Community Fund, and Build to Bond. Key Facts Partner: Article 25 Type: Humanitarian architecture charity Year: 2019 Mission: Design to improve health, livelihoods and disaster resilience "We use design to improve health, livelihoods and resilience to disasters." — Article 25

body: In July 2022, BBC attended the Image Bamboo Festival in Birmingham and collaborated with Ghana Bamboo Bikes to jointly showcase bamboo bicycles — creating a bridge between the UK and African bamboo bicycle communities. title: BBC Forms an Education CIC: Mission Made Official

summary: Organisational | National | December 2025 At the end of 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club announced the formation of a Community Interest Company (CIC) specifically to run and grow all its education projects. After 13 years of education work, BBC mad...
body: At the end of 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club announced the formation of a Community Interest Company (CIC) specifically to run and grow all its education projects. After 13 years of education work, BBC made it official. The CIC sits alongside the commercial workshop and kit business, ring-fencing the education mission with its own legal structure — enabling access to grants, programme funding, and impact investment unavailable to standard companies. The announcement came alongside confirmation of multiple new funders: TNL Community Fund, Big Issue Invest, and Innovate UK's Growth Programme — three major endorsements in one year alongside Investec and the FT/Timpson coverage. 2025 was the year BBC stopped describing itself as a bicycle company that sometimes teaches, and started describing itself as what it has always been: an education organisation that builds bicycles. Key Facts Structure: Community Interest Company (CIC) Year: 2025 Funders: Investec, TNL Community Fund, Big Issue Invest, Innovate UK Significance: Education mission ring-fenced with dedicated legal structure "We formed a CIC to run and grow all our education projects." — James Marr, December 2025

title: Manish: Bamboo Bikes Have a Negative Carbon Footprint
tags: carbon footprint, environment, impact, research, sustainability
summary: Sustainability Research | London | October 2024 Manish, founder of a sustainable AI company, cycled 70 miles London to Brighton then came to BBC to build a bamboo bicycle. As a sustainability professional, he ran the carbon numbers....
body: Manish, founder of a sustainable AI company, cycled 70 miles London to Brighton then came to BBC to build a bamboo bicycle. As a sustainability professional, he ran the carbon numbers. His calculation compared the lifecycle carbon footprint of a BBC bamboo bike against a conventional carbon fibre bicycle. The result: a BBC bamboo bike has a negative CO2 footprint. Bamboo sequesters carbon as it grows. BBC's manufacturing uses hand tools and bio-resin with no power-intensive machining. The frame stores that captured carbon for its lifetime. Carbon fibre bicycles, by contrast, require energy-intensive autoclave manufacturing and cannot be recycled at end of life. Manish's analysis adds independent professional credibility to BBC's sustainability story. It is not BBC saying its bikes are green — it is a sustainability professional calculating it and finding that bamboo bikes are, in fact, carbon negative. Key Facts Researcher: Manish, sustainable AI founder Finding: BBC bamboo bike = negative CO2 footprint Comparison: vs conventional carbon fibre bicycle Published: October 2024 "His bamboo bike has a negative CO2 footprint." — Manish, October 2024

title: Jock's Ride to Norway: 3,000km for PAPYRUS
tags: charity, cycling, impact, mental health, Norway, PAPYRUS
summary: Charity Cycling | London → Bergen | August 2023 Jock built a bamboo bicycle at BBC. Then he cycled 3,000 kilometres from London to Bergen, Norway — to raise money for PAPYRUS, the charity preventing young suicide. He made the ride in memory of his ...
body: Jock built a bamboo bicycle at BBC. Then he cycled 3,000 kilometres from London to Bergen, Norway — to raise money for PAPYRUS, the charity preventing young suicide. He made the ride in memory of his university friend Joe, who died by suicide in early 2022. Jock describes Joe in detail — his humour, his generosity, the memories that don't fade — and explains that when Joe died, the absence 'felt harrowing to the point where it felt surreal.' The 3,000km ride was his response. PAPYRUS works specifically to prevent young suicide and promote mental health in young people — precisely the cause that resonates in the university world Jock and Joe inhabited. The bamboo bike Jock built was the craft project that preceded the journey; the months of building that preceded the months of riding; the physical expression of a decision to do something with grief rather than be consumed by it. Key Facts Rider: Jock Route: London → Bergen, Norway Distance: 3,000 km+ Charity: PAPYRUS Prevention of Young Suicide In memory of: Joe "This ride is for Joe — and for everyone who has lost someone to suicide." — Jock, 2023

title: 2 by Bamboo: 11,300km Across 6 Countries
tags: adventure, endurance, expedition, impact, South America
summary: Adventure Expedition | South America | 2018 In July 2018, two riders completed 11,300 kilometres across 6 countries, finishing in Cartagena, Colombia on BBC-built bamboo bikes....
body: In July 2018, two riders completed 11,300 kilometres across 6 countries, finishing in Cartagena, Colombia on BBC-built bamboo bikes. 11,300km is the equivalent of cycling from London to the Middle East and back. Across 6 countries. On hand-built bamboo frames. If there was any remaining question about whether bamboo bicycles are robust enough for serious long-distance cycling, this answers it. 2 by Bamboo ran alongside Kate Rawles' South American journey in the same period — two separate bamboo bicycle expeditions crossing South America simultaneously, both built at BBC. Adventures like this require a bike the rider trusts completely. The fact that BBC bikes are chosen over commercial alternatives is the most compelling endorsement the company has. Key Facts Expedition: 2 by Bamboo Distance: 11,300 km Countries: 6 Finish: Cartagena, Colombia Year: 2018 "After 6 countries, 11,300km, a bloody long mountain range, lots of laughs, a few sobs, and 1,620 rice-based meals — we made it." — 2 by Bamboo, 2018

title: Dr Tom and Dr Nick: UK to Singapore for MSF
summary: Charity Expedition | UK → Singapore | 2014 In 2014, two doctors built BBC bamboo bikes and cycled from the UK to Singapore to raise money for Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) — over 12,000 kilometres across Europe, the Middle...
body: In 2014, two doctors built BBC bamboo bikes and cycled from the UK to Singapore to raise money for Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) — over 12,000 kilometres across Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia. Completing this route on hand-built bamboo frames is a statement about what the material can withstand: cold mountain passes, desert heat, monsoon rain, and months of accumulated road wear. The charity dimension matters. MSF operates in conflict zones and humanitarian emergencies. Two doctors choosing to raise for MSF by cycling 12,000km on bamboo bikes is a powerful story: sustainable transport in the service of sustainable medicine. Dr Tom and Dr Nick's ride was the first of many BBC-community charity expeditions — setting a template that Jock (PAPYRUS, 2023), Alec (WaterAid, 2015), and others have followed. Key Facts Riders: Dr Tom and Dr Nick Route: UK to Singapore (~12,000+ km) Year: 2014 Charity: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) "Riding from the UK to Singapore to raise money for Doctors Without Borders." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, 2014

body: BBC taught Hilton Bankside staff to build bamboo bikes — bikes that then became part of the hotel's public hire fleet. A complete example of BBC's education-to-impact pipeline: teach people to build, they build the bikes, the bikes go into service. Hilton Bankside is a design-led London hotel positioned at the intersection of sustainability and premium hospitality. BBC's bamboo hire bikes fit naturally: a distinctive, sustainable, locally-built product that tells a story to guests. The hire bikes were subsequently spotted by @zacefron, documented on his zero-to-earth sustainability platform by @zacdowntoearth — BBC's bamboo bikes visible to a global audience through unexpected celebrity connection. body: In 2022, BBC delivered a team-building workshop for GM Motors in Zurich — taking its mobile education offer across Europe to one of the world's largest automotive companies. Building bamboo bikes with an automotive company carries symbolic weight. GM's business is built on the combustion engine. BBC's mission is to offer the world's most sustainable transport. Jigs, materials, tools, and instructor travel to the client — hotel event spaces and international locations are equally viable. GM Zurich expanded BBC's European corporate credentials significantly, demonstrating appetite for its sustainability-led model in the Swiss and German corporate markets. title: The Macallan Whisky: Masters of Their Craft

body: Macallan Whisky brought participants in its UK advocacy platform, 'Masters of Their Craft,' to BBC's London workshop to build bespoke bamboo bicycles. Ten bikes were built. The connecting theme: bamboo makes up 80% of the bike, just as oak casks contribute 80% of Macallan's whisky flavour. Both organisations make premium, handcrafted, natural-material products that require time, skill, and patience. The BBC session gave participants a visceral experience of what craft actually feels like. Ten bikes from one session is one of BBC's largest single-day outputs — requiring serious logistical coordination across multiple groups with quality control throughout. Macallan adds a powerful brand to BBC's corporate client list alongside Four Seasons, GM Motors, and Hilton — positioning BBC as a premium sustainable brand experience. title: Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire: Senior Team Builds a Bike in Three Hours
tags: corporate, Four Seasons, impact, sustainability, team building
summary: Corporate Team Building | Hampshire | April 2025 Twelve senior managers from Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire swapped spreadsheets for spoke keys and built a bamboo bike frame in three hours. BBC brought its mobile workshop to the hotel's events barn — ...
body: Twelve senior managers from Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire swapped spreadsheets for spoke keys and built a bamboo bike frame in three hours. BBC brought its mobile workshop to the hotel's events barn — bamboo, jigs, tools, and an instructor. The session covered every stage of frame building: measuring and marking bamboo, precision cutting with Japanese pull saws, mitre-fitting joints, dry-fitting the triangle, and applying bio-resin epoxy. The result: a complete, structurally sound bamboo frame, built in an afternoon. Four Seasons asked for a hands-on, sustainability-driven team-building experience. What BBC delivered was something more: a shared experience of making something difficult together, under time pressure, with a real, tangible outcome. The Four Seasons build is the premium expression of BBC's corporate offer: fully managed, mobile, premium-brand-compatible, producing a finished object and a lasting story. Key Facts Client: Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire Participants: 12 senior managers Duration: 3 hours Output: 1 complete bamboo bike frame "In just three hours, twelve senior managers swapped spreadsheets for spoke keys." — Bamboo Bicycle Club

body: In September 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club was selected as one of four national winners of the Investec Beyond Business 2025 programme — receiving approximately £24,000 in funding alongside ongoing mentorship and access to Investec's professional network. The programme has been running for 15 years, supporting socially-driven entrepreneurs in Tower Hamlets, Newham and Hackney.
