title: Outdoor Philosophy: Why Kate Rawles Built a Bamboo Bicycle
tags: 2016, bamboo, build, eden-project, kate-rawles, outdoor-philosophy, press, woody
body: Outdoor Philosophy 29 November 2016 | outdoorphilosophy.co.uk | Kate Rawles Published immediately after the BBC workshop build, before the Life Cycle expedition departure “For James at the Bamboo Bicycle Club, the main reasons are to do with empowering people to build their own machines. That’s his vision: hundreds and eventually thousands of people, who have been through the unique process of building their bicycle, to their specifications, from scratch; from, literally, a pile of sticks. There is something really powerful about disentangling bikes from remote expertise and making them, their construction and their maintenance, a whole lot more accessible.” — Kate Rawles, Outdoor Philosophy, November 2016 Outdoor Philosophy — Kate Rawles’ website and writing platform, covering environmental adventure, ecology, and the philosophy of outdoor experience — published this account in November 2016, immediately after Kate had built Woody at BBC’s London workshop and weeks before she departed for Colombia to begin the Life Cycle expedition. It is the earliest first-person account of the BBC workshop experience by Kate Rawles, written in the immediate aftermath of building Woody — before any of the expedition’s outcomes were known. Kate’s account is notable for its focus on the why of the build rather than the what . She does not describe the technical process of building the frame — the jig, the bamboo selection, the hemp wrapping. She describes what the process means: the philosophy of making something yourself, from raw materials, rather than purchasing the finished object from a factory. This is the lens through which Kate Rawles — an environmental philosopher — approached everything, including her bicycle. The Eden Project bamboo Kate’s account of the material provenance is precise: the bamboo came from the Eden Project in Cornwall; the hemp joints from Yorkshire; the eco-resin from European plant-based sources. As far as anyone could confirm, it was the UK’s first home-grown bamboo bicycle — not just in the sense that it was built in the UK, but in the sense that the primary structural material grew in UK soil. This material specificity mattered to Kate philosophically. She was about to ride 8,288 miles through South America raising awareness of biodiversity loss — the same systems that produce bamboo, hemp, and flax. The frame and the mission were not separate. The bike was made of the world Kate was trying to protect. “The heart of this bike is local and low impact. The joints are made from Yorkshire hemp soaked in a European plant-based eco-resin. The bamboo came from the Eden Project in Cornwall. Truly a ‘home grown bicycle’ in these respects at least.” — Kate Rawles, Outdoor Philosophy, November 2016 The most important BBC workshop testimonial Kate Rawles’ articulation of James Marr’s vision — “disentangling bikes from remote expertise and making them, their construction and their maintenance, a whole lot more accessible” — is the clearest third-party description of BBC’s founding purpose ever written. Kate is not a journalist summarising a press release. She is a philosopher who attended the workshop, built the frame, and then articulated what the experience meant in terms she uses professionally. The Outdoor Philosophy piece was published in November 2016, before any of the expedition’s outcomes were known. Kate wrote about why she was going. Woody was complete. The 8,288 miles lay ahead. The philosophy she articulated then was proven, over the following 14 months, by every mountain pass, every salt flat crossing, and every Patagonian headwind that Woody survived without mechanical failure. The BBC workshop philosophy she described in November 2016 rode those miles too. Read the full piece on Outdoor Philosophy →

title: Swoop Patagonia: Why Kate Rawles Cycled Across Patagonia on a Bamboo Bike
tags: 2024, bamboo-bike, expedition, kate-rawles, patagonia, press, swoop-patagonia, woody
body: Swoop Patagonia August 2024 | Adventure Travel Blog Photography: Chris Loynes | Kate Rawles guest contribution “My trusty steed for the duration was called Woody, a bike I’d built myself at a course run by the Bamboo Bicycle Club in London, with a frame crafted from bamboo grown at the Eden Project in Cornwall. All bikes are like magicians, transforming interactions with people and landscapes alike, but a bamboo bike multiplies that a hundredfold.” — Kate Rawles, Swoop Patagonia, August 2024 Swoop Patagonia — one of the leading adventure travel specialists for Patagonia expeditions, with a global readership of serious adventure cyclists, hikers, and wilderness travellers — published Kate Rawles’ first-person account of cycling across Patagonia on Woody in August 2024, more than six years after the expedition’s completion. The piece appeared as a guest contribution on Swoop’s travel blog, reaching an audience of people actively planning or considering Patagonia expeditions — exactly the community most likely to understand what 8,288 miles on a bamboo bike actually means. Swoop Patagonia’s platform is authoritative for adventure travel in the region: it covers route planning, logistics, gear, and trip reports from real expeditions. Kate Rawles’ contribution placed BBC at the centre of the most significant bamboo bicycle expedition ever undertaken — in a context where the audience could fully appreciate the terrain, the distances, and the challenge. The bamboo bike as expedition tool Kate’s description of Woody as a “magician” for transforming human interactions — and a bamboo bike as multiplying that effect “a hundredfold” — captures something specific about bamboo bicycles that conventional cycling equipment cannot replicate. Throughout 8,288 miles of riding through Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina, Woody generated conversations that opened doors to communities, contacts, and experiences that Kate could not have accessed on a standard aluminium touring bike. For Swoop Patagonia’s readers — people planning their own Patagonia adventures — the bamboo bike story raises a genuine question: what equipment choices, beyond the practical, shape the quality of an expedition? Kate’s account suggests that building your own frame — knowing every joint, every bamboo node, every material decision — creates a relationship with the bike that a purchased frame cannot. That relationship, across 14 months of solo riding, proved to be an asset as much as any technical specification. “The final distance of my ride was 8,288 miles, and Woody made it with virtually no mechanical issues at all.” — Kate Rawles Six years on The Swoop Patagonia piece was published in August 2024 — more than six years after the expedition’s February 2018 completion and three years after Kate’s book The Life Cycle was published. Its appearance in 2024 demonstrates the longevity of the Kate Rawles / Bamboo Bicycle Club story: it is not a news cycle that expires but a durability proof that becomes more compelling with time. Every year that passes without Woody failing is another year of evidence. Swoop Patagonia’s global audience of adventure travel enthusiasts represents a significant reach for BBC in 2024: people who understand what cycling through Patagonia requires, who are planning their own expeditions, and who are making equipment decisions informed by real-world evidence rather than manufacturer specifications. Kate Rawles’ testimony — 8,288 miles, virtually no mechanical issues — is the kind of evidence that informs those decisions. Read the full article on Swoop Patagonia →

title: Designboom: Bamboo Bicycle Club Lets You Build Your Own Sustainable Commute
tags: 2023, design, designboom, diy, gravel-bike, kit, press, sustainable
body: Designboom 26 January 2023 | Editor: Ravail Khan | Photography: Adam Gasson DIY Submissions feature | 14 million+ monthly readers “Promoting local manufacturing, DIY, and independence, Bamboo Bicycle Club’s Bamboo Gravel Bike Build Kit revolutionises our relationship with cycling. Designed by James Marr, the kit allows users to take control of their commute and become a maker of their own vehicle, allowing them to construct their own sustainable built bicycle in their front room.” — Designboom, January 2023 Designboom — the world’s largest online design magazine, with 14 million+ monthly readers across architecture, industrial design, product design, and sustainable innovation — featured BBC’s Bamboo Gravel Bike Build Kit in January 2023, with professional photography by Adam Gasson and editorial by Ravail Khan. The article appeared in Designboom’s DIY Submissions section, which features genuine innovations submitted by designers and studios and selected for editorial coverage on their own merits. The January 2023 feature was BBC’s second Designboom appearance — following the November 2020 mccloy + muchemwa city bike collaboration. In three years, the design-world narrative had shifted: where the 2020 piece focused on BBC as a fabrication partner for architects, the 2023 piece positioned the gravel kit as an independent consumer product with a design rationale that Designboom’s audience could immediately understand. The gravel kit The Bamboo Gravel Bike Build Kit combines recycled aluminium lugs with bamboo tubes — a hybrid approach that addresses the central challenge of bamboo bicycle construction: jointing. Traditional bamboo builds use hand-wrapped hemp fibre and epoxy resin at every connection point, a process that is beautiful, strong, and time-consuming (the original BBC workshop kit required 70–80 hours to complete). The recycled aluminium lug system creates precision connections that hold the bamboo tubes in exact alignment, cutting build time by approximately 75%. The modular dropout design allows any gearing configuration; drop stays are included for improved ride quality; and fittings for racks and mudguards are integrated, making the gravel kit a practical commuter and adventure frame as well as a design object. Adam Gasson’s photography for Designboom presented the finished kit bike with the same visual quality that Designboom applies to high-end product design features — making the bamboo gravel bike legible to a global design audience. “Despite being more sustainable and of higher quality, bamboo bicycle frames are difficult and time consuming to build. By combining the lug with bamboo, it offers a natural vibration dampening and resolves the current bicycle market’s lack of flexibility and high costs.” — Designboom, January 2023 Design rationale Designboom’s framing — “revolutionises our relationship with cycling” — is strong editorial language from a publication that applies it carefully. The Designboom editor identified the gravel kit not just as a product but as a different model of bicycle production: local, manual, personalised, and repairable. In a market dominated by factory-produced aluminium and carbon frames that are difficult or impossible to repair and offer no customisation beyond colour, a kit that a rider builds themselves from natural and recycled materials addresses a genuine gap. Designboom’s global readership of design professionals and design-educated consumers understood this immediately. The gravel kit’s January 2023 Designboom feature generated traffic from design studios, architecture practices, engineering consultancies, and individual makers worldwide — the international audience that BBC’s kit business depends on for sustained growth beyond the UK workshop market. title: Inside Time: Bamboozling Way to Build Bikes — Bamboo Bicycle Club at Lowdham Grange
tags: 2025, build-to-bond, inside-time, lord-timpson, lowdham-grange, press, prison, rehabilitation
body: Inside Time November 2025 | National Newspaper for Prisoners “Innovative workshop course provides ray of light at troubled jail” “The bamboo bike course offers more than just technical training — it provides an avenue for creativity, teamwork, and self-expression.” — Sally Allsopp, Industries Manager, HMP Lowdham Grange Inside Time — the national newspaper for prisoners, distributed inside UK prisons and available online — published a full feature on the Bamboo Bicycle Club’s Build to Bond programme at HMP Lowdham Grange in November 2025. The article, headlined “Innovative workshop course provides ray of light at troubled jail”, provided the most detailed public account of the programme’s operation to date: six prisoners per cohort, a six-week course, a waiting list, three prisoners trained as instructors, and a Level 2 certificate in Sustainable Design and Manufacturing on completion. Inside Time’s readership is the programme’s own community — prisoners, their families, prison staff, and criminal justice advocates. Coverage in Inside Time is not just media validation; it is communication directly to the people the programme serves and the professionals who run the institutions where it operates. For potential partner prisons considering the programme, an Inside Time feature is the most credible possible endorsement: the programme’s recipients speaking to its value. The programme At Lowdham Grange — a Cat-B men’s prison with approximately 900 residents, including a significant proportion serving life sentences — Build to Bond operates in the industrial workshop. BBC’s bamboo is cut and shaped with hand tools; no specialist machinery is required, which makes it viable in a prison workshop environment where power tools and precision equipment may be restricted. James Marr identified bamboo’s specific advantage precisely: same tensile strength as steel, entirely hand-tool workable. The Inside Time article documented an aspect of the programme rarely covered in mainstream press: the final week, in which frames built during the course are disassembled so materials can be reused by the next cohort. This constraint — which might seem like a disappointment for participants who cannot keep their builds — is also, the article noted, what makes the programme financially sustainable. The participants who progress to the Build to Bond follow-up programme build a children’s bamboo bike to gift to their own son, daughter, nephew, niece, or grandchild. That bike they keep. “Finding employment after release reduces the chance of reoffending significantly, which is why we are improving opportunities to help prisoners turn their lives around. Innovative projects, such as Build to Bond, support rehabilitation and help people leave prison as better citizens, boosting the economy and keeping our streets safe.” — Lord (James) Timpson, UK Prisons Minister Ministerial endorsement Lord Timpson’s endorsement of Build to Bond — reproduced in full in the Inside Time article — is significant in the context of the publication. Timpson, appointed as Prisons Minister in 2024, is himself a former employer of hundreds of ex-offenders through Timpson the shoe repair company, and is one of the few senior government ministers with direct commercial experience of post-release employment. His endorsement of a specific rehabilitation programme by name, published in the national newspaper for prisoners, carries weight that no press release or charity award citation can replicate. The Inside Time feature appeared in November 2025, the same year as BBC’s Financial Times Weekend profile (September 2025) and Investec Beyond Business award (September 2025). Together, these three pieces of coverage made 2025 the highest-profile year in BBC’s 13-year history — with the Build to Bond programme receiving its first sustained national and specialist media attention simultaneously. title: Total Women's Cycling: Kate Rawles on Solo Cycling Through South America on a Bamboo Bike
tags: 2018, cycling, expedition, kate-rawles, press, south-america, total-womens-cycling, women
body: Total Women’s Cycling 6 July 2018 | Feature Interview | Kate Rawles “The bike was unexpectedly brilliant. That was the first time I’d ever built a bike and I really didn’t know if I was going to get to the end.” — Kate Rawles, on Woody, her BBC-built bamboo frame Total Women’s Cycling — one of the UK’s leading cycling publications focused on women in the sport, covering everything from sportive training to expedition adventure — published a full interview with Kate Rawles in July 2018, five months after she completed the Life Cycle expedition. The interview covered her experience building Woody at BBC’s London workshop, the physical and mental demands of 8,288 miles through South America, and her relationship with bamboo as a material. Kate Rawles was not a lifelong cyclist. She was an environmental philosopher who chose cycling as her mode of adventure because it was slow enough to pay attention, fast enough to cover ground, and low-carbon enough to be consistent with the values she was advocating. The BBC workshop gave her a bike that matched those values precisely: built from a plant, by her own hands, at low cost, with nothing manufactured that didn’t need to be. The first-time framebuilder Kate’s description of Woody as “unexpectedly brilliant” — combined with the admission that she genuinely didn’t know if she’d get to the end of the build — is one of the most useful testimonials in BBC’s press archive. It is honest, specific, and addresses directly the anxiety that most BBC workshop customers bring to their first session: can I actually do this? Kate Rawles built her frame from scratch with no prior experience and rode it 8,288 miles. The answer to the anxiety is not reassurance but evidence. Total Women’s Cycling’s readership — women cyclists at every level, from beginners to competitive racers to expedition adventurers — is a community that responds to exactly this kind of evidence. Kate Rawles was not a sponsored athlete with a team of mechanics. She was an independent adventurer who built her own bike and rode it alone through some of the most demanding terrain in the world. That story is relatable across every level of the Total Women’s Cycling audience. “There’s something lovely about anteaters. They never eat all the ants, they always leave enough for the anthill to regenerate, and I just think there’s a great message for humans: ‘don’t eat all the ants.’” — Kate Rawles, Total Women’s Cycling, July 2018 The expedition’s message Kate’s anteater observation — made in conversation with Total Women’s Cycling — is characteristic of her approach to environmental communication: specific, surprising, and immediately comprehensible. She didn’t lead with statistics about species extinction rates. She led with an anteater that never eats all its ants. That precision of communication — finding the concrete image that carries the abstract argument — is part of why the Life Cycle story resonated far beyond the environmental press and reached women’s cycling media, lifestyle publications, and university news services simultaneously. BBC was the starting point for that journey: the London workshop where Kate built Woody in November 2016. Total Women’s Cycling’s July 2018 interview reached the cycling audience that Kate’s expedition most directly inspired — women who cycle, or want to cycle, and who understand adventure as something you do yourself rather than something that happens to you. Read the full interview on Total Women’s Cycling →

title: The Monopolitan: Crea tu propia Bicicleta de Bambú — Spanish Language Feature
tags: 2017, international, kit, monopolitan, press, spain, spanish, workshop
body: The Monopolitan June 2017 | Spain | Lifestyle & Design “Bamboo Bicycle Club es un proyecto que nace con la intención de motivar a las personas a construir sus propias bicicletas de bambú.” (“Bamboo Bicycle Club is a project born with the intention of motivating people to build their own bamboo bicycles.”) — The Monopolitan, Spain, 2017 The Monopolitan — a Spanish-language lifestyle and design publication based in Spain — featured Bamboo Bicycle Club in a full article in June 2017, introduced to a Spanish-speaking audience for the first time by this international coverage. The article was re-featured and updated in January 2022. BBC’s home-build kits — available internationally — made Spain and the Spanish-speaking world a natural market; The Monopolitan’s feature was among the first to reach that audience in their own language. The article positioned BBC as a community and philosophy, not just a product: “un proyecto que nace con la intención de motivar a las personas a construir sus propias bicicletas” — a project born with the intention of motivating people to build their own bicycles. This framing, in 2017, was consistent with the BBC brand message in every language. The emphasis was on empowerment, craft, and sustainability over consumerism. “Bamboo Bicycle Club se ha convertido, hoy en día, en una comunidad de entusiastas movidos por la idea de revolucionar la manera en que nos transportamos, ofreciendo una alternativa ultra personalizada, durable, económica y amigable con el medio ambiente.” (“Bamboo Bicycle Club has become, today, a community of enthusiasts driven by the idea of revolutionising the way we travel, offering an ultra-personalised, durable, affordable and environmentally friendly alternative.”) — The Monopolitan International reach BBC’s home-build kit business was explicitly international by 2017 — with 70% of kit sales going to customers outside the UK, across 36+ countries. Spain and Latin America represent a significant potential market: warm climate cycling culture, an appreciation for artisan craft, and a growing sustainability movement. The Monopolitan’s description of BBC as “ultra personalizada, durable, económica y amigable con el medio ambiente” — ultra-personalised, durable, affordable, and environmentally friendly — captures the kit’s international value proposition precisely. The Monopolitan feature also reflects BBC’s broader cultural resonance: a London social enterprise built around bamboo bicycles had, by 2017, accumulated enough international press attention to attract Spanish-language lifestyle media independently. No specific Spanish-market outreach was required. The story — build your own sustainable bike from a natural material — travelled without translation. Read the full article on The Monopolitan →

title: Wharf Life: How Bamboo Bicycle Club Helps Its Customers Build Their Own Rides
tags: 2022, canning-town, east-london, kit, press, wharf-life, workshop
body: Wharf Life 3 August 2022 | By Jon Massey | East London & Docklands “Visitors to the Canning Town workshop can see all sorts of machines created from bamboo including tricycles, electric variants and rides with oversize chunky backbones.” — Jon Massey, Wharf Life, August 2022 Wharf Life — the East London and Docklands community newspaper covering Canary Wharf, Isle of Dogs, Royal Docks, and Canning Town — published a full feature on Bamboo Bicycle Club in August 2022, following BBC’s relocation from Hackney Wick to Caxton Works in Canning Town. Journalist Jon Massey visited the workshop in person and documented the operation at its new East London base. Wharf Life’s readership is hyperlocal — the communities along the Lea Valley and Royal Docks corridor, from Canary Wharf to Stratford. For BBC, coverage in Wharf Life was both a local press milestone (introducing the new Canning Town address to its immediate community) and a signal of the workshop’s continuing commitment to East London as its base after nearly a decade in Hackney Wick. The move to Canning Town BBC relocated from Hackney Wick to Caxton Works, Canning Town in 2020 — driven in part by the rising rents that have displaced many creative enterprises from Hackney Wick since the post-Olympics development boom. Caxton Works is a cluster of studios and workshops in Canning Town that has attracted makers, designers, and small manufacturers seeking affordable space in the Royal Docks area. BBC’s move maintained its East London creative-manufacturing identity while accessing a new community. Massey’s feature documented the variety of BBC’s workshop output: not just road and mountain bike frames but tricycles, electric cargo bikes, and experimental geometries. The “oversize chunky backbones” description reflects something real about bamboo as a material — the larger-diameter sections of Guadua bamboo used in cargo and utility frames have a visual presence quite different from racing or commuter frames. A BBC workshop contains objects that don’t look like anything manufactured in a standard bicycle factory. “The spirit of the original club still forms the spine of the business. They don’t sell finished bikes — only kits and building sessions in workshops.” — Jon Massey, Wharf Life, August 2022 Ten years on, the model holds Massey’s observation — that “the spirit of the original club still forms the spine of the business” — was published in August 2022, ten years after BBC launched in September 2012. In that decade, the company had expanded from monthly workshops to weekly sessions, launched home-build kits available globally, developed the Build to Bond prison programme, opened workshops in Amersfoort and Toulouse, and won the Investec Beyond Business award. But the founding principle — no finished bikes, only building sessions and kits — had not changed. For the Wharf Life readership of young East London professionals, the BBC workshop in Canning Town represented exactly the kind of local business the area needed: skilled, original, community-oriented, and rooted in East London’s manufacturing tradition. Massey’s feature introduced BBC to its new Canning Town neighbours and documented an operation that, after a decade of growth, still operated on its founding principle. title: Designboom: mccloy + muchemwa × Bamboo Bicycle Club — The Bamboo Urban Mini Velo
tags: 2020, architecture, biocomposite, city-bike, collaboration, designboom, mccloy-muchemwa, press
body: Designboom 26 November 2020 | Photography: Sophie Percival Collaboration: mccloy + muchemwa (architects) × Bamboo Bicycle Club “At mccloy + muchemwa we challenge the conceptualisation and the functionality of each design, even on the smallest scales. As with our projects for public spaces and street furniture, we wanted the bike design to bring a moment of joy and imagination. The bamboo bicycle club workshop is an incredible opportunity for anyone, not just designers, to learn the satisfaction of handmaking a complex and beautiful object like a bicycle frame.” — Steve mccloy, Architect, mccloy + muchemwa Designboom — one of the world’s largest design media platforms, covering architecture, product design, art, and technology for a global readership of design professionals — published a full feature on the Bamboo Urban Mini Velo in November 2020: a custom city bike designed by architects mccloy + muchemwa in collaboration with Bamboo Bicycle Club, facilitated through humanitarian architectural charity Article 25. The Bamboo Urban Mini Velo was commissioned as a practical portfolio carrier: a split-frame, small-wheeled city bike with a central cargo compartment accommodating an A3 portfolio and laptop case, without the bulk of a basket or the discomfort of a laden backpack. The frame uses BBC’s standard biocomposite construction — bamboo tubes, flax-fibre bindings, plant-based resin — engineered to an architectural brief rather than a standard cycling specification. The design mccloy + muchemwa is an emerging London architectural practice with a focus on public space and social infrastructure. Their approach to the BBC collaboration was architecturally rigorous: every material choice was considered in terms of both performance and appearance. The black-and-white component palette was chosen to contrast with and amplify the natural tones of the bamboo. The biocomposite bindings were sculpted into bone-like nodes. Recessed lights emerged from protruding stalks — a hint of “friendly zoomorphism” in an otherwise restrained design language. The first prototype was built at BBC’s London workshop, with mccloy and the BBC team working directly with the raw bamboo and flax materials. The collaboration required bridging two distinct disciplines: architectural design precision (tight specifications, standardised dimensions, clear load requirements) and organic material variability (bamboo culms differ from each other; flax bindings require skilled application). Sophie Percival photographed the finished bike for Designboom’s feature. “There is freedom for creativity when working with bamboo because the tooling is low-tech, safe and accessible. But as a designer you have to stand out too — we wanted to push the club’s existing format into something special, but also found inspiration in all the various processes and working with the raw materials during the build. The straightforward black and white colour palette and choice of understated but high-quality accessories allow the natural tones of the bamboo to really pop!” — Steve mccloy, mccloy + muchemwa BBC as a design fabrication partner The Designboom feature positioned BBC in a register that cycling press coverage rarely captures: as a sustainable fabrication partner for architects and designers. The Bamboo Urban Mini Velo was not a kit build or a workshop project — it was a commissioned design object, meeting an architectural brief, photographed professionally, and published on one of the world’s most widely-read design platforms. This is a significant expansion of BBC’s narrative. BBC is not solely a cycling company. It is a bamboo fabrication workshop capable of working to external design briefs, in collaboration with professional practices across disciplines. The Article 25 facilitation — through a humanitarian architecture charity — reinforces this: BBC’s skills in bamboo composite construction are genuinely transferable across applications beyond cycling. title: Cornwall Live: Eden Project's Bamboo Bike Comes Home After Epic 8,000-Mile Journey
tags: 2018, cornwall-live, eden-project, expedition, kate-rawles, press, south-america, woody
body: Cornwall Live 5 May 2018 | By Tom Gainey | Reach plc “Woody has proved to be an extremely tough and reliable bike, coping with extremes of heat and cold, rain, dryness and altitude. Bamboo is a brilliant material for building bikes. It’s so great that we can say the UK’s first home-grown bike came from right here at Eden.” — Kate Rawles, at the Eden Project reunion, May 2018 Three months after completing an 8,288-mile journey through South America, Kate Rawles returned to Cornwall with Woody — the bamboo bicycle she had built at BBC’s London workshop from canes grown at the Eden Project — to reunite with the team who had provided the raw material. Cornwall Live, part of Reach plc’s regional news network, covered the homecoming with a full feature by journalist Tom Gainey. Cornwall Live’s readership is concentrated in Cornwall and the West Country — a community with a particular relationship with the Eden Project as a local institution. The article reached an audience for whom the Eden Project’s bamboo canes were not an abstract sustainability claim but a familiar presence on the hillside outside the Rainforest Biome. The “UK’s first home-grown bicycle” was genuinely local news in Cornwall. The homecoming Kate Rawles visited the Eden Project with her partner Chris Loynes to reunite Woody with the team that had grown the bamboo. The canes for Woody’s frame had been cut from a mature clump on a hillside outside the Rainforest Biome — grown to maturity in Cornwall, cut, dried, and transported to BBC’s London workshop, where Kate built them into the frame she would ride for 14 months through the Andes. The Eden Project team received Woody as a local story: a bike made from their bamboo, built in London, ridden 8,288 miles through South America, and returned to Cornwall. Dr Mike Maunder, Eden’s Director of Life Sciences, described the homecoming as “thrilling” and praised Kate’s leadership in raising awareness of biodiversity loss. Eden shared Kate’s sense of urgency about what she had seen travelling through South America’s most biodiverse ecosystems. “I love the human-magnet effect that Woody has, and the fact that I was on a biodiversity ride on a bike that used to be a plant. I was riding ten, 11, 12 hours a day and wild camping wherever I got to at nightfall. I’ve never pushed so hard physically in my life, but I think it’s good to reach your limits occasionally — and then keep going.” — Kate Rawles, Cornwall Live, May 2018 The complete picture Cornwall Live’s article was the third major press piece to document the Woody story in 2018 — following the University of Cumbria announcement in February and the PA wire completion coverage in September 2018. Together, these pieces created a complete narrative arc for BBC’s most publicly visible project: bamboo grown in Cornwall, built in London by a first-time framebuilder, ridden 8,288 miles through South America, and returned to its origins. Each piece of press added a different angle and reached a different audience. Cornwall Live added the Eden Project community. Tom Gainey’s article noted that Kate had placed BBC’s London workshop at the centre of the story — “she put her mountain bike together at the Bamboo Bicycle Club in London” — giving BBC a direct reference point in a regional press piece that reached Cornwall’s community. The Eden Classic sportive was also referenced, with the Eden Project continuing its connection to cycling alongside the Woody homecoming. Read the full article on Cornwall Live →

title: University of Cumbria: 8,000 Miles on a Bike Made of British Bamboo
tags: 2018, bmc-award, cumbria-university, eden-project, expedition, kate-rawles, press, south-america
body: University of Cumbria News 27 February 2018 | Academic press release “Woody has proved to be an extremely tough and reliable bike, coping with extremes of heat and cold, rain, dryness and altitude.” — Dr Kate Rawles, associate lecturer, University of Cumbria The University of Cumbria — where Dr Kate Rawles holds an associate lectureship and is an associate of the Institute for Leadership and Sustainability — published a news release on 27 February 2018 confirming that Rawles and Woody had completed the Life Cycle expedition: 8,288 miles from northern Colombia to Ushuaia, Patagonia, following the spine of the Andes. The university’s press release stated explicitly: “University of Cumbria associate lecturer, Dr Kate Rawles, built the bike at the Bamboo Bicycle Club in London from bamboo grown at Cornwall’s world-renowned Eden Project” — confirming both BBC’s role in building Woody and the Eden Project bamboo origin for the academic record. The article linked directly to bamboobicycleclub.org. The BMC award The Cumbria University article revealed a previously little-publicised detail: a film of Woody’s construction at the BBC London workshop, made by Cumbria outdoor studies student Lizzi Gilson, won Best Student Film at the British Mountaineering Council’s Women in Adventure film competition in 2017. This was the first independent film award associated with BBC’s work — recognised by the UK’s primary mountaineering institution for its artistic and storytelling quality. The film documented the physical process of building Woody at BBC: the bamboo selection, the jig setup, the hemp-and-epoxy lug wrapping, and the finished frame. Its award at the BMC Women in Adventure competition — a category that celebrates women doing remarkable things outdoors — recognised both the craftsmanship of the BBC build and the significance of what Kate was about to do with it. “And of course, everyone was intrigued by the bamboo bike. I love the human-magnet effect that Woody has, and the fact that I’m on a biodiversity ride on a bike that used to be a plant! Just when I thought there was no way I could make it, I got lucky with a tailwind that lasted for ninety-nine miles!” — Dr Kate Rawles, University of Cumbria News, February 2018 The human-magnet effect Kate Rawles’ phrase “the human-magnet effect” captures something specific about bamboo bicycles in public spaces. Wherever Woody appeared — in Colombian cities, Ecuadorian mountain towns, Bolivian salt flat villages, Chilean fishing ports, Patagonian estancias — it attracted attention, questions, and conversations. Kate’s mission was raising awareness of biodiversity loss; Woody’s presence opened the conversations that let her do it. This effect is consistent across BBC’s 14 years: workshop participants, kit builders, and expedition riders universally report that a bamboo bicycle generates more public engagement than any conventional frame. The bamboo material is immediately recognisable as unusual; the fact that it’s a rideable bicycle creates genuine curiosity. BBC has never needed to explain its sustainability argument in the abstract. The frame does it. Kate returned to the UK by cargo ship from Valparaiso via the Panama Canal — consistent with her zero-flying policy for the expedition. She arrived at Tilbury Docks in April 2018. Woody is now on permanent display in a museum. Read the full article on University of Cumbria News →

title: Kate Rawles: The Life Cycle — BBC-Built Woody Completes 8,288-Mile South America Expedition
tags: 2017, bamboo-bike, eden-project, expedition, kate-rawles, life-cycle, press, south-america, woody
body: Kate Rawles — katerawles.org December 2016 – February 2018 | The Life Cycle Expedition 8,288 miles | Colombia to Cape Horn | Bamboo bike built at BBC, London “As for Woody, the bamboo bike proved to be extremely tough and reliable, coping with extremes of heat and cold, rain, dryness and altitude. I had virtually no mechanicals on the whole journey!” — Kate Rawles, on Woody — her BBC-built bamboo expedition frame In November 2016, Dr Kate Rawles — environmental philosopher, author, and adventurer — came to Bamboo Bicycle Club’s London workshop and built a bamboo bicycle frame from canes grown at the Eden Project in Cornwall. As far as anyone could confirm, it was the UK’s first home-grown bamboo bicycle. She named the bike Woody. Six weeks later, she took Woody to Colombia and set off on one of the most significant cycling expeditions in recent years: the Life Cycle — a 8,288-mile journey from Cartagena, Colombia to Cape Horn at the southern tip of Patagonia, following the spine of the Andes. Woody and Kate arrived at Ushuaia, the southernmost city in the world, in February 2018. The frame built in a London workshop survived 14 months of Andean riding: Pacific coast highways, 5,000-metre mountain passes, Bolivian salt flats, the Atacama desert (the driest on Earth), and the notoriously savage winds of Patagonia. The expedition The Life Cycle was not a cycling holiday. It was a long-form environmental investigation: Kate visited biodiversity and conservation projects throughout South America — turtle conservation schools, Titi monkey protection projects, indigenous fishing communities threatened by industrial trawlers, and organic coffee farmers growing in biodiversity-compatible forest systems. In Patagonia, she met Kris McDivitt Tompkins, whose foundation was in the process of donating millions of acres — including what became Patagonia National Park — to the Chilean government. The bamboo bike was not incidental to this narrative. Kate rode a material that grew in Cornwall. She rode it to raise awareness of biodiversity loss — the same systems that produce bamboo, hemp, and flax, the materials in a BBC workshop frame. The frame and the mission were materially connected. “As far as we know this is the UK’s first home-grown bicycle. We’re delighted to have built it, and to be launching it on this mountainous environmental adventure.” — Kate Rawles, Guardian, November 2016 What Woody proved Kate Rawles had no prior framebuilding experience before arriving at BBC’s London workshop. Woody was the first bamboo bicycle frame she built. Over 14 months and 8,288 miles, across six countries and the most demanding terrain in the western hemisphere, she had virtually no mechanical problems with the frame. The BBC-built bamboo frame was, in this respect, more reliable than most of the support vehicles, logistics arrangements, and equipment Kate travelled with. The Life Cycle expedition is BBC’s most powerful durability proof. No test rig, no lab, no technical paper can substitute for 8,288 miles of Andean riding. Woody is now in a museum. Kate’s book — The Life Cycle: 8,000 Miles in the Andes by Bamboo Bike — was published in 2021 and is widely available. Every copy carries BBC’s story to its readers. title: road.cc: Dave Builds a Bamboo Bike — The 5-Part BBC Kit Video Series
tags: 2018, build-series, cycling, diy, kit, press, road-cc, video
body: road.cc April–May 2018 | 5-Part Build Video Series | Dave Atkinson UK’s largest online cycling publication — 2 million+ monthly readers “Time for a new series of videos! Our Dave has been interested in building a bamboo bike for a while, and he’s finally bitten the bullet with a kit from the Bamboo Bicycle Club, which purports to contain everything you need for the job. With the possible exceptions of hand-eye co-ordination and patience.” — road.cc, April 2018 road.cc — the UK’s largest cycling website, with 2 million+ monthly readers — launched a five-part video documentary series in April 2018 following staff writer Dave Atkinson as he built a Bamboo Bicycle Club kit from scratch. The series ran every Friday from April into May 2018, documenting the complete frame build from jig construction to first ride. Road.cc’s audience of experienced cyclists, many of whom are sceptical of anything that deviates from aluminium, carbon, steel, or titanium as frame materials, represented a genuinely challenging editorial context. Dave Atkinson was not a bamboo advocate or a sustainability journalist. He was a road cyclist who wanted to know if a BBC kit could produce a real bike that could race. Road.cc gave him five weeks to find out. The series The five-part build series was structured as a real-time documentary, with Atkinson reporting each stage honestly as he encountered it. Part 1 documented jig construction — the alignment frame that holds the bamboo tubes in position while the lugs cure. Parts 2 and 3 covered tube fitting and lug wrapping: the hand application of hemp fibre and epoxy resin that forms the structural joint at each connection point. Part 4 covered finishing, painting, and component prep. Part 5 was the first ride — and the plan to race the finished frame at a Cat 3 criterium. Road.cc’s tone — “Dave’s making a bike out of sticks and glue. We can’t see how that could go wrong” — was characteristic of the publication’s dry, technically-informed humour. The scepticism was genuine and the audience shared it. But the series ran to completion, the bike was built, and Atkinson rode it to the Cat 3 race he had committed to — one of the most memorable road.cc features of 2018. “Dave’s making a bike out of sticks and glue. We can’t see how that could go wrong. He’s underway with the task of building it, with the stated aim of rocking up to a 3rd cats race at some point in the summer to general derision.” — road.cc, April 2018 What the series demonstrated Five weekly videos from the UK’s largest cycling website, featuring a staff member building a BBC kit from scratch and racing the result, is the most thorough product documentation any cycling media outlet has produced for a BBC kit. Unlike a standard first-ride review, the road.cc series showed the entire process: the jig, the lugs, the hours, the uncertainty, the finished frame, and the first race. For the 2 million road.cc readers who watched across five weeks, the series answered every practical question about BBC kits with evidence rather than marketing. The series also prefigured the easy build kit launch. In a follow-up article in 2020, road.cc noted that BBC had reduced the kit build time from the original 70+ hours to approximately four hours with pre-moulded carbon lugs — a direct evolution of the process Atkinson documented in 2018. The kit price at the time of the series: £275 for the road bike version. Legacy The road.cc build series is one of BBC’s most useful press assets. A five-episode video documentary, produced independently by a credible cycling media outlet, showing BBC kit construction in real time — with no editorial control by BBC — is a transparency artefact that no amount of marketing copy can replicate. When potential kit customers ask “can I really build this?”, five road.cc videos are a more persuasive answer than any brochure. Watch the series on road.cc →

title: IFB2016: Bamboo Bicycle Club Selected for UK Government GREAT Britain Innovation Showcase

body: TheBusinessDesk.com & Liverpool Echo June 2016 | International Festival for Business 2016, Liverpool UK Government GREAT Britain export campaign showcase “Bamboo is officially the fastest growing plant in the world, which should make these the fastest bicycles in the world: light, hollow-tube construction, supremely engineered by nature. But they are not too fast to buy. You have to join the club and build one yourself.” — Kevin McCloud, Grand Designs TV presenter, on BBC’s Home Build Kit In June 2016, Bamboo Bicycle Club was selected to exhibit at the Innovation is GREAT stand at the International Festival for Business 2016 (IFB2016), Exhibition Centre Liverpool — the UK Government’s export promotion showcase. BBC was placed alongside Airbus Defence and Space (whose Mars Rover was exhibited), Zaha Hadid Architects, Framestore (Academy Award-winning VFX studio), what3words, BAFTA, BBC Worldwide, and Apple Corps (Abbey Road Studios). IFB2016 ran through July 2016 at one of the UK’s largest convention venues. Both TheBusinessDesk.com (the North West’s leading business publication, by journalist Nick Jackson) and the Liverpool Echo (one of the UK’s largest regional daily newspapers, by journalist Tony McDonough) covered BBC’s presence at the exhibition. Kevin McCloud’s endorsement The Kevin McCloud quote reproduced in TheBusinessDesk’s IFB2016 coverage is one of BBC’s most enduring press moments. McCloud — best known as the presenter of Channel 4’s Grand Designs — had chosen BBC’s Home Build Kit for his Grand Designs Live ‘Green Heroes’ selection earlier in 2016. His description of the kit captures the paradox that makes BBC compelling: bamboo is faster-growing than any other plant material used in manufacturing, yet the bamboo bicycle is not purchased — it is earned by being built. “You have to join the club and build one yourself.” IFB2016’s context amplified this endorsement. At a government-sponsored innovation showcase attended by international investors, trade buyers, and business journalists, Kevin McCloud’s quote framed BBC as a design and innovation story, not just a cycling novelty. TheBusinessDesk’s article reached the North West’s business community; the Liverpool Echo reached 170,000+ daily readers in the region. “Bamboo Bicycle Club: founded by James and Ian, two engineers who love cycling. After their own enthusiastic experiments in building bamboo bikes, they decided to create a bicycling community interested in building beautiful, robust and environmentally friendly bamboo bicycle frames using 3D technology.” — Liverpool Echo, IFB2016 exhibitor listing, Tony McDonough, June 2016 The IFB2016 context TheBusinessDesk confirmed several important historical details in its IFB2016 coverage. BBC started in the Brecon Beacons, Wales — where founding engineers James Marr and Ian McMillan first tested bamboo frames, glues, jig setups, and designs before moving the operation to Hackney Wick, East London. The IFB2016 article also documented two significant early commissions: a sustainable rear-loaded cargo tricycle built with UCL students for use by farmers in developing agricultural industry, and touring bikes built with two Doctors Without Borders charity cyclists for a London-to-Singapore route, designed to survive extreme climate conditions. Being selected for the GREAT Britain innovation showcase — by the UK Government’s Department for International Trade — placed BBC in a category of British businesses identified as internationally competitive, export-ready, and representative of British innovation. At a festival attended by trade delegations from across the world, this institutional endorsement reached well beyond the cycling press and the sustainability media into the business and investment communities. body: Inhabitat 21 January 2016 | Green Design & Innovation 14 million+ monthly readers “The team behind Bamboo Bicycle Club recently created the world’s most advanced bamboo bike which is currently on display at the ‘Cycle Revolution’ exhibition in London’s Design Museum until June 2016.” — Inhabitat, January 2016 Inhabitat — one of the world’s leading green design and architecture publications, reaching 14 million+ monthly readers — covered Bamboo Bicycle Club’s aerodynamic bamboo racing bike in January 2016, as it went on display at the Design Museum’s landmark Cycle Revolution exhibition in London. The Cycle Revolution exhibition ran from autumn 2015 to June 2016 at the Design Museum on Kensington High Street, attracting 70,000+ visitors. It was the most significant cycling design exhibition staged in the UK in decades, showcasing bicycle innovation from the Victorian safety bicycle to cutting-edge lightweight composites. BBC’s aerodynamic bamboo racing bike was exhibited in this context — a statement about natural materials, engineering ambition, and the gap between what bamboo could do and what the cycling industry assumed it could do. The aerodynamic racing bike BBC’s engineering team spent years developing the aerodynamic bamboo racing frame. The challenge was significant: bamboo resists conventional machining and shaping, yet an aerodynamic racing bicycle demands tight tolerances, consistent tube profiles, and precise joint geometry. The frame exhibited at the Design Museum represented the then-current limit of bamboo fabrication technology: aerodynamic tube shaping combined with BBC’s refined hemp-and-epoxy lug construction. The bike was positioned as a proof of concept rather than a production model. Its purpose was to answer a specific sceptic question that BBC encountered constantly in its first four years: can bamboo actually perform at a competitive level? The aerodynamic racing bike’s presence at the Design Museum’s Cycle Revolution exhibition — alongside icon racing machines from across cycling history — was BBC’s answer to that question. Inhabitat’s coverage of the exhibition amplified that answer to a global sustainability audience. “The aerodynamic bamboo racing bike demonstrates that natural, sustainable materials don’t have to compromise on performance — bamboo’s tensile strength and vibration dampening properties make it an ideal candidate for high-performance cycling applications.” — Inhabitat, January 2016 Inhabitat’s audience and the sustainability argument Inhabitat covers green design, sustainable architecture, and environmental innovation for a global audience of design professionals, environmentally-conscious consumers, and green building practitioners. Its readership is distinct from the cycling press: these are people who understand materials science, building performance, and lifecycle assessment — and who are sceptical of greenwashing. Inhabitat’s positive coverage of the aerodynamic racing bike was significant precisely because this audience would probe any sustainability claim rigorously. The cover story — that bamboo is not just a novelty material but a genuine engineering medium capable of producing competitive racing frames — held up under that scrutiny. Bamboo’s properties (tensile strength comparable to steel, natural damping characteristics superior to aluminium, carbon-positive in growth) are genuine and documentable. Inhabitat covered them accurately and sympathetically, giving BBC a sustainability credibility boost with one of the most demanding sustainability audiences in media. Legacy The aerodynamic bamboo racing bike that appeared at the Design Museum in 2016 prefigured the lugged frame innovation documented by Bikerumor in 2022 and the technical R&D work with LSBU’s Innovation Hub. Each generation of BBC engineering builds on the previous — the racing frame to the 3D-printed frame to the pre-moulded carbon lug to the easy build kit. title: Core77: Build a Bamboo Bike in Under 5 Hours — BIY Kit Named Best of 2016

body: Core77 2016 | Industrial Design & Making | Best of 2016 feature “I think it would make a wonderful tool for mechanically inclined people, and could lead to some interesting DIY bike design.” — Core77 Core77 — the world’s leading industrial design publication and community, read by professional designers, engineers, makers, and design-educated consumers — covered Bamboo Bicycle Club’s BIY (Build It Yourself) 2 Kickstarter campaign in 2016, then named it the most hands-on bike moment of the year in their annual Best of 2016 roundup. Core77’s selection of BBC for the Best of 2016 recognition placed the BIY kit alongside professional design projects, product innovations, and industrial milestones. For a design-educated audience that evaluates objects on their structural and conceptual merits, this was a significant endorsement — not of cycling, but of the kit as a design object and tool. The BIY 2 kit The Build It Yourself 2 kit represented a significant refinement of BBC’s original home-build concept. Where the first iteration required complex lug preparation and extended build times, the BIY 2 promised a complete bamboo frame in under five hours — a claim that Core77 specifically highlighted. Starting at $249 USD, the kit included all materials, pre-cut bamboo, connection components, and full instructions. The Kickstarter campaign format — a funding model familiar to Core77’s maker-culture readership — gave the campaign extra legitimacy within the industrial design community. Kickstarter-backed products in 2016 were understood as genuine manufacturing innovations seeking their first production run, not marketing exercises. BBC’s campaign in that context signalled seriousness of purpose and manufacturing readiness. “The most hands-on bike moment of 2016 was the return of the Bamboobee build-it-yourself bamboo bike kit, which promised the BIYer a bike frame in under five hours.” — Core77, Best of Bikes 2016 Core77’s perspective Core77’s framing was precise and revealing: the BIY kit was “a wonderful tool for mechanically inclined people” that “could lead to some interesting DIY bike design.” This is not the language of a product review; it is the language of a design critic evaluating a new platform. Core77 saw the BBC kit not as a fixed product but as an enabling tool — something that, in the right hands, could generate new bicycle geometries, new materials explorations, and new approaches to personal transportation design. That framing remains accurate a decade later. BBC’s workshop alumni include engineers, architects, designers, and artists who have built non-standard frames, integrated unusual materials, and used the BBC kit structure as a starting point for genuine design experimentation. Core77 in 2016 recognised the BBC kit’s potential before most of those experiments had occurred. About Core77 Core77 was founded in 1995 and has grown to become the most widely-read industrial design publication globally. Its mix of editorial coverage, design competitions, job listings, and community forums makes it the daily destination for professional designers worldwide. A feature in Core77 — and a Best of Year mention — reaches an audience of design professionals, design students, and design-educated consumers who understand craft, manufacturing, and the gap between concept and execution. title: BikeBiz: Bamboo Bicycle Club and Oxford Brookes Build World's First 3D Printed Bamboo Bike
body: BikeBiz 13 April 2016 | Industry News “It was always going to be a challenge combining highly engineered products with an artesian style build, especially using such an unprocessed natural material such as bamboo. After an intense but ultimately successful weekend, this type of modular construction has really shown the potential to create truly bespoke bicycle frame design at home, perhaps taking a little more time!” — Dr James Broughton, Oxford Brookes University BikeBiz — the UK’s leading trade publication for the cycle industry, covering news, product launches, and business for retailers, distributors, and manufacturers — reported on Bamboo Bicycle Club’s live build of the world’s first bamboo and 3D-printed bicycle at the Design Museum in April 2016, in collaboration with Oxford Brookes University. The event took place during the Design Museum’s landmark Cycle Revolution exhibition, which ran from autumn 2015 into 2016 and attracted 70,000+ visitors. BBC had already been displaying the world’s first aerodynamic bamboo bicycle in the exhibition. The 3D printing build event — carried out live, in public, over a weekend — was a separate and distinct innovation milestone: proving that bamboo bicycle construction could be combined with digital fabrication technology to produce a rideable frame. The technology The critical engineering challenge in bamboo bicycle construction has always been the joint — the connection point where bamboo tubes meet at the bottom bracket, the head tube, and the chainstays. Traditional BBC construction uses hand-wrapped hemp fibre and epoxy resin, a process that takes hours but produces extremely strong bonds. The 3D printing experiment replaced the hand-wrapped lug with a precision-designed nylon-reinforced carbon fibre joint — the same material used in Formula 1 car components — printed over two weeks by a team at Oxford Brookes. Dr James Broughton, lead academic partner from Oxford Brookes, documented both the challenge and the outcome with precision. The combination of highly engineered printed components and natural, unprocessed bamboo presented specific adhesion and tolerancing problems. The urethane adhesive glue used to bond the bamboo to the 3D-printed lugs required careful application and cure time. The build was completed; the bike was ridden at the Design Museum on Sunday afternoon. “This process is expected to become a lot faster in the future and could have a huge impact on British manufacturing.” — BikeBiz, April 2016 Legacy: the easy build kit The 3D-printing experiment at the Design Museum in April 2016 was the direct ancestor of the BBC easy build home kit. The insight from the Oxford Brookes collaboration — that precision-engineered joints could replace hand-wrapped fibre lugs, dramatically reducing build complexity and time — was refined over the following years into pre-moulded carbon lugs that ship as part of the home kit. The current easy build kit, which reduces frame build time from 70+ hours to approximately 4 hours, exists because James Marr and Oxford Brookes proved the concept live at the Design Museum in 2016. BikeBiz’s trade audience — retailers, buyers, and cycle industry professionals — understood the significance immediately. A bamboo frame with 3D-printed, F1-material lugs, built live at one of London’s premier design institutions, in collaboration with a university engineering department, was not a workshop curiosity. It was a manufacturing proof of concept with genuine industry implications. Community collaboration The build event was supported by BBC’s Hackney Wick community at Autumn Yard — including Studio Bark (one of Britain’s most sustainable architects, as seen on Grand Designs), Great Coat Films, and A Marr + Associates. The collaboration reflects BBC’s deep roots in the East London creative and manufacturing community — a network that has supported the organisation’s R&D, marketing, and development since 2012. title: Time Out London: Bamboo Bike Workshop — Things to Do in London

body: Time Out London 10 February 2016 | Things to Do — Classes & Workshops “These two-day workshops teach participants how to make their very own bike frames using bamboo. The classes allow participants to be as creative as they wish, with help from expert frame builders who’ll provide all the skills needed to create strong and sturdy structures to ride home on.” — Time Out London, February 2016 Time Out London — the definitive guide to London life, with 10 million+ monthly readers globally — listed the Bamboo Bicycle Club workshop in its Things to Do section in February 2016. Being included in Time Out’s curated listings is not automatic: the editorial team selects only experiences they believe are genuinely worth a Londoner’s time and money. A spot in the Things to Do section placed BBC alongside West End theatre, gallery openings, food festivals, and the best of London’s cultural calendar. The listing Time Out’s coverage captured the workshop at a specific moment in its development: a two-day experience at £590, with a maximum of four participants per class, led by expert frame builders. The intimate format — never more than four people in a session — was by design. BBC is not a factory. The workshop is a genuine learning environment where expert instruction can reach every participant simultaneously, answer every question, and ensure every frame is structurally sound before it leaves the building. The price point (£590 in 2016) positioned the BBC workshop within Time Out’s premium experiences tier — comparable to specialist cooking courses, aviation lessons, and professional photography workshops. For an audience who spent money on experiences rather than things, this positioning was exactly right. “Top up days are available if you want to add extra components and bamboo beer is supplied at the end of each day. Classes are for a maximum of four people and need to be booked in advance via the Bamboo Bicycle Club website.” — Time Out London, 2016 The bamboo beer detail Time Out included the bamboo beer. This is significant not because beer matters to frame construction, but because it reveals something precise about the BBC workshop experience: it ends with a drink, a finished frame, and a shared sense of achievement among four people who arrived as strangers two days ago and leave as fellow builders. The beer is not a gimmick. It is the moment of completion and community — the social reward for a weekend of genuine effort. Time Out journalists, who spend their professional lives evaluating London experiences, put the bamboo beer in the listing. They knew their readers: people who want an experience worth talking about, with an object worth taking home at the end. A bamboo bicycle frame, made with your own hands, is both. Time Out’s reach and significance Time Out London was founded in 1968 and has grown into one of the world’s most trusted urban guides. Its readership of design-conscious, culturally engaged Londoners — and the tourists who rely on Time Out for authoritative experience recommendations — includes the exact demographic most likely to book a BBC workshop. A listing in Time Out’s Things to Do section is a commercial signal, not just a press clipping: it reaches people who are actively looking for something to do this weekend, with money and time available to do it. title: Uncrate: They Build Bikes from Custom Bamboo Frames, and They Love What They Do
tags: 2014, early-press, lifestyle, press, uncrate, usa, video
body: UNCRATE 19 September 2014 | Video & Travel — Events “They build bikes from custom bamboo frames, and they love what they do.” — Uncrate, September 2014 Uncrate — one of the most influential product discovery platforms for men in the United States, with 4 million+ monthly readers — featured Bamboo Bicycle Club as a Video pick in September 2014. In Uncrate’s editorial format, a feature is exactly this: a short, definitive editorial observation and an embedded video. No padding. No equivocation. Just the thing, and why it’s worth your time. Uncrate’s readership is a specific and valuable audience: discerning men who combine an appreciation for craft, design, and quality with genuine purchasing power and a preference for unusual objects over generic ones. Being curated into Uncrate’s Video section in 2014 — two years after BBC launched — was a transatlantic endorsement from one of the most taste-conscious editorial operations in US lifestyle media. The selection criteria Uncrate does not publish sponsored content or reviews of everything submitted. The editorial team selects products, brands, and experiences they genuinely believe are worth knowing about. In September 2014, they selected Bamboo Bicycle Club. The eight-word description they chose — “They build bikes from custom bamboo frames, and they love what they do” — is as good a summary of BBC’s essence as any press description produced before or since. The feature was classified in Uncrate’s Video / Travel & Events category, positioning BBC not as a product to buy but as an experience worth seeking out — consistent with the workshop model and the BBC brand more broadly. You don’t buy a bamboo frame from BBC. You come to Hackney Wick and build one yourself. Uncrate got that distinction immediately, and their categorisation reflected it. “Bamboo Bicycle Club — Video / Travel & Events” — Uncrate editorial category, September 2014 What a US lifestyle feature means By September 2014, BBC had been covered by Huck Magazine, the Guardian, and cycling specialist press in the UK. The Uncrate feature extended the story into American lifestyle media for the first time — reaching an audience of US men who had never heard of BBC, never visited East London, and were unlikely to travel to Hackney Wick for a weekend workshop. But they could order a kit. And Uncrate introduced them to the idea. BBC’s home-build kit business — which now sells internationally across 36 countries — traces part of its early international demand to US lifestyle press coverage in the 2014–2016 period. Uncrate, Fast Company, and CNN Money collectively introduced the kit concept to a US audience large enough to make international shipping economically viable. Uncrate’s September 2014 feature was among the first signals that the bamboo bike workshop was a global story, not just a London one. Watch on Uncrate →

title: Hindustan Times: Build It Yourself at UK's First Bamboo Bike Workshop (2012)
body: Hindustan Times 19 November 2012 | World News | London Bureau The earliest known major press coverage of Bamboo Bicycle Club “It’s Saturday morning in Hackney Wick, east London, and apart from a mechanic deep in the bowels of a truck, the only sign of life among the small factories on a backstreet is a whine of machinery from an upper window — work has begun at Bamboo Bicycle Club.” — Hindustan Times correspondent, London, November 2012 The Hindustan Times, with 7 million+ daily readers across India and a substantial diaspora readership in the UK, published this article on 19 November 2012 — just two months after Bamboo Bicycle Club launched in September 2012. It is the earliest known major press coverage of the organisation, and it found James Marr and Ian McMillan in Hackney Wick, running Britain’s first and only bamboo bike workshop. The piece appeared in the newspaper’s World News section from its London bureau. Its readership — Indian professionals and diaspora communities in the UK — proved to be a significant early audience for BBC: a community with deep cultural appreciation for both handcraft and engineering, and with bamboo as a familiar material from daily life in South Asia. The founding story The article captured BBC at its most nascent: a workshop that had been running for just two months, with James and Ian still working full-time as engineers while running courses at weekends. The £389 monthly course bought participants a computer-designed custom bamboo frame — road or mountain bike — built over a fun weekend alongside a maximum of a handful of other builders. The origin story was documented precisely: two years of R&D in a garden shed in Brecon, Wales. James and Ian had originally set out to become boutique bamboo frame manufacturers — competing with Calfee Design ($2,995 per frame) and Yorkshire’s Bamboo Bikes (£1,199 per frame). They produced a refined, marketable product. Then they changed their minds. “Bamboo is one of the most interesting trends to emerge in bike construction. Names like Californian manufacturer Calfee Design or Yorkshire’s Bamboo Bikes have revived a construction method pioneered as early as 1894.” — Hindustan Times, November 2012 Community over commerce The insight the HT reporter captured — that BBC chose community and knowledge-sharing over premium manufacturing — was the core business decision that determined everything that followed. While competitors sold finished frames at premium prices, BBC charged for the experience of making. That positioning, identified in the first major press coverage two months after launch, has remained BBC’s defining characteristic across 14 years. The article noted the workshop’s energy: “Woodwork class was never like this.” Three participants, jigs set for three custom frames, bamboo selected from the stockpile, crossbars and seatposts being cut to blueprint specifications. A sense, the correspondent wrote, of energy and industry — and of fun. That description, from November 2012, remains accurate today. Historic significance Being covered by the Hindustan Times within eight weeks of launching gave BBC its first truly international press moment. James and Ian were still employed as engineers. The workshop was a weekend project. Yet here it was — in one of the world’s most widely-read newspapers — presented as an international story about craft, sustainability, and the democratisation of bicycle building. That early framing set the tone for 14 years of press coverage that has spanned every major UK national newspaper, the Financial Times, CNN, Fast Company, and the BBC. title: Wallpaper*: Bamboo Bicycle Club Featured in Konstantin Grcic's Paris 2024 Olympic Exhibition

body: WALLPAPER* March 2024 | by Anna Sansom | Design & Interiors “It would be true to say that sport was my first design teacher. When I was a kid, I was obsessed with looking at sports equipment and studied catalogues about it for days, weeks, months, years. I think it really informed my becoming a designer.” — Konstantin Grcic, exhibition designer and curator Wallpaper* — the world’s leading design, interiors and architecture magazine, reaching an international audience of designers, architects and cultural tastemakers — covered the ‘Match, Design & Sport — A Story Looking to the Future’ exhibition at the Musée du Luxembourg, Paris, in March 2024. The exhibition was curated by German industrial designer Konstantin Grcic and commissioned by GrandPalaisRmn to coincide with the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. Bamboo Bicycle Club was featured in the exhibition and photographed for the official record by GrandPalaisRmn’s photographer. The exhibition Grcic’s ‘Match’ exhibition explored the relationship between sport and design across a century of material and manufacturing innovation — from classical sporting sculpture to contemporary robotics. The selection was deliberately wide: a reproduction of Myron’s Discobolus , Boston Dynamics’ Atlas Humanoid Robot, Olympic torches, racing wheelchairs, and purpose-built sporting equipment from across disciplines. Among this context, the Bamboo Bicycle Club team and their frames represented the handmade, natural-material counterpoint to high-technology manufacturing. The Wallpaper* feature noted Grcic’s perspective on the intersection of sport and design as a formative influence — a designer who had grown up studying equipment catalogues and found in sporting objects a clarity of purpose that informed his own industrial practice. BBC’s bamboo frames share this quality: objects designed to do a specific thing, with every material choice determined by function. “Bamboo Bicycle Club Team” — Image caption, Musée du Luxembourg, Paris, 2024 | Credit: GrandPalaisRmn Why it matters Being featured in Wallpaper* ’s coverage of a Paris Olympic Games exhibition — alongside work curated by Konstantin Grcic, one of the world’s most respected industrial designers — places BBC within a design conversation that has nothing to do with cycling as a sport. This is about material thinking, craft intelligence, and the relationship between making and meaning. The Wallpaper* audience of architects, designers, and cultural decision-makers includes many people who would not describe themselves as cyclists but who understand immediately what it means to build something structural from a natural material. For BBC, coverage in Wallpaper* positions the organisation in the design canon — a different register entirely from cycling press coverage, and arguably more durable as a credibility signal. The Musée du Luxembourg is part of the Réunion des musées nationaux — Grand Palais network, one of the most significant institutional presences in European cultural life. BBC’s presence at the Musée du Luxembourg in 2024 follows its appearance in the museum’s exhibition programme in 2023 — suggesting a sustained relationship with this cultural institution across two consecutive years. title: CNN Money: How Bamboo Bicycle Club Sells Build-Your-Own Bikes to the World
tags: 2016, cnn, cnn-money, international, kits, press, small-business
body: CNN Money 7 October 2016 | Small Business | London Bureau “To get one of these bamboo beauties you go on a two-day course to make your own — although home-build kits are now available too.” — CNN Money, 2016 CNN Money — CNN’s business and small enterprise section, reaching tens of millions of readers globally — covered Bamboo Bicycle Club in October 2016 from its London bureau. The piece appeared in the Small Business section and introduced BBC’s workshop model and home-build kit business to a North American and international audience. The business model CNN Money’s coverage identified what made BBC commercially unusual: it did not manufacture products for retail. Instead, it charged for the experience of manufacturing. Workshop participants paid for two days of instruction and left with a custom bamboo bicycle frame they had built themselves. Home-build kit customers paid for all the materials and instructions required to build a frame at home, without attending a workshop. At the time of coverage, BBC’s DIY kits were priced between $360 and $460, in road, mountain bike, and tandem configurations. Seventy percent of kit sales were going to customers outside the UK — predominantly in Europe, the United States, and Australia. For a small East London workshop operation, this level of international reach by 2016 — just four years after launch — was notable. “Bamboo Bicycle Club is a London-based company that sells bamboo bicycle building kits and runs workshops showing customers how to build their own bamboo bicycle frame.” — CNN Money, Small Business, 7 October 2016 Material properties and durability CNN Money noted bamboo’s key advantages over conventional frame materials: natural shock absorption (bamboo’s cellular structure dissipates road vibration more effectively than steel or aluminium), lighter weight than steel, and exceptional durability. BBC estimated frame lifespans of 10–15 years minimum — longer than many carbon frames, and entirely consistent with bamboo’s properties as a natural composite material. The article also noted the accessibility benefits: riders with injuries or sensitivity to vibration reported bamboo’s damping qualities as a significant improvement over metal frames. For a publication focused on small business innovation, this represented the kind of product differentiation — genuine, material, difficult to replicate — that makes a niche business sustainable. About CNN Money CNN Money was CNN’s dedicated business and finance platform, reaching a global audience of investors, entrepreneurs, and business professionals. Coverage of BBC’s Small Business section introduced the bamboo kit concept to a North American audience considerably larger than any European cycling publication could reach. The piece was filed from CNN’s London bureau in October 2016 — four years into BBC’s existence and just as the home-build kit business was establishing its international distribution.
