title: Investec Beyond Business 2025: Bamboo Bicycle Club wins £24,000 award
tags: 2025, award, beyond-business, investec, press, social-enterprise, verified
body: Investec Beyond Business 29 September 2025 | Announcement “A truly inspiring cohort — each of these social enterprise businesses are focused on addressing important societal issues, delivering meaningful impact in their communities.” — Ruth Leas, CEO, Investec Bank plc Bamboo Bicycle Club was named one of four winners of the Investec Beyond Business 2025 programme on 29 September 2025 — receiving a share of approximately £100,000 in funding plus ongoing mentorship and business support from Investec colleagues. The Investec Beyond Business (IBB) programme has run for 15 years in East London, backing purpose-driven social enterprises in Tower Hamlets, Newham and Hackney. In 2025, a record 148 applicants competed for four places. BBC was selected alongside Round Retail, Feeling Social, and TrailFam — the full cohort collectively receiving c.£100,000 from Investec. What Investec saw in BBC The Investec programme page described Bamboo Bicycle Club as an organisation that “reconnects excluded learners with education by delivering hands-on, industry-relevant, accredited programmes in sustainable design and mobility to open pathways into further study, employment or enterprise.” This description captures something precise about BBC’s positioning: it is not primarily a cycling business. It is an education and social mobility organisation that uses bicycle building as the mechanism. The programme doesn’t teach people to cycle — it teaches them to make something, which changes something in them. Investec’s judges understood this distinction. The judging panel The 2025 IBB judging panel included two former IBB winners (Eve Wagg of Well Grounded, David Schluter of Fluid IT), Marc Kahn and Deborah Sayagh from Investec, and Ruth Leas, CEO of Investec Bank plc. A 148-application field was reduced to four. The process was competitive; BBC’s selection required demonstrating both social impact credibility and commercial viability. Programme history “Bamboo Bicycle Club reconnects excluded learners with education by delivering hands-on, industry-relevant, accredited programmes in sustainable design and mobility to open pathways into further study, employment or enterprise.” — Investec Beyond Business programme description (investec.com) Since 2011, Investec has committed over £1 million to the IBB programme, which has launched 72 social enterprises and created over 430 jobs combined. BBC joins a cohort of graduates who have gone on to grow and scale significant social businesses in London and beyond. What the funding enables At BBC, the Investec award accelerates three areas: expanding community workshop access (schools, community groups, rehabilitation settings); building a skills and employment pipeline through sustainable manufacturing training; and scaling the Build to Bond prison programme — which was, at the time of the award, already running at HMP Lowdham Grange with a waiting list of participants. The award was announced the same month (September 2025) that BBC was profiled by the Financial Times in FT Weekend. The combination of FT coverage and an Investec award in the same period represented BBC’s highest-profile month in its 13-year history. Read the full announcement at Investec →

title: Inside Time: Making bike-building accessible to everyone in prisons
tags: 2025, accessibility, inside-time, press, prison, rehabilitation, verified
body: Inside Time National Newspaper for Prisoners | November 2025 “The bamboo bike course offers more than just technical training — it provides an avenue for creativity, teamwork, and self-expression.” — Sally Allsopp, Industries Manager, HMP Lowdham Grange Inside Time — the UK’s national newspaper for prisoners, reaching over 100,000 readers in prisons across England and Wales — published a feature on Bamboo Bicycle Club’s Build to Bond programme at HMP Lowdham Grange in November 2025. The article opened with characteristic directness: “Pandas eat it. Schoolchildren used to be caned with it. But now prisoners at Lowdham Grange have found a surprising new use for bamboo — making bicycles out of it.” How the programme works At HMP Lowdham Grange — a Category B men’s prison in Nottinghamshire — six prisoners at a time join a six-week bamboo bike building course. When one group completes the course, another begins; a waiting list testifies to its popularity. Inside Time noted that bamboo has the same tensile strength as steel yet can be cut and shaped with hand tools — making it particularly suitable for a prison workshop environment. The programme operates on a cost-recovery model: profits from BBC’s £695 public workshops fund the prison courses. Bikes made on the course are dismantled in the final week so materials can be reused by the next cohort. Three prisoners have been trained as instructors and help facilitate each session. Participants who complete the course earn a Level 2 certificate in Sustainable Design and Manufacturing. The most engaged participants become eligible for Build to Bond — BBC’s follow-up programme in which a prisoner builds a children’s bamboo balance bike to gift to their own child, grandchild, niece or nephew. The bike is sent home. The father stays inside. The prison context Inside Time noted that the programme provides “a ray of light at Lowdham Grange,” where many of the 900 prisoners are lifers. The prison transferred from private management to the public sector following a period of concern about drug use, violence, and what an inspection report described as “almost non-existent” incentives for prisoners. The bamboo bike course was one of the few consistently popular and purposeful activities available. Government endorsement “Finding employment after release reduces the chance of reoffending significantly, which is why we are improving opportunities to help prisoners turn their lives around. Innovative projects, such as Build to Bond, support rehabilitation and help people leave prison as better citizens, boosting the economy and keeping our streets safe.” — Lord (James) Timpson, Prisons Minister Lord Timpson’s endorsement — published in Inside Time, the publication read in every prison in England and Wales — placed Build to Bond directly in front of the audience most relevant to its mission: prisoners, prison staff, and the people who work in the criminal justice system. The Prisons Minister’s explicit naming of the programme is rare; most endorsements from government ministers are generic. This one was specific. The Inside Time feature was published in November 2025, one month after the Financial Times’ FT Weekend profile, and alongside an ongoing inquiry by the House of Commons Justice Committee into what actually works to reduce reoffending. Bamboo Bicycle Club featured in both contexts within the same month. Read the full article on Inside Time →

title: Grand Designs Live: Kevin McCloud's Green Heroes
tags: 2018, grand-designs, green-heroes, kevin-mccloud, press, tv, verified
body: Grand Designs Live — ExCeL London May 2018 | Kevin McCloud’s Green Heroes “Bamboo is officially the fastest growing plant in the world, which should make these the fastest bicycles in the world: light, hollow-tube construction, supremely engineered by nature. But they are not too fast to buy. You have to join the club and build one yourself.” — Kevin McCloud, Grand Designs presenter (Channel 4) Bamboo Bicycle Club was selected as one of Kevin McCloud’s Green Heroes at Grand Designs Live 2018 — the annual sustainable design showcase held at ExCeL London, curated by Grand Designs presenter Kevin McCloud. The Green Heroes section highlights the most innovative eco-conscious businesses and designers exhibiting at the show, selected personally by McCloud. Kevin McCloud’s selection McCloud’s quote captures precisely what makes the Bamboo Bicycle Club model unusual in the sustainable products landscape. Most sustainable product companies make things and sell them. BBC doesn’t. It teaches people to make things themselves. McCloud — whose Grand Designs philosophy has always centred on the relationship between the maker and the made object — identified this distinction immediately. The observation that bamboo is “supremely engineered by nature” is technically precise. Bamboo’s cellulose microfibre structure gives it a tensile strength comparable to steel, vibration-damping properties superior to aluminium, and a growth cycle of 3–5 years versus 60+ years for hardwoods. It is, as McCloud noted, an extraordinary material that happens to grow extremely fast. Grand Designs Live Grand Designs Live is the UK’s largest home building and renovation show, attracting 50,000+ visitors across its London run at ExCeL each May. The show is an extension of Channel 4’s Grand Designs television series, hosted by Kevin McCloud since 1999. McCloud personally curates the Green Heroes section each year, selecting businesses that demonstrate genuine innovation in sustainable design and construction. The selection criteria for Green Heroes are demanding: originality of concept, credibility of sustainability credentials, and practical viability as a product or service. BBC’s workshop model — using a fast-growing grass instead of mined or synthesised materials, teaching participants to build rather than consuming pre-made products, creating frames with design lifespans of 10–15 years — met all three criteria. “Kevin McCloud’s Green Heroes” is listed as a key credential on bamboobicycleclub.org alongside the Investec Beyond Business 2025 award and OCN Level 2 Accredited Education — three of BBC’s most significant institutional endorsements. — bamboobicycleclub.org (as of March 2026) McCloud’s BBC endorsement in context Kevin McCloud’s endorsement carries unusual weight in the sustainable design world. Unlike award bodies or press features, his selection is personal and publicly attributed. When McCloud says a product is a Green Hero, he is putting his name and his audience’s trust behind it. His Grand Designs audience of homebuilders, architects and design professionals represents exactly the demographic most likely to value BBC’s combination of craft, sustainability and hands-on engagement. The credential has remained on BBC’s website for six years. Its longevity reflects both the durability of McCloud’s endorsement and the consistency of BBC’s positioning in the sustainable materials space. Note: The original granddesignslive.com page for this feature is no longer live as of March 2026. Kevin McCloud’s quote is confirmed via independent reporting in TheBusinessDesk (June 2016) and the BBC website credential listing. Grand Designs Live website →

title: BikeRadar: Building your own bamboo bicycle — the charm of handmade
tags: 2015, bikeradar, cycling, handmade, press, review, verified
body: BikeRadar 29 January 2015 | by Gregor MacGregor | Rider: Joe Norledge “It would be churlish to try and measure a bike like this against a state of the art carbon machine — that’s not the point of one of these rides. Forget the tiny flaws and rough look to the build — that’s a huge part of the charm.” — Gregor MacGregor, BikeRadar In January 2015, BikeRadar — the UK’s largest cycling website — published its first ride video of a Bamboo Bicycle Club frame, produced by then-Communities Editor Gregor MacGregor and ridden by BikeRadar’s Joe Norledge. It was BBC’s first major coverage in the professional cycling media. The first ride BikeRadar received a Bamboo Bicycle Club frame and put it through a standard first ride assessment — the same format used for professional carbon, steel and aluminium bikes. The results were filmed as a video, with Norledge providing his rider impressions on camera. MacGregor’s written assessment was precise about what BikeRadar was evaluating. A bamboo workshop bike is not a race bike. Comparing it to carbon would miss the point entirely. The ride characteristic that mattered was different: the feel of something you built yourself, in a material you chose, to dimensions fitted to your body. “To get one of these bamboo beauties you go on a two-day course to make your own — although home-build kits are now available too.” — Gregor MacGregor, BikeRadar What the coverage meant BikeRadar is owned by Immediate Media and reaches millions of cyclists monthly across its website, app and YouTube channel. A first ride feature on BikeRadar — in 2015, just over two years after BBC launched — was a significant validation signal. It told the cycling world that the bamboo workshop concept was credible enough to be evaluated on the same terms as any other bike. The video format was particularly valuable. First-person video of someone riding a BBC-built bamboo frame gave potential workshop participants something they couldn’t get from photos: a sense of what the bike actually felt like in motion. Smooth, quiet, comfortable. Characterful. Not a race bike, not a utility bike, but something with its own distinctly physical personality. MacGregor’s editorial framing — “forget the tiny flaws, that’s part of the charm” — was borrowed and adapted by dozens of subsequent reviewers. It became one of the most accurate and frequently-cited characterisations of what a handmade bamboo bike actually is. Not a precision instrument, but something more interesting: a bike that carries the marks of the person who made it. Historic significance This was BikeRadar’s first-ever coverage of Bamboo Bicycle Club. Since January 2015, BikeRadar has returned to BBC multiple times — covering the home build kits (2018), the gravel build (2019), and later in depth features on workshop participants. Each subsequent piece of BikeRadar coverage built on the foundation of this first ride video. The article also marked an important moment in the evolution of BBC’s product offering: home build kits had just been launched, and BikeRadar’s coverage was one of the first mainstream publications to note their existence. This introduction to a national cycling audience directly contributed to the early growth of the kit business. title: road.cc: Bamboo Bicycle Club Easy Build Kit — 70 hours to just 4
tags: 2020, cycling, easy-build, kit, press, road-cc, verified
body: road.cc, December 2020 — by Anna Marie Hughes Thanks to pre-molded carbon lugs, you can DIY a custom sustainable bamboo bike at home within a day. "Slashing the time to construct its bamboo road frame from around 70 hours (with the previous kit) down to just four hours with their new easy build option, the Bamboo Bicycle Club has impressively improved the accessibility of building a bamboo bicycle." — Anna Marie Hughes, road.cc, December 2020 Founded in London in 2012 by James Marr, bamboo is said to have ideal properties for bike construction with its "excellent vibration dampening effects", resistance to stress and durability. The Bamboo Bicycle Club's easy build home kit (£395) contains pre-molded carbon lugs which removes the process of creating your own connections between each bamboo length — reducing frame build time by 75%, from around 70 hours down to just four. "Founded in London in 2012 by James Marr, bamboo is said to have ideal properties for bike construction with its 'excellent vibration dampening effects', resistance to stress and durability." — road.cc, December 2020 The new easy build process: shape the bamboo, insert into the carbon lugs, allow to dry, apply any finish, fit components. Carbon lugs weigh 0.7kg; bamboo 1–1.5kg. Tyre clearance of 32mm, mudguard and pannier mounts, internal cabling and a disc brake frame adapter are all included. Bamboo Bicycle Club promises "no mess simple construction" — the frame comes with a detailed build manual, a full-scale drawing, an alignment jig and high strength bonding glue. A standard table (1200mm × 600mm) plus sandpaper, a hobby knife, masking tape and disposable gloves is all you need. The 70-hour original kit (£285) remains available for those who want the full craft experience: setting up a jig, shaping and cutting bamboo to size, tacking the frame together, creating flax fibre lugs with epoxy resin, sanding and finishing. A club atmosphere is encouraged with the "build with a buddy" scheme — 25% off a second kit. Full support via telephone, email and video call if you hit any hurdles. Gravel and city bike kits also available. Key facts: Easy Build Kit £395 | Build time ~4 hours | Carbon lugs 0.7kg | Bamboo 1–1.5kg | Tyre clearance 32mm

title: Huck Magazine: The Bamboo Bicycle Club making sustainable cycling accessible
body: HUCK Working Artisans’ Club 2014 | Photography: James Cannon “In a quiet corner of Hackney Wick, Ian McMillan and James Marr are helping Londoners customise their rides. Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products.” — Huck Magazine In 2014, Huck Magazine selected Bamboo Bicycle Club as one of the standout artisan businesses in their Working Artisans’ Club series — a collaboration with surf brand O’Neill that celebrated modern makers across Europe. The full feature was photographed by James Cannon at the Hackney Wick workshop. Knowledge-sharing over profit-making Huck’s coverage captured something the cycling press of the time often missed: the philosophy behind the workshop model. Bamboo Bicycle Club wasn’t trying to compete with Calfee or Canyon. It was doing something structurally different — selling the experience of making rather than the product made. Huck, whose readership spanned skaters, surfers, climbers, and independent creatives, immediately understood this positioning. The article positioned BBC alongside other Working Artisans’ Club members: board-builders, guitarists, brewers, bag-makers. Makers who had chosen craft and community over conventional careers. In this context, BBC’s workshop model — two days, one frame, yours to ride home — was entirely legible as a statement of values, not just a service offering. Photography by James Cannon brought the Hackney Wick workshop to life: the bamboo stacks, the jigs, the hemp-wrapped joints mid-build. Visual content that positioned BBC within the maker movement at its peak, in a magazine read by exactly the kind of early-adopter audience that would later form the core of BBC’s customer base. The Working Artisans’ Club Huck’s Working Artisans’ Club was an editorial project produced throughout 2014, culminating in exhibitions in London and Munich. The Munich exhibition ran at Art:ig Galerie, 16–19 October 2014. BBC was among a small group of European makers featured in both the magazine and at the exhibitions. The project was presented by Huck and O’Neill. “The old way of doing things is dead. Resource depletion, environmental destruction and financial crises are just a few of the factors that raise questions about relying on a system shaped by mass-production, designed obsolescence and death by focus group. We have to think about buying less, using things longer and making products with quality and care.” — Huck Magazine, Working Artisans’ Club editorial introduction, 2014 Huck was founded in 2006 and has built a global readership across surf, skate, snowboard, art and independent music communities. Its editorial voice — characterised by an affection for craft, autonomy and countercultural values — made it an ideal home for BBC’s story. In 2014, when “maker culture” was at its cultural peak, Huck’s selection of BBC as a Working Artisans’ Club subject placed the workshop at the intersection of cycling and the broader handmade movement. Historical significance The 2014 Huck feature was one of BBC’s earliest appearances in lifestyle and culture media beyond the cycling press. Where BikeRadar and road.cc reached cyclists, Huck reached people who hadn’t yet decided they wanted a bike — people drawn to the idea of making something with their hands, regardless of the object. This audience became one of BBC’s most durable customer segments: non-cyclists who built their first bamboo bike and never looked back. It also signalled something important about BBC’s brand positioning. Being featured alongside surfboard shapers, guitar builders and brewers — not just bike brands — told a story about craft, values and community that pure cycling press could not tell. title: The Guardian: How to make a £500 bespoke bicycle from bamboo
tags: 2015, cycling, guardian, homemade, press, stuart-heritage, verified
body: 17 June 2015 "Going to the workshop was hands-down one of the best things I've ever done. Yes, at almost £500 it's a lot of money, but you're making a bespoke creation that's structurally sound and leaves a tiny carbon footprint." — Stuart Heritage, The Guardian Stuart Heritage, writing for The Guardian's Homemade Life series, documented his experience building a bamboo bicycle at our London workshop. After leaving London and escaping the terror of city cycling, he wanted to get back in the saddle with something special. The Workshop Experience Day one involved visualising three-dimensional measurements, choosing bamboo poles, sawing them to size, drilling holes, whittling them, and assembling the basic frame shape. Day two focused on gluing — soaking hemp cloth in epoxy and wrapping it around joints. Heritage returned twice more to sand the frame and fit wheels and handlebars. The result was a unique creation that reflected his personality. "My bike is charmingly flawed, clearly the work of someone who charges into things without thinking them through and then hopes for the best. The bike is me. I don't think I could love it any more than I do." — Stuart Heritage, The Guardian Read the full article on The Guardian → The Bamboo Bicycle Club was founded in September 2012 in Hackney Wick, east London — at the time, Britain's only bamboo bike building course. Engineers James Marr and Ian McMillan spent two years researching bamboo frame construction before pivoting from selling finished frames to teaching others to build their own. The £389 course included a computer-designed custom frame (road or mountain bike) plus a full weekend of hands-on building, hosted once per month. Guardian journalist James Stewart visited the workshop on a Saturday morning, observing the two-day process firsthand. Day one involved selecting bamboo for strength, mitring joints, and setting tubes in jigs — with chromoly tubes inserted for handlebars, forks and seatpost. Day two focused on building hemp wraps around joints with epoxy to form the strong bonds that give the frame its structural integrity. Stewart took James's personal bamboo bicycle for a test ride and reported that "the ride is light, stiff and smooth thanks to bamboo's ability to dampen vibration. Impressive, considering I target every pothole." He noted the aesthetic appeal — comparing it to punk versus Coldplay: "less up against the big names than creating a bike that is about DIY and will engender more passion than the average factory-line model."

title: The Guardian: Build it yourself at the UK's first bamboo bike workshop
tags: 2012, cycling, guardian, hackney-wick, launch, press, verified
body: The Guardian — Bike Blog Friday 16 November 2012 | by James Stewart “I take James’s bike for a spin and the ride is light, stiff and smooth thanks to bamboo’s ability to dampen vibration. Impressive, considering I target every pothole.” — James Stewart, The Guardian Bike Blog It’s Saturday morning in Hackney Wick, east London, and apart from a mechanic deep in the bowels of a truck, the only sign of life among the small factories on a backstreet is a whine of machinery from an upper window — work has begun at Bamboo Bicycle Club. Guardian journalist James Stewart arrived at the workshop to find three men in their late-20s already three hours into building their custom bamboo frames. Jigs had been set, bamboo selected from a stockpile, crossbars and seatposts being cut to lengths specified on each participant’s blueprint. “There’s a sense of energy and industry. And of fun. Woodwork class was never like this,” he wrote. The origins of Bamboo Bicycle Club The article described how bamboo had emerged as one of the most interesting trends in bicycle construction, with Californian manufacturer Calfee Design reviving a method pioneered as early as 1894 — but at a cost of up to $5,852 ready to ride, far out of reach for most cyclists. Engineers James Marr and Ian McMillan had spent years researching bamboo frame construction in a shed in Brecon, Wales — refining techniques, experimenting with joint construction, developing the vocabulary of “close-noded thick-wall tubes” that would define their process. Their original plan was to establish a boutique bamboo bicycle manufacturer. They abandoned it when they realised the real value lay in something different: sharing the craft rather than selling the product. The Bamboo Bicycle Club launched in September 2012 — more community than company. The £389 course price included a computer-designed custom frame and a weekend of building. Monthly workshops ran in Hackney Wick. Gear packs for road-ready builds were available from £218. Two days in the workshop Stewart documented both days of the course in detail. Day one: selecting bamboo for strength (not just diameter, but ensuring proposed cuts fall between nodes), mitring joints, setting tubes in jigs. The front triangle used 40mm diameter bamboo; seat and chainstays used thinner, more precise tubes. Chromoly inserts were fitted for handlebars, forks and seatpost; stainless steel dropouts slotted into the chainstays. Day two was for the lugs — what Marr and McMillan called the wraps. Hemp webbing wrapped around each joint and dropout, then saturated with epoxy to form bonds that dispersed loads across the frame rather than concentrating them at a single point. The result looked rougher than a professional frame. That was part of the point. Stewart noted that all participants on this particular workshop were engineers by trade — but observed that this was “no coincidence” given that the course attracted people drawn to understanding how things work. He tried and failed to find a reason the bikes wouldn’t hold together. Ian McMillan had been commuting 16 miles a day on his for over a year. title: Financial Times: How Bamboo Bicycle Club is helping to break the prison cycle

body: September 5, 2025 The 2,000 sq ft workshop space at HMP Lowdham Grange where prisoners learn bamboo bicycle construction. title: Introducing Our New Bamboo Bicycle Frame-Building Jig
body: We’re excited to share the launch of our latest product: the Bamboo Bicycle Club Frame-Building Jig – Version 6 , now available at £595 . After years of refining our designs through workshops, builds, and community feedback, this new jig is our most streamlined and user-friendly version yet. What Is a Frame-Building Jig? A frame-building jig is the foundation of bicycle construction. It securely holds each tube in place, ensuring precise alignment while you join them together. This version is optimised for bamboo but can also be adapted for other frame materials. Key Features Version 6 includes: Durable aluminium construction – CNC-machined plates for accuracy and stability Engraved measurement scales – etched directly onto the plates for easy geometry setup Fully adjustable fixtures – vertical posts and sliding rails for different frame sizes and styles Hand-operated knobs – black nylon with yellow caps for quick, tool-free adjustments Engraved branding – Bamboo Bicycle Club logo and details, clearly displayed on each jig How It Works The jig makes frame building straightforward: Adjust the geometry using the built-in scales Secure bamboo (or other) tubes in place Maintain perfect alignment while joining the lugs Experiment with different bike styles by adjusting the setup What’s New in Version 6 This sixth iteration builds on everything we’ve learned from earlier versions: Simplified design with fewer parts for faster setup A more intuitive adjustment system Cleaner, more open workspace around the frame Refined fixtures for smoother handling Specifications Price: £595 Material: CNC-machined aluminium Assembly: Some self-assembly required Shipping: UK and international delivery available Included: All jig components plus setup instructions Who It’s For This jig is designed for: First-time builders looking for precision and reliability Workshop leaders running bamboo bike courses Enthusiasts exploring custom geometry Schools and universities teaching engineering or sustainable design About Bamboo Bicycle Club We provide tools, kits, and workshops for bamboo bicycle building, helping people design and build their own sustainable bikes. summary: Four Seasons × Bamboo Bicycle Club: From Boardroom to Bike Frame Twelve senior managers at Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire traded their usual strategy sessions for saws and bamboo, crafting a complete bicycle frame in just three hours. The team-building workshop delivered hands-on sustainability lesson
body: Building With Bamboo: How Four Seasons' Senior Team Crafted a Bike in Three Hours Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire × Bamboo Bicycle Club Team-build | 3 hours | 12 leaders | One unforgettable frame Why a Bamboo Bike? When Four Seasons Hotel Hampshire asked us for a hands-on, sustainability-driven team-building experience, we knew a bamboo bike frame would hit the sweet spot between creativity, collaboration, and eco-awareness. In just three hours, twelve senior managers swapped spreadsheets for spoke keys—discovering firsthand how fast raw bamboo can turn into a ride-ready frame. Setting the Scene Our mobile workshop rolled into the hotel's events barn, bringing: Pre-cut, responsibly sourced Tonkin bamboo Stainless-steel frame jigs mounted on portable boards A travel kit of saws, files, biodegradable epoxy, and safety gear From Tubes to Triangles Measure & Mark – Each duo matched bamboo diameter to the seat-stay, down-tube, and chain-stay positions. Precision Cutting – Using Japanese pull saws, they trimmed tubes to ±1 mm accuracy (yes, really!). Mitre Perfection – Files and sandpaper shaped each joint until no daylight showed between tubes. Dry Fit & Epoxy – With guidance, the full triangle went into the jig, ready for curing. Team Takeaways Cross-department bonding – Directors from Rooms, F&B, and Spa worked shoulder-to-shoulder. Sustainability in action – Bamboo sequesters more CO₂ per hectare than timber and needs no fertiliser. Rapid prototyping mindset – Leaders experienced agile thinking: measure, cut, test, iterate . Ready to Ride (Almost!) By the end of Hour 3 the epoxy was curing, the smiles were wide, and every participant had signed the inside of the seat tube—leaving a hidden team signature for the rider who'll eventually roll this bike down the lanes of Hampshire. Sustainable Full Circle As part of Four Seasons' corporate social responsibility initiative, all completed bikes were donated to Upcycle in Brixton, supporting their community cycling programs and ensuring these sustainable creations continue to make a positive impact. body: Bamboo Bike Building: Transforming Lives at Lowdham Grange Prison In an inspiring development for prison rehabilitation programs, HMP Lowdham Grange has partnered with Bamboo Bicycle Club to launch an innovative training initiative focused on bamboo bike construction. This groundbreaking program, which began in March 2025, is designed to equip inmates with valuable skills in mechanics, design, and craftsmanship – creating pathways to employment and entrepreneurship upon release. The six-week course takes place in a dedicated workshop built specifically for this purpose on the prison grounds. What makes this program particularly special is its peer-learning component: trusted inmates assist staff in delivering the training, creating a collaborative environment that builds leadership skills alongside technical knowledge. From Frame Building to Future Building Participants engage in comprehensive sessions totalling 18 hours weekly, covering everything from: Frame construction techniques Bicycle mechanics and assembly Design principles Finishing methods and quality control Each cohort consists of twelve carefully selected inmates who develop not only practical skills but also the discipline and focus essential for successful reintegration into society. The program's sustainable approach is evident in its materials management – at the course conclusion, frames are deconstructed, with connections reused for future courses and bamboo components recycled. A Turning Point for Lowdham Grange This initiative arrives at a crucial time for HMP Lowdham Grange, a Category B male training prison in Nottinghamshire. Following a challenging period marked by internal difficulties and a December 2023 management takeover by HM Prison and Probation Service (HMPPS), the facility has been seeking effective rehabilitation programs. The bamboo bike building scheme represents a fresh approach to addressing these challenges, offering purposeful activity that positively influences behavior while developing marketable skills. As James Marr, founder of Bamboo Bicycle Club, explains: "Training prisoners in the building of frames and mechanics of bikes so they can build themselves a brighter future." Looking Forward: Growth and Community Impact The program's future looks promising, with plans already underway to develop an online platform featuring instructional videos and theoretical content to support the in-person training. Weekly check-ins from founder James Marr ensure continuous improvement based on participant feedback. Perhaps most exciting is the next planned phase – establishing an enterprise scheme that would allow completed bikes to be sold to the community, creating a sustainable business model while strengthening connections between the prison and local residents. If the pilot proves successful, Bamboo Bicycle Club intends to expand the scheme to other prisons and establish a Community Interest Company (CIC) to secure government grants and formal accreditation. By separating the balancing skill from the pedalling skill, balance bikes allow children as young as 18 months to develop genuine cycling confidence before they ever touch a pedal. Children who learn on balance bikes typically transition to pedal bikes years earlier than those who start on stabilisers. Cycle the 70 miles between London and Brighton. I went through tremendous self-doubt - often wondering what I had got myself into. I trained for three months and did some meticulous planning. And suddenly it was the day. On a crisp London morning, I said bye to my family and close friends and as they cheered me, began the 7 hour ride to Brighton. I have never been so happy to see the sea! It was a tough ride, but ultimately felt truly rewarding. As I was preparing for this event, I quickly realised that long distance cycling can be complicated while requiring a lot preparation. One thing that bothered me involved buying many accessories for the trip which are full of plastic (Lycra clothing, lightweight plastic water-bottles, a sturdy helmet, cycling cleats… even the protein bar packaging). I had decided to cycle to create a more sustainable lifestyle. Buying all these plastic essentials made me question whether I was actually on a sustainable cycling lifestyle A Bicycle is one of the oldest and simplest forms of transport, It is great for our mind, body and for the environment. However, the cycling industry is increasingly damaging the environment. It has a formidable carbon footprint owing to aluminium bike frames and nowadays carbon fibre, a wonder composite material required to make high performance bicycles. The production of such bicycles consumes huge quantities of water and energy and generates lots of waste. According to the UCI (the world governing body of cycling sport) in 2021 the sports industry was the third largest user of carbon fibre worldwide. Most sports equipment using this material has an average lifespan of three years and 90% ends up in landfills. I wondered if there could be a viable solution to this problem. To make cycling even better for the environment. To make it a fantastically sustainable way of transport. The answer turned out wilder than you could ever imagine. Grass. Well, not grass as you know it. But a special type of grass that we have all heard of, and we all know about… only not so much in the context of a sustainable lifestyle. Did you know that Bamboo is a type of grass? Bamboo is a nature-based carbon fibre which belongs to the grass family of plants. It grows faster than any other plant on the planet with some species growing up to 1 meter a day! Bamboo has super carbon sequestration capabilities. Bamboo is a renewable and regenerative resource, one which can be harvested every year and will continue to sequester carbon year after year. There are more than 1600 known species of bamboo which largely grow in tropical and subtropical to mild temperate regions globally. The tensile strength of bamboo is higher than that of steel, it has amazing vibration dampening capabilities and is light weight. This makes it ideal for construction industries which use engineered bamboo which lasts for decades with proper care. No wonder it’s been nicknamed Green Gold. Last year, after completing my 70-mile bicycle ride on my 'Specialized' aluminium bike, I decided to build my own Bamboo Bicycle at a workshop here in London. title: New Video- How to protect your frame
summary: How to protect your bamboo frame and improve longevity.
body: D escription: In this video, we dive into the best ways to protect your bamboo frame, ensuring it stays durable and beautiful for years to come. Whether it's a bamboo bike, furniture, or another project, we explore various product options you can use to keep your bamboo looking great. From car finishes to yacht varnishes, learn how these products provide superior protection against moisture, UV damage, and wear. Whether you're a DIY enthusiast or a seasoned craftsman, this guide will help you choose the right solution for your bamboo frame. 🔧 Topics Covered: Why bamboo frames need protection Benefits of using car finishes on bamboo How yacht varnish enhances bamboo’s resilience Application tips for the best results Long-term maintenance strategies for bamboo frames 💡 Products Mentioned: Yacht Vanish Tung Oil Car Finish 📌 Don’t forget to like, subscribe, and hit the notification bell for more DIY tips and product reviews! #BambooFrame #BambooProtection #DIYBamboo #CarFinish #YachtVarnish #WoodProtection #SustainableDIY "Founded in London in 2012 by James Marr, bamboo is said to have ideal properties for bike construction with its 'excellent vibration dampening effects', resistance to stress and durability." — road.cc, December 2020 Protecting your bamboo bicycle frame is an important step that many first-time builders underestimate. Bamboo is a natural material with specific vulnerabilities — particularly to prolonged moisture exposure and UV degradation — that are easily managed with the right protective treatments. This video covers everything you need to keep your BBC frame looking great and performing well for years. Why bamboo needs protection: Bamboo culms naturally contain moisture when harvested and continue to exchange moisture with the environment after curing. Unprotected bamboo can absorb rainwater through the end-grain sections at tube joints, leading to internal moisture accumulation, degradation of the culm wall, and in severe cases, cracking as the bamboo expands and contracts. UV radiation bleaches and dries the surface, eventually causing surface checking (fine surface cracks). A good protective coating prevents both problems. Primary protective coating options: Outdoor lacquer: The simplest option. A two-part polyurethane lacquer applied in three coats gives excellent UV and moisture protection with a glossy or satin finish that shows the natural bamboo grain. Recoat every 2–3 years. Epoxy sealer + lacquer: For frames used in consistently wet conditions, a first coat of penetrating epoxy sealer (applied to bare bamboo, warm and thin) followed by lacquer provides superior moisture exclusion at the cost of a slightly more industrial appearance. Natural oil finish: Tung oil or Danish oil gives a warm, matte finish that allows the bamboo to breathe while providing moderate weather protection. Requires more frequent reapplication (annually) but is easily applied without professional equipment. "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 The protection video demonstrates each method on real BBC frames, including surface preparation, application technique, and drying times. It also covers joint-specific protection — sealing the flax or carbon lug ends where the most moisture ingress risk exists — and how to touch up protective coatings after minor damage without full refinishing.

BOOK A WORKSHOP VISIT THE LONDON DESIGN FESTIVAL WEBSITE "In a quiet corner of Hackney Wick, Ian McMillan and James Marr are helping Londoners customise their rides." — Huck Magazine, 2023 "In today's consumer driven mass produced society, little thought is given to the design, function and making process of the items we purchase." — James Marr, Founder — Luxembourg Museum Exhibition, 2023 Bamboo Bicycle Building at London Design Festival London Design Festival is one of the world's most significant design events — a week-long celebration of creativity and innovation that attracts over 600,000 visitors and thousands of designers, makers, and cultural institutions from across the globe. For the BBC to participate in London Design Festival is to place bamboo bicycle building squarely within the broader conversation about sustainable design, craft practice, and the future of making. The BBC's installation offered visitors the opportunity to watch bamboo bicycle building in progress, handle raw bamboo culms and finished frames, and understand the engineering principles that make bamboo such an effective structural material. For many visitors, this was their first encounter with the idea that a bicycle frame could be grown rather than manufactured — and the realisation was genuinely surprising. Design Festival audiences bring a different perspective to bamboo bicycle building than cycling audiences. Where cyclists ask about performance and handling, designers ask about material sourcing, manufacturing process, end-of-life recyclability, and the aesthetics of craft marks left visible in the finished product. These questions push the BBC to articulate its proposition in new ways — and in doing so, sharpen the understanding of what bamboo bicycle building is really about. The BBC's presence at London Design Festival reflects a belief that sustainable design is not a niche category — it is the future of all design. Bamboo bicycle building is one model for how that future might look: materials that grow rather than being extracted; products made by their users rather than by factories; objects that carry meaning because of how they were made and by whom.

title: Adam's Flax Build Video Series
summary: This series of videos show the process of building a bike using a kit from Bamboo Bicycle Club
body: "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 Adam's flax build video series documents his complete BBC bamboo bicycle build using the traditional flax fibre lug method — the original BBC approach that produces frames of extraordinary character and depth. Unlike the Easy Build Kit's pre-moulded carbon lugs, the flax method involves hand-wrapping each joint with layers of woven flax fabric impregnated with bio-epoxy resin. It is slower, more demanding, and — for many builders — more rewarding. Flax fibre composites have a natural warmth and texture that carbon fibre lacks. The finished lugs show the weave pattern of the fabric beneath the surface coating, giving each joint a distinctive handmade quality that is unique to this building method. The material also has genuinely excellent vibration-damping properties — arguably superior to carbon in this respect — making flax-lugged bamboo frames particularly prized by riders who spend long hours in the saddle. Adam's series covers all stages of the flax build: bamboo selection and preparation; jig setup; front triangle assembly; rear triangle construction; flax fibre lug application, including wet layup technique, bubble removal, and peel ply finishing; curing and post-cure sanding; and final finishing with primer, paint, and lacquer. "Founded in London in 2012 by James Marr, bamboo is said to have ideal properties for bike construction with its 'excellent vibration dampening effects', resistance to stress and durability." — road.cc, December 2020 The full Adam's Flax Build series is available on the Bamboo Bicycle Club YouTube channel. It is the BBC's most comprehensive documentation of the traditional flax build process and is an essential resource for anyone considering this build method.

The parallels with bamboo bicycle building are not superficial: both involve working with natural materials that have been given time to develop their character, applying skilled craft to shape them into something of lasting value. The Macallan team's corporate workshop with Bamboo Bicycle Club brought together senior executives and team members who spend their professional lives talking about craft and quality — and gave them the experience of practising it directly. There is a profound difference between understanding craft intellectually and experiencing what it demands: the precision required, the patience when things don't go as planned, the satisfaction when they do. Ten bamboo bicycle frames were built during the Macallan workshop — each one unique, each carrying the decisions and effort of the individuals who built it. The frames were completed over the course of the day and taken home by their builders: a tangible, functional outcome of a day's genuine work. For The Macallan, the BBC workshop represented an authentic expression of their brand values in a completely different context. For the BBC, the workshop demonstrated what sustainable, craft-based corporate experiences can offer: not entertainment, but genuine engagement. Not a team-building exercise, but actual team building — through the shared experience of making something real, together. BBC corporate workshops are available for groups of 6 to 20 participants in London and at venues across the UK. Each workshop results in finished bamboo bicycle frames that participants keep. title: Reimagining Bicycle Craftsmanship- LUXEMBOURG MUSEUM
summary: Reimagining Bicycle Craftsmanship - LUXEMBOURG MUSEUM James Marr, Founder, Bamboo Bicycle Club This a short article written for the Luxembourg Museum Paris for a upcoming exhibition which will feature our home build kit and we were invited to write a article for the exhibition manual
body: Reimagining Bicycle Craftsmanship - LUXEMBOURG MUSEUM James Marr, Founder, Bamboo Bicycle Club This a short article written for the Luxembourg Museum Paris for a upcoming exhibition which will feature our home build kit and we were invited to write a article for the exhibition manual In todays consumer driven mass produced society, little thought is given to the design, function and making process of the items we purchase. Most everyday products - including bicycles - are not built to suit individual needs but are a “one size fits all” option. As Founder of Bamboo Bicycle Club I have always challenged this, as I believe we should all be able to modify, create and improve everything we own, giving us agency over both a products function and aesthetic. As humans we have engaged in the act of making for thousands of years, and I strongly believe in the importance of physically touching, crafting and tweaking a design and its’materials, until you have a unique finished product. I founded Bamboo Bicycle Club in 2012 and over the last eleven years have built approximately 4,000 unique bike frames for people all over the world. These range from road bikes to mountain bikes, tandems, cargo bikes, wheelchairs and more, for people of all different heights and body shapes. We decided to use bamboo to construct bikes as it is an interesting engineering material that is under utilised. With over 1,500 species it can be grown almost anywhere in the world making it both accessible and sustainable for builders globally. It also has many qualities that make it ideal for bicycle construction; it has a natural aerodynamic tube shape and comes in various diameters, it has a high weight to strength ratio, and a unique vibration dampening characteristic. Bamboo also has a negative carbon footprint, as it absorbs 30% more CO2 than traditional timber, making it one of the key materials in climate change migration. Bamboo can however can be difficult to join due to its’ wall thickness and structure. As part of our build techniques we therefore incorporate lugs (socket like connections that join the main triangle tubes) to construct the frame, which are made from recycled aluminium. These can be seen in the home built kit on display in this exhibition. But for more complex builds we also use other materials in our process to make these connections such as flax composite and carbon fibre, which when combined with bamboo to form a unique bio composite bicycle frame. Education, sharing our knowledge and empowering people to have the confidence to build their own bikes has always been fundamental to our ethos. In addition to our London based bike building workshops and home build kit offerings, we also run a number of training hubs utilising locally grown bamboo in Kenya and Ethiopia as well as hubs in cities across Europe. We are also committed to supporting the next generation of engineers, and work in partnership with universities and schools to support research projects and build prototypes which push boundaries and provide further knowledge. Do visit our website, build your own bike from the home kit in this exhibition, or get in touch if you have a crazy idea that you want to bring to life! title: Long Video exploring Sustainability and Bicycle Riding
body: The Life Cycle: Bamboo Bike Ride through South America with Kate Rawles Join Kate Rawles on an unforgettable odyssey across South America, as she pedals the paths less traveled on her sustainable bamboo bike. 🚴‍♀️🍃 **About This Video:** In "The Life Cycle," Kate Rawles beautifully blends adventure with environmental consciousness. Dive deep into the magnificent landscapes of South America, all while exploring the potential of bamboo as a beacon for sustainable living. * *Highlights:** - 🌱 Marvel at the symbiosis between the natural strength of bamboo and Kate's determination, as they take on diverse terrains and challenges. - 🏞️ Journey from the towering Andes to the dense Amazon rainforests, unveiling the hidden gems of South America. - 🤝 Connect with the local communities, as Kate immerses herself in their rich traditions, fostering dialogue about sustainable practices. - 🌏 Delve into discussions about the urgency of environmental conservation, and the innovative approaches we can embrace. **Engage & Explore:** Hit the subscribe button and ring the bell 🔔 to stay updated with Kate's adventures and eco-initiatives. Your insights and experiences are valuable; share them with us in the comments below! **Championing Eco-conscious Expeditions:** Supporting this content amplifies the message of sustainable exploration. "In today's consumer driven mass produced society, little thought is given to the design, function and making process of the items we purchase." — James Marr, Founder — Luxembourg Museum Exhibition, 2023 "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 Bamboo, Bicycles, and the Bigger Picture The long-form sustainability video represents the BBC's most comprehensive attempt to place bamboo bicycle building in its full environmental and social context. The film covers not just the mechanics of building a bamboo frame but the material science of bamboo itself, the carbon economics of bicycle production, and the social dimensions of what it means to build rather than buy. Bamboo sequesters more carbon per hectare than most tree species, grows to harvestable size in three to five years (compared to 30–50 years for hardwood timber), and can be harvested without killing the plant. A bamboo bicycle frame built with bio-epoxy and flax fibre has a carbon footprint approximately 90% lower than an equivalent carbon fibre frame — a material that requires energy-intensive industrial processes and is effectively non-recyclable at end of life. The bicycle itself is one of the most carbon-efficient forms of transport ever devised — approximately 50 times more energy-efficient per passenger-kilometre than a car, and with zero operational emissions. Combining the most efficient form of transport with the most sustainable structural frame material is not a compromise: it is the logical conclusion of taking sustainability seriously. The film also addresses the social dimension: the BBC's workshops operate on a knowledge-sharing model that prioritises accessibility over profit maximisation. Building skills are democratised — made available to anyone who wants to learn, regardless of technical background. This model, combined with materials that can be grown rather than mined, points toward a different relationship between people and the objects they use.

body: My name is Jock and this summer I will be embarking on a cycling journey over 3,000km from London, England to Bergen, Norway on a bike I made to raise money for the prevention of young suicide. This trip is dedicated to my friend Joe who took his life at the beginning of 2022. PLEASE DONATE BY VISITING - https://www.justgiving.com/page/jstancer-l2b I met Joe right at the beginning of my university life along with many other fantastic people. Joe was a close friend whom I lived with for well over a year and was someone who, regardless of the situation, could always bring a smile to the faces of all those around him. Over the course of knowing Joe, many of those who spent time with him such as myself and many others gained more fond memories of the time we spent together that I could count, be it through the conversations and jokes or adventures and misadventures. I had never before met anyone like Joe, with all the memories I have of him being ones that will never fade, and I can’t imagine that I will meet anyone else like Joe ever again. When I found out what had happened, the feeling could only be described as though there was an immense absence that was harrowing to the point where it felt surreal. Unfortunately, suicide is something that is far too common, and I hope that through this fundraising event, even in a small part, it may go on to help others. The charity I have chosen for the money raised to go to is PAPYRUS, which is the national UK Charity for the Prevention of Young Suicide. During 2018, over 1,800 young people in the UK took their own lives and young suicide remains the largest killer of those under the age of 35. There is still so much that needs to be done to be able to provide the support for those who need it which is why all the money raised will be going to PAPYRUS. Our innovative approach transitioned from a labor-intensive flax lug prototype to a refined lug concept, reducing construction time by 90%. By leveraging bamboo and
body: E-Cargo Trike Evolution At Bamboo Bicycle we help people to build there own bicycles from scratch, Our neighbour is the contemporary equivalent of the classic milkman, delivering milk and bread using e-cargo bikes. However, the costs of these bikes were a hurdle to there growth. Challenged by this, we embarked on a mission to design an e-cargo delivery bike from the ground up. In our research, we examined numerous designs featuring different components like boxes, canopies, and drivetrains. We noticed significant design shortcomings. While some were sturdy, they lacked user-friendliness and ergonomic considerations. Many canopy designs were overly rigid, leading to excessive vibrations and compromised visibility. The component choices in many models left much to be desired, with subpar parts repurposed from cheap motorcycles. Additionally, the predominant drivetrain designs often had a single drive wheel, resulting in undue wear on the bearings and chain. After extensive research and enjoyable test rides, we crafted our design objectives: - A robust all-wheel drive differential. - Hydraulic discs with a dual-lever system. - Strengthening through the incorporation of Guadua Bamboo (100mm). - A load capacity of 250KG. - Utilization of standard bicycle components wherever feasible. - Creation of the rear box using recyclable modular sheets for easy adaptability. - Vibration reduction to protect the cargo and ensure rider comfort. From our previous venture into building bamboo bikes using flax connections, we recognized bamboo's strength, confirmed by exhaustive tests in collaboration with universities testing facilities. This technique became our choice as it eliminated the need for initial investments in moulds or welding—making it ideal for prototyping. We meticulously designed the complete bicycle ensuring the main chassis fit comfortably within major bike lanes, and did not exceed 1m by 2.5m dimensions. For the delivery box, we selected a recyclable, lightweight honeycomb material supplied as sheet material. Its design simplicity means shapes can be modified based on delivery needs, and it's easily shipped for DIY assembly at home. Given the variable weather conditions of Northern Europe, ensuring rider comfort was paramount. Our canopy, crafted from laminated bamboo, is both durable and flexible, moving in harmony with the trike while maintaining its form. Optimal visibility was a key design criterion. Our final design showcases the potential of a modest budget paired with innovative materials and expertise. The mid-drive motor ensures reduced maintenance, and our choice of an internal gear hub permits a consistent, durable chainline. The primary chassis is impressively robust and supports versatile box adaptability. As we look ahead, our goal is to diminish the build time by 90% via a modular system with pre-fabricated lugs, simplifying the assembly process, and enabling anyone to construct a trike tailored to their delivery needs. As we continue to refine our design, we're eager to collaborate. If our journey intrigues you, please reach out. We're excited to partner with like-minded enthusiasts in the next stages. title: NEW VIDEO - BUILDING THE FRONT TRIANGLE
summary: New video series! building the front triangle.
body: New video: How to build the front triangle of your bamboo bicycle frame — the most critical stage of your build. The front triangle is the heart of your bamboo bicycle frame. It consists of the down tube, top tube, head tube, and seat tube — the four main tubes that form the primary structural diamond. Getting the front triangle right sets up the entire rest of the build, and this new video walks you through every step in real time. "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 Why the Front Triangle Matters The front triangle determines your frame's geometry: head tube angle, stack height, reach, and standover clearance all come from how the front triangle is assembled. In a bamboo frame, the natural variation of each culm means every front triangle is subtly unique — this is not a flaw but a feature. Your frame will flex and respond in a way no machine-made frame can replicate. What the Video Covers Selecting the right bamboo culms for each tube position Setting up the alignment jig to your custom geometry Mitring tube ends for a tight joint fit Inserting chromoly dropouts and head tube inserts Tacking the frame with initial wraps before full lug application Checking frame alignment before and after tacking Common mistakes and how to correct them Key Tips from the Video The most common mistake builders make when constructing the front triangle is rushing the jig setup. Taking an extra 30 minutes to ensure the jig is perfectly aligned and level will save hours of remediation later. Check alignment from multiple angles — front, side, and top — before committing to any resin application. Bamboo culm selection is equally critical. The down tube carries the highest compressive load during riding, so choose a culm with consistent wall thickness and no visible cracks. The top tube carries primarily tensile loads and can be slightly lighter — but don't compromise on quality here either. "Founded in London in 2012 by James Marr, bamboo is said to have ideal properties for bike construction with its 'excellent vibration dampening effects', resistance to stress and durability." — road.cc, December 2020 Watch the full front triangle build video on the Bamboo Bicycle Club YouTube channel, and see the complete build series playlist for all stages from bamboo selection to final finishing.

body: New video series: Building a 20" cargo bike from bamboo — the complete BBC build journey. This new video series documents the complete build of a 20" wheel bamboo cargo bike — one of the most ambitious and practical builds in the Bamboo Bicycle Club's history. Cargo bikes represent the frontier of bamboo bicycle engineering, combining the load-carrying demands of a working bicycle with the sustainable material properties that make bamboo so exciting as a frame material. "The current trend is for carbon frames that lack environmental credentials. Carbon uses more energy to produce than steel and is difficult to recycle. However, Bamboo is easy to grow and offsets its carbon footprint, combined with flax and bio composites it has the potential to offer a viable alternative." — Gravel Cyclist, April 2021 Why a Cargo Bike? Cargo bikes are transforming urban transport. With e-assist options now widely available and the growing movement away from car dependency in cities, a well-built cargo bike can replace a van for many everyday journeys. Building one from bamboo takes this sustainability proposition even further — a frame material that is carbon-neutral, rapidly renewable, and fully biodegradable at end of life. The 20" Wheel Specification The 20" wheel configuration gives the cargo bike a lower centre of gravity, essential for stability when loaded. The smaller wheels also allow a longer wheelbase without making the bike unwieldy — critical for the extended front loading platform. Key specifications include: 20" front and rear wheels with wide-section tyres for load stability Extended bamboo top tube for front cargo platform mounting Reinforced bottom bracket shell for higher pedalling loads Hydraulic disc brakes front and rear for reliable stopping when loaded Internally routed gear cables through bamboo tubes Custom dropouts with pannier rack mounts What the Video Series Covers The series follows the complete build from raw bamboo selection to finished, rideable cargo bike. Each episode covers a specific stage: bamboo preparation and geometry design; jig construction; front triangle assembly; rear triangle with extended chainstays; cargo platform fabrication; finishing and component installation; and final test ride loaded with real cargo. "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 Watch the full cargo bike build series on the Bamboo Bicycle Club YouTube channel. The series is ideal for experienced builders looking to push the limits of what's possible with bamboo.

title: New video series - complete build introduction.
summary: New series of build videos.
body: Introducing the Bamboo Bicycle Club complete build video series — your guide to building a bamboo bicycle from scratch. This introductory video sets the stage for the BBC's most comprehensive build series to date. Whether you're a complete beginner or an experienced cyclist who wants to understand the craft behind bamboo bicycle construction, this series covers everything you need to know — from selecting the right bamboo culms to taking your finished bike out for its first ride. "The whole goal of Bamboo Bicycle Club is to make bike-building accessible to everyone." — James Marr, Founder — Inside Time, November 2025 What the Series Covers The complete build series is structured around the BBC's workshop curriculum, adapted for self-guided learning at home. The series is divided into seven modules: Introduction to bamboo: Understanding the material — species selection, culm harvesting, curing and storage Geometry and design: Reading a geometry chart, adjusting for your body measurements, marking out tubes Jig setup: Building and setting up the alignment jig for your specific frame geometry Front triangle: Assembling the main diamond — down tube, top tube, head tube and seat tube Rear triangle: Chain stays, seat stays, and dropout installation Lugs and finishing: Wrapping joints with flax fibre, curing, sanding, and finishing Component installation: Fitting drivetrain, brakes, bars and wheels — making it rideable Who This Series Is For The series is designed for BBC home kit builders, but the techniques and principles apply to anyone interested in bamboo frame construction. Previous experience of bicycle mechanics is helpful but not essential — the series assumes no prior frame-building knowledge and explains every step from first principles. Tools needed throughout the series: workbench or stable table, hand saw or mitre saw, drill and bits, mixing cups and brushes for resin, sandpaper (80–400 grit), disposable gloves, and the BBC build manual included with your kit. title: My perilous 8,000-mile solo bike ride across South America
summary: What motivates a cyclist to spend 13 months riding a homemade bamboo bike from Colombia to Cape Horn? Kate Rawles relives her once-in-a-lifetime adventure
body: What motivates a cyclist to spend 13 months riding a homemade bamboo bike from Colombia to Cape Horn? Kate Rawles relives her once-in-a-lifetime adventure t was early February when I cycled through the small town of Taraza in northern Colombia, noticing a custard-yellow church in the square and merengue leaking from the windows of multicoloured houses. Not long after, the beat of the music still upping my pedalling rate, I rounded a corner in the heat and there they were, rearing up in front of me like a wall — the Andes mountains, or at least the northern end of the Cordillera Occidental, one of the three immense spines that track roughly northeast to southwest. I was in Colombia at the start of the Life Cycle: a largely solo bike ride the length of South America through six countries, following the line of the Andes, the longest mountain chain in the world. And I was about to begin a multi-day climb up into these Andean giants, then follow their spine all the way south. My route would take me from Cartagena on Colombia’s Caribbean coastline, palm trees swaying against the turquoise ocean, to the spiky white peaks of the Peruvian Cordillera Blanca; from cloud and rainforests, some of the most life-rich habitats on Earth, to the Bolivian salt flats and the Atacama desert, before finishing in Ushuaia, Argentina. I’d started my 13-month journey by crossing the Atlantic on a cargo ship, a privileged glimpse into the largely invisible world that underpins our modern, industrialised civilisations. The other two passengers and I spent the eleven-day passage roaming the cargo decks, revelling in the extra hour of sleep and daily increase in sunshine as we powered west, and swaying to the bow for the sunset flying-fish watch. The acres of containers being loaded and unloaded off ships every time we docked offered a compelling visual image of the madness of the sheer quantity of stuff in transit around the world. Ironically that same voyage reduced the environmental impact of my journey; my carbon footprint was about 50kg compared with two tonnes for a return transatlantic flight. Kate Rawles built her bike after taking a course in London This was especially important to me because the heart of the Life Cycle journey was an exploration of biodiversity — what it is, what’s happening to it, why it matters and above all, what can be done to protect it — and climate change is an increasingly significant driver of the current catastrophic rate at which we are losing it. My ride took me through the subject I was exploring. And, on a bike, you are really in the landscapes you travel through. This can be as heartbreaking as it is wonderful. In the Ecuadorian Amazon rainforest, I experienced the diversity and abundance of life — and its indisputable value — in a way that is visceral. From the azure flash of blue morpho butterflies, to hundreds of parrots descending noisily through liana-crowded trees, to the caiman whose half-closed eyes were just visible above a long, mostly submerged snout, a rugged grey back stretched out like a tyre tread just above the brown water. It leaves you with an absolute certainty that rainforests are vital. Then rounding a corner, this time on a boat, gas flares. To confront the reality of oil-drilling in the Yasuni National Park, one of the most biodiverse places on Earth in one of the most biodiverse continents, is to be confronted with the short-sighted stupidity of economic activity that undermines our own life-support system. The highlights, however, included learning more about the intricate interactions and interdependencies that underpin life the world-over; feasting my eyes on astonishing plants and animals; and meeting a range of brilliant people working to protect it all. In Colombia I visited a project that worked with the local community to conserve endangered, pint-sized titi monkeys by collecting waste plastic and turning it into highly durable — and sellable — fence posts: the income helped reverse

title: KATE RAWLES NEW BOOK!
summary: We worked with Kate to build her own bicycle. All the materials where sourced in the UK making it the lowest carbon footprint bicycle possible. She then cycle 8000 miles!
body: We worked with Kate to build her own bicycle. All the materials where sourced in the UK making it the lowest carbon footprint bicycle possible. She then cycle 8000 miles! 'A gripping read for anyone who cares about what we're doing to the planet and how we can change it' DAVID SHUKMAN, FORMER BBC NEWS SCIENCE EDITOR 'Searing observations focused on our need to protect biodiversity - A tour de force' SIR TIM SMIT OBE, CO-FOUNDER OF THE EDEN PROJECT 'An informative, uplifting and truly important book' JONATHON PORRITT, AUTHOR AND CAMPAIGNER One woman's journey through South America - and the devastating story of our planet's disappearing biodiversity Pedalling hard for thirteen months, eco adventurer Kate Rawles cycled the length of the Andes on an eccentric bicycle she built herself. The Life Cycle charts her mission to find out why biodiversity is so important, what's happening to it, and what can be done to protect it. From the Pacific Ocean to rainforests and salt flats, Kate learns that armadillos can cross rivers by holding their breath, that Colombia has more species of birds than North America and Europe combined, and that in threatening species and ecosystems, we're tearing down our own life support system. En route, she witnesses the devastation of goldmining and oil drilling but finds hope in the incredible people working to regenerate habitats and communities. As she reaches the 'end of the world', she realises that to tackle biodiversity loss we all have a role to play. ORDER HERE - https://www.amazon.co.uk/Life-Cycle-Miles-Andes-Bamboo/dp/178578787X "In today's consumer driven mass produced society, little thought is given to the design, function and making process of the items we purchase." — James Marr, Founder — Luxembourg Museum Exhibition, 2023 "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 The Life Cycle: Kate Rawles and Her BBC-Built Bamboo Bicycle Kate Rawles' book The Life Cycle documents her 8,000-mile solo journey from Colombia to Cape Horn — one of the most demanding cycling adventures ever undertaken — aboard Woody, her BBC-built bamboo bicycle. The book is not simply a cycling adventure memoir: it is a serious engagement with the biodiversity crisis, the state of the world's ecosystems, and the question of what responsible adventure travel looks like in an era of climate emergency. Kate chose a bamboo bicycle specifically because the material embodied the values she was trying to articulate through her journey. A frame grown from the earth, built by hand, made from materials that will return to the earth — carried through landscapes under extreme environmental pressure — made an argument through its presence that no manufactured bicycle could make. Woody became a character in the story as much as a tool of transport. The BBC built Kate's frame specifically for the Cordillera expedition: reinforced joints for the high-altitude passes of the Andes; custom geometry to accommodate heavy touring loads; a conservative head tube angle for stability on unpaved mountain descents. The frame survived the entire 8,000 miles without structural failure — a testament to both the material and the build quality. The Life Cycle was published to critical acclaim and was shortlisted for multiple outdoor writing awards. It introduced bamboo bicycle building to a readership primarily engaged with environmental writing — and made the BBC's work visible to an audience that cares deeply about the intersection of human activity and the natural world.

title: TEAM BUILDING WITH GM MOTORS
summary: We built 10 frames with 50 people in 4 hours with GM motors Zurich
body: Bamboo Bicycle Team Building with GM Motors in Zurich a unique team-building activity that involves building bicycles using bamboo as the primary material. This activity is designed to promote teamwork, communication, problem-solving, and collaboration among participants. We built 10 frames with 50 people in 4 hours! During the bamboo bicycle team building activity, participants where divided into small teams and given the task of building a functioning bicycle frame using bamboo as the frame material. The teams where encouraged to work together, communicate effectively, and use their problem-solving skills to overcome any challenges that may arise during the building process. "Bamboo Bicycle Club taps into 'the IKEA effect' — that extra bit of affection people reserve for objects they put together themselves." — Financial Times, September 2025 "Bamboo Bicycle Club follows a niche-manufacturing business model that prioritises knowledge-sharing over profit-making retail, charging for workshops and kits rather than pre-made products." — Huck Magazine, 2023 Team Building with GM Motors — Why Corporate Bamboo Builds Work Corporate team-building activities often struggle with a fundamental problem: they feel artificial. Participants know they're doing an exercise, and the artificial nature of the activity undermines the genuine connection it's meant to create. Bamboo bicycle building sidesteps this problem entirely — because the task is real, the outcome is real, and the challenge is genuinely shared. The GM Motors team brought a cross-functional group to the BBC workshop: engineers, marketers, operations staff, and senior leaders working side by side on identical challenges. The bicycle frame doesn't care about job title or departmental hierarchy — it demands the same precision, patience, and collaborative problem-solving from everyone. The BBC workshop structure is designed to surface natural team dynamics. The build requires different skills at different stages: strategic thinking during geometry planning, precision during tube selection and measurement, creative problem-solving when joints don't fit as expected, and calm under pressure during the time-sensitive resin application stages. Watching how a team navigates these different challenges — who steps up, who supports, who communicates — reveals more about team dynamics than any structured exercise. The GM Motors team left the workshop with completed bicycle frames, a shared experience of genuine accomplishment, and — most importantly — a new understanding of each other. The BBC has delivered team-building workshops for companies including Four Seasons Hotels, Macallan Whisky, and many others. Each workshop is tailored to the group's size, objectives, and time available. To enquire about a corporate BBC team-building workshop, contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org.

title: BAMBOO BICYCLE CLUB AT KEW GARDENS
