The surfaces change constantly, the gradients surprise you, the descents test your nerve. Having a bike you built yourself means understanding exactly how to fix it when something needs adjusting. The natural bamboo looks perfect against that terracotta brick. There's a colour harmony that feels accidental but probably isn't — Paul clearly has an eye for this stuff. Building your own bike means moments like this aren't frustrations; they're conversations. The bike tells you what it needs, you listen, you respond. Partnership rather than ownership. Gears sorted, Italy awaits. Andiamo, Paul. 🇮🇹

title: Build by Aurelian for his girlfriend! Nice guy! .
body: Aurelian built this for his girlfriend. That's the kind of project that raises the stakes — you're not just building for yourself, you're building for someone whose opinion matters more than your own. She's riding it here, puffer jacket against the chill, heading somewhere in what looks like suburban France. The teal painted lugs pop against natural bamboo, a colour choice that clearly landed well. Action shots capture what static photos miss: the posture of someone comfortable on their bike, the relaxed grip, the forward lean that says "this is easy." First rides are often awkward. This one clearly isn't. Building a bike for someone else means guessing at their preferences, asking questions you might not think to ask yourself, paying attention to details that wouldn't bother you but might bother them. When it works, it's the best kind of gift. The spec is practical: disc brakes for confident stopping, comfortable geometry for daily riding, flat bars for an upright position. This is a bike built for actually using, not posing with. Aurelian called himself a "nice guy" for doing this. He's underselling it. Building someone a bike is a declaration of care that lasts years longer than flowers or dinners. Properly thoughtful. Well done, Aurelian. 💚

title: We're well into cyclocross season! If your looking for a durable Gravel or Cross bike then bamboo is
body: Cyclocross season means this: snow on the ground, dead leaves still clinging to branches, and a gravel bike that doesn't care about either. The blue painted lugs add contrast that works beautifully in this winter forest. Against the white snow and brown leaves, the natural bamboo and blue accents create a colour palette that looks almost planned. Apidura bags — frame pack and saddlebag — suggest this isn't just a CX racer but a bikepacking-capable machine. Mud on the tyres confirms it's been through the conditions, not just posed in them. Building a bike for CX means accepting abuse. These frames get shouldered over barriers, dropped in transitions, ridden through conditions that would make road cyclists weep. Bamboo handles it because the fibres flex rather than fatigue. Winter riding demands commitment. Cold hands, numb feet, that moment when you question why you're not on the sofa. Then you look around at scenery like this and remember: this is why. The setting is perfect woodland: single trees providing framing, the trail visible in the background, that magical quality of winter light that photographers chase and riders happen upon. CX season is short but sweet. Ride it while you can. ❄️

title: Build by @aleportante finished using a #sram groupset and #huntwheels.
body: Red. Bold, unapologetic red. Alex's build makes a statement with painted lugs that demand attention against natural bamboo tubes. The spec matches the confidence: SRAM groupset, Hunt wheels, Apidura top tube bag. This is a build where everything was chosen deliberately, from the red bar tape echoing the frame accents to the component spec that backs up the aesthetics. Standing in late summer grassland, the bike looks ready for exactly what it was built for: long rides on mixed terrain, the kind of routes where road turns to gravel turns to track turns to adventure. Hunt wheels have become the gravel standard for good reason: they're built for abuse, tubeless-ready, and look the business while handling the substance. Paired with SRAM's gravel-focused groupsets, this bike is ready for serious riding. The colour contrast works because it's decisive. Not a hint of red, not a subtle accent, but full commitment to the choice. That's confidence. Flared drops give extra control on rough descents — the slight outward angle at the drops provides leverage when the trail gets choppy. A detail that matters more than most riders realise until they need it. Red bamboo done right. Ready to ride. 🔴

title: Paul with his finished bamboo road bike 🚴‍♀️ built at a weekend workshop, join now to creat
body: That smile. That wave. That energy. Paul isn't just happy with his bike — he's absolutely buzzing with it. The Pro Cycle Hire Mallorca jersey matches the orange painted lugs perfectly. Coordination like this doesn't happen by accident — Paul clearly planned this moment, wanted the colours to align, wanted the photo to pop. And it does. Deep section ICAN carbon wheels, brown leather bar wrap for warmth against all that speed, road geometry built for Spanish climbs. This is a bike designed to hang with the serious riders on Mallorca's famous roads. The grin tells you everything about how the build went. Workshop complete, bike assembled, first photos taken — and the result exceeded expectations. That's the feeling we work towards. Mallorca has earned its reputation as cycling's paradise. The roads climb into mountains, descend to coasts, wind through villages where cyclists are welcome. Taking a handmade bamboo bike there is taking something special to somewhere special. Those carbon wheels aren't cheap. That jersey isn't either. Paul clearly invests in his cycling — and now he's invested in building his own frame to complete the picture. Pure joy, captured perfectly. Keep smiling, Paul. 🧡

title: Bamboo Bicycle Build
body: Sometimes the best photos are the simplest: bike against wall, nothing competing for attention, just clean lines and honest construction. The concrete background sets this gravel build apart. Natural bamboo tubes, black flax lugs, Panaracer tyres ready for mixed terrain. The spec is thoughtful without being flashy — disc brakes, comfortable geometry, clearance for when the road deteriorates. Studio shots reveal details that get lost in action photos. The curve of the top tube, the proportions of the triangle, the way the dark lugs anchor the visual weight at the joints. This builder clearly understood that bamboo bikes photograph well against industrial textures. The component choices speak to experience: drop bars for long rides, enough gearing for hills, tyres that roll fast on tarmac but grip on gravel. Nothing exotic, everything functional. A bike built to ride rather than admire. Gravel bikes have become the default for people who want one bike that does everything. Road rides? Yes. Fire trails? Yes. That shortcut through the park? Obviously. This frame handles all of it. Workshop complete, first ride pending, adventures loading. 🎋

title: Toby touring on his bamboo gravel frame. Bamboo combined with flax is well suited to touring as bamb
body: Whitewell 2. Clitheroe 11. Lancaster 15. Trough of Bowland ahead. The fingerposts of northern England point in every direction, and Toby's bamboo gravel bike is ready for all of them. This is proper British touring: red Ortlieb pannier loaded with essentials, tan-wall tyres gripping the verge, ferns reaching into the frame of a photo that could only happen in summer. The Forest of Bowland sits at the heart of some of England's quietest riding. The white painted lugs pop against natural bamboo — a colour choice that works surprisingly well against all that green landscape. Drop bars with white tape continue the theme, giving the bike a distinctive look without trying too hard. Touring in the UK means dealing with hills, wet roads, and navigation that assumes you can read a fingersign while moving. The gravel setup handles all of it: wide enough tyres for unpredictable surfaces, gearing for climbing, position comfortable enough for all-day rides. Lancaster one way, Slaidburn another, decisions everywhere. That's the joy of touring — every junction offers choices, every choice leads somewhere worth going. Bowland awaits. Keep pedalling, Toby. 🇬🇧

title: Build by Hasan. SRAM aphex groupset with lugs finished in black. Thru axle rear dropout.
body: The details matter. Gold pinstripes on black chainstays, the mechanical precision of a SRAM Apex derailleur, Continental Gatorskins chosen for puncture resistance rather than speed. Hasan's build shows restraint that speaks to confidence. Black lugs finished cleanly, that subtle gold accent adding warmth without demanding attention. This is a builder who understood that too many colours compete while focused choices harmonise. Close-up photos reveal what wide shots miss: the quality of the wrapping, the tension of the chain, the cleanliness of the cassette before its first real ride. This drivetrain is ready for thousands of kilometres. Gatorskins are a statement of intent. Not the fastest tyres, not the lightest, but arguably the most reliable. Commuters choose them. Randonneurs choose them. People who hate punctures choose them. Hasan clearly has places to be. The blue stripe at the base of the frame — Greece colours, perhaps? — adds one more considered detail to a build full of them. Excellence lives in the details. Hasan found it. 🔧

title: Good morning, early start at our London workshop! Will have these 6 frames all finished by 5pm! .
body: Good morning from the workshop. Six frames, six stages, six stories unfolding at once. This is what an early start at our London workshop looks like: frames in jigs, tubes being aligned, different builds progressing through different stages. The numbered photos track progress — 1 through 5, then the full spread of organised chaos. Each frame represents someone's vision becoming real. The tubes are cut, the geometry is set, the joints are wrapped, and gradually a pile of bamboo transforms into something rideable. Workshop days move fast. Instructors circulate between builds, answering questions, demonstrating techniques, catching errors before they become problems. The collective energy of multiple builders creates momentum — seeing others progress motivates your own work. Tools line the walls: handsaws, clamps, measuring devices, the accumulated equipment of years of frame building. Nothing fancy, everything functional. You don't need expensive machinery to build a bamboo bike — just patience, guidance, and attention to detail. By day's end, some of these frames will be wrapped and curing. Others will need another session. All of them will eventually become bikes that someone rides with pride. Workshop life, one frame at a time. ☕

title: Just been helping Benjamin lacquer up his world touring frame. He built as a home build and popped i
body: Fresh lacquer, still drying. Benjamin's world touring frame sits on protective paper, black lugs glistening as the finish cures. This moment — just after lacquering — is where anticipation peaks. The frame is structurally complete but not yet rideable. The lugs have that wet-look shine that will settle into satin. Everything is almost ready. World touring demands specific considerations. Extra clearance for wider tyres. Multiple mounting points for racks and bottles. Geometry that prioritises comfort over speed because when you're riding across continents, daily comfort trumps hourly performance. Benjamin built this with that journey in mind. The proportions read as serious equipment — not a weekend toy but a tool for covering serious distance over serious time. The overhead view reveals the triangle clearly: top tube flowing into seat tube, down tube anchoring the whole structure. Clean lines, confident joints, a frame ready for whatever comes next. Lacquer cures, patience wears, adventure approaches. Soon this frame will carry Benjamin to places none of us can predict. World touring frame, world-ready builder. 🌍

title: Bike of the year 5/11! #bamboobicyclegravel
body: Bike of the Year 2018. The badge says it all — this gravel build beat every other frame we saw that year. The camo bar tape started a trend. After this photo appeared, we saw more builds experimenting with wild patterns, military aesthetics, tape choices that made statements. Sometimes one build changes what everyone else considers possible. Against the corten steel backdrop, the natural bamboo and black lugs create a palette that photographers dream about. Warm rust, golden bamboo, dark accents — the colours work because they're all organic tones. The spec is serious gravel: disc brakes, clearance for proper tyres, geometry that handles all-day rides on mixed terrain. The Tour de Sands sticker suggests an owner who knows their events. Winning Bike of the Year requires more than just good construction. It needs vision — that extra element that makes people stop and look twice. This builder found it in the details: the camo tape, the confident stance, the way everything comes together. 2018 was a good year for bamboo builds. This one set the standard. Award-winning for a reason. 🏆

title: Build by Tamas.  3 speed with a belt drive
body: Three speeds and a belt drive. Tamas built simple on purpose, and the result speaks for itself. Royal blue painted lugs make a statement against natural bamboo. The tan-wall tyres continue the warm palette. Standing in his Patagonia fleece against industrial shutters, Tamas looks like someone who's thought carefully about what cycling means to him — and decided less is more. Belt drives eliminate chain maintenance entirely. Internal hub gears remove derailleur hassle. Three speeds handles flat terrain perfectly. This is a bike designed for city riding without the complexity of performance builds. Sometimes the best bikes are the ones that disappear into daily life. No special clothes required, no pre-ride checks, no post-ride cleaning. Just get on and go. Tamas clearly understood this. The colour coordination runs deep: blue lugs matching the quieter tones of his fleece, tan tyres warming the whole composition. Deliberate choices that add up to a cohesive look. Simplicity is harder than complexity. Anyone can add features. Knowing what to leave out requires confidence. Tamas found that balance. Three gears, zero hassle, infinite style. 💙

title: Women’s bamboo road bike out in France. .
body: Late autumn in France. Bare trees, fallen leaves, a quiet road winding through woodland. And a bamboo road bike waiting by the verge. White painted lugs give this women's build a distinctive character against the muted browns of the forest floor. The bike almost disappears into the scene — natural material in a natural setting, the kind of photo that feels unplanned even when it clearly wasn't. French roads are made for cycling. The network of quiet D-roads connects villages, climbs through forests, descends to valleys. This build is specced for exactly that: drop bars for efficient position, disc brakes for confident descents, geometry that says "road bike" without saying "race bike." The frame size suggests this was built for a specific rider — geometry tailored rather than compromised. That's what workshop builds offer: not stock sizing but actual fit, dimensions chosen for the person rather than the average. Somewhere nearby, the rider is probably stretching, checking the phone, enjoying a moment off the bike before the next kilometres. These pauses are part of touring — the quiet appreciation of where cycling takes you. French woodland, perfect setting, adventure continues. 🇫🇷

title: Tandem build by Marco in the Netherlands. All coming together, built using a custom home build kit.
body: From above, Marco's tandem build spreads across the workbench like a puzzle coming together. Frame triangle assembled, chainstays laid out, the geometry drawing visible beneath the bamboo. Tandems are ambitious builds. Double the length, double the joints, double the complexity. Two head tubes, two bottom brackets, everything needing to align across a frame that's longer than most single bikes by a significant margin. The overhead view shows the planning: tubes matched to the paper drawing beneath, stays waiting to be positioned, the careful progression from concept to construction. Marco is building this in the Netherlands, adding to our community of builders across Europe. Workshop details populate the edges of the frame: tools, tape, scissors, the small equipment that makes builds possible. OSB board workbench, coffee cups nearby, the environment of serious making. Tandems carry two people, which means building for a relationship as much as for a rider. The conversations that happen on a tandem are different — constant communication, shared effort, destinations reached together. Coming together in the Netherlands. Keep building, Marco. 🇳🇱

title: Road bike build by Hugo in France. All our bikes can be fitted with racks from round the world touri
body: Lake Annecy at sunset. Mountains catching alpenglow. A bamboo bike resting against a bench while someone breathes in one of the most beautiful views in France. Hugo built this road frame and brought it here — to the place where the Alps meet the water, where the light at golden hour paints the peaks pink and orange. The B'Twin pannier suggests a longer journey, the Casco helmet speaks to proper riding, the scene screams "this is why we cycle." Some photos justify entire builds. This is one of them. Whatever Hugo invested in time, materials, and workshop fees paid back the moment this view appeared around a corner. Lake Annecy draws cyclists from across Europe. The circuit around the lake is a classic, the climbs into the mountains legendary, the descents technical enough to demand respect. Bringing a handmade bamboo bike elevates the experience from riding to pilgrimage. The bamboo tubes glow in the same warm light hitting the mountains. Natural material, natural scenery, natural moment. Everything aligned. This is what bikes are for. Getting us to places like this. Letting us stop and stare. Reminding us why we pedal. Annecy at sunset. Worth every kilometre. 🏔️

title: Team Limitless crossing the Pyrenees. Team limitless built some 29er touring bikes with is over the
body: Camping at altitude in the Pyrenees. Two loaded bikes, a picnic spread on the ground, snow-capped peaks in every direction. Team Limitless is exactly where they planned to be. This is what world touring looks like during the pauses: setting up camp at a col, unpacking food after a long climb, taking a moment to absorb views that made every pedal stroke worthwhile. Both bikes are built for this — bamboo frames carrying serious loads through serious mountains. The bags are stuffed with gear for self-sufficient travel: shelter, cooking equipment, the minimum necessities for moving through landscapes on your own terms. The Pyrenees offer some of Europe's most demanding cycling. The passes are high, the gradients steep, the descents technical. Crossing them on loaded touring bikes is an achievement worth documenting. One rider stands looking at the mountains, processing the scale of what they're doing. It's a reflective moment in an expedition that will include hundreds more. Every summit reached leads to another climb; every boundary crossed reveals new terrain. Team Limitless built their bikes specifically for this journey. The confidence of knowing your equipment comes from having made it yourself. Pyrenees conquered. More mountains ahead. Keep climbing. 🏔️

title: Build by Toby and his Dad Jim. Built over a weekend workshop and finished at home.
body: Father and son, weekend workshop, one finished bike. Toby and Jim built this together, and the result shows what happens when two generations collaborate. Classic fixed-gear aesthetics: Aventon wheels, brown leather bar wrap matching the Brooks saddle, polished silver components against natural bamboo. The styling nods to vintage while the construction is entirely modern. Building a bike together creates memories that outlast the frame itself. The conversations over alignment, the shared problem-solving, the quiet satisfaction of seeing something emerge from raw materials — these become part of the bike's story. The black painted lugs provide contrast without competing with the bamboo. Simple, confident, clean. This is a builder (or builders) who understood that restraint creates elegance. Weekend workshops are intense: two days of focused work, learning techniques that take practice to master. Having a partner helps — one person can hold while another wraps, questions get discussed rather than just pondered. The finished bike leans against the wall, casting a shadow that suggests it's ready to move. Whatever Toby and Jim talked about during construction, they'll talk about again every time this bike gets ridden. Built together, memories made. Nice one, both of you. 👨‍👦

title: Interested build by Daniel! Any when used a @laufcycling fork before, are they worth it?
body: That's what a properly ridden bike looks like. Daniel's "Giant Panda" build is caked in mud, leaning against a rusted farm gate, somewhere in flat British farmland. The Lauf fork is the standout choice here — that distinctive leaf-spring suspension that smooths out rough terrain without the weight and complexity of traditional forks. It's bold, unusual, and clearly effective given how hard this bike has been ridden. Mud on the tyres, mud on the frame, mud spattering up the seat tube. This isn't a garage queen; it's a working tool that gets used in all conditions. The "Giant Panda" name painted on the downtube adds personality. The setting is proper British gravel: pylons on the horizon, stubble fields stretching to nothing, the kind of flat openness that means wind in your face no matter which direction you're heading. Rust on the gate, rust on the bike isn't — the finish is holding up even after serious abuse. That's what matters: not how clean a bike stays but how well it performs when conditions turn difficult. Giant Panda, small conditions. Keep riding, Daniel. 🐼

title: 🚴‍♂️ Ever thought about building a bamboo bike? Our latest blog dives into one cyclist's jo
body: Forest green lugs, orange bar tape, pine needle carpet. This gravel build absolutely sings in its natural habitat. The colour scheme is inspired: deep green painted lugs matching the forest, orange tape adding warmth, tan-wall tyres bridging the two. Standing among pine trees, the bike looks like it grew there rather than being placed for a photo. Tan sidewalls have become the gravel standard for good reason — they soften the visual impact of black rubber, complement natural bamboo perfectly, and age gracefully as they pick up trail dust. The spec is serious gravel: flared drops for control on rough terrain, disc brakes for confident stopping, enough clearance for whatever the forest floor throws up. Topeak saddlebag suggests someone planning longer rides. Pine forests offer perfect riding: soft surfaces, dappled light, the smell of resin warming in sunlight. The trails wind without destinations, every junction an opportunity to choose a new direction. Building a bike with painted lugs means making a commitment to colour. Get it wrong and you're stuck with it; get it right and you have something like this — a frame that belongs in certain landscapes. Forest green dreams, perfectly executed. 🌲

title: Bike packing on a bamboo #cyclocross, build by @andrzejbraga using a home build kit.
body: Deep snow, high mountains, brilliant sunshine. Andrzej's cyclocross build is bikepacking somewhere that makes most riders' "epic" rides look like commutes. The photo is stunning: bike silhouetted against fresh snow, mountain peaks framing the horizon, the sun creating long shadows across untouched white. This isn't a road — there's no road. Just Andrzej, his bike, and terrain that would stop most expeditions. The frame bag and saddlebag carry enough gear for self-sufficiency in conditions where help isn't coming. Fat tyres handle the snow, disc brakes work regardless of temperature, the bamboo frame absorbs the constant chatter of mixed terrain. Cyclocross frames make excellent adventure bikes. The clearances handle conditions road bikes can't touch, the geometry balances carrying capacity with handling. Add bikepacking bags and you can go anywhere. There's a particular type of cyclist who seeks conditions like this: not despite the difficulty but because of it. The harder it is to reach somewhere, the more meaningful the arrival. Andrzej built a bike and took it to places that test everything. That's the point of making your own equipment — trusting it enough to push limits. Snow, sun, summit. Absolutely epic. 🏔️

title: Very nice gravel build by David. Finished with @hunt.beyond with @campagnolo_ekar
body: Dark green lugs with gold striping, orange bar tape, "BAMBOO BICYCLE CLUB" running down the head tube. David's gravel build knows exactly what it is. The colour palette is rally-car inspired: British racing green with gold accents, that satisfying combination that works in motorsport and works equally well on bicycles. The orange tape adds the finishing touch of personality. Hunt wheels handle the heavy lifting — their gravel-specific builds have become the default choice for serious riders. Paired with tan-wall tyres and positioned against a wooden country fence, this bike looks ready for any lane it encounters. Rural England provides the backdrop: trees, hedgerow, that slightly damp quality of light that suggests rain was recent or imminent. Gravel riding conditions, in other words. The saddlebag and bottle setup suggest rides that push past the quick-loop distance. This is a bike for exploration, for lanes that don't quite appear on maps, for riding until you're not sure where you are anymore. The BBC branding on the head tube is a badge of origin: built at our workshop, using our methods, by someone who learned the craft and made something remarkable. Green, gold, and ready to roll. Beautiful work, David. 🎋

title: Bamboo Gravel frame fully loaded in Slovenia.
body: The Julian Alps rise behind Lake Jasna, and a fully loaded bamboo bike rests against a pine tree. Slovenia delivers views like this casually, around corners, as if extraordinary scenery were nothing special. The frame is loaded for touring: saddlebag, frame bag, bottles, all the gear needed for multi-day adventures through one of Europe's most underrated cycling destinations. The orange bag adds a colour pop against all that alpine green. Slovenia combines Italian drama with Austrian organisation at a fraction of either's tourist density. The roads climb through forests to passes, descend to lakes of impossible blue-green, connect villages where cyclists are welcomed with curiosity rather than annoyance. The lake in the background is the kind of postcard scene that makes people question whether your photos are real. They are — Slovenia just looks like that. Bringing a handmade bamboo bike to terrain like this elevates the experience. Every view is framed differently when you're carrying something you built, every climb feels more significant when your equipment has a story. The helmet rests on the seat, suggesting a break for swimming or just admiring what's in front of the lens. Some views demand you stop moving. Slovenia summers, perfectly captured. 🇸🇮

title: New build by Craig. Gravel lugged build finished with a GRX groupset
body: Golden hour on a British field, a church steeple breaking the treeline, and Craig's teal-lugged gravel bike leaning against an oak tree. Photography doesn't get better than this. The colour of those lugs is perfect: somewhere between teal and petrol blue, catching the warm sunset light and glowing against natural bamboo. Hunt wheels and Schwalbe G-One tyres complete a spec built for serious gravel riding. The setting is quintessentially English: ploughed field, distant village, that quality of light that happens for about twenty minutes and makes photographers run for their cameras. Craig timed this perfectly. Flat bar gravel bikes offer a more upright position than drop-bar equivalents — comfortable for long rides, excellent visibility for traffic, relaxed enough for all-day exploration. The saddlebag suggests Craig plans to be out for a while. Oak trees make the best bike stands. The bark provides grip, the trunk won't scratch the frame, and there's something right about leaning organic materials against each other. The church steeple in the distance anchors the photo to place and time — a village that's been there for centuries, surrounded by fields worked for longer. Cycling connects us to landscapes like this. Perfect light, perfect build, perfect moment. 🌅

title: Gravel flat bar handlebar. Built by Becca for commuting. Can accommodate a upto a 50mm tyre. #pannie
body: Outside our workshop, Becca's commuter sits against the brick wall. Slate blue lugs, flat bars, her name written on the downtube. This is a bike built for daily life. Look closely and you'll see our logo in the window behind — this photo was taken right where the bike was made. There's symmetry in that: a build returning to its birthplace, documented before disappearing into city traffic. The colour scheme is subtle: muted blue-grey that works with any outfit, any season, any London weather. Not shouting for attention, just quietly getting things done. That's commuter design at its best. Flat bars make sense for urban riding. You sit higher, see further, react faster. The wide tyres handle potholes and tram tracks without drama. The geometry says "relaxed" rather than "racing." Having your name on the downtube matters. It transforms an object into something personal, a declaration that this bike belongs to someone specific. Becca built this, Becca rides this, Becca's name stays on it. The workshop churns out frames that scatter across the country. Some stay local. This one clearly does — we'll probably see it rolling past occasionally. Local builder, local rider, local bike. Proper. 🎋

title: Paul’s build of a lightweight #touringbicycle.
body: Camo bar tape, camo saddle, Tour de Sands sticker. Paul's lightweight touring build has serious character against that corten steel backdrop. The military aesthetic runs through the whole bike: greens and tans in the tape pattern, functional simplicity in the component choices, a stance that suggests readiness rather than decoration. Lightweight touring means going fast with what you need, not crawling under maximum load. That Tour de Sands sticker is a statement — one of the UK's best gravel events, and Paul clearly knows the scene. Building a bike specifically for this kind of riding shows commitment. The corten steel panels behind create the perfect backdrop: rust tones that complement the natural bamboo, industrial texture that contrasts with organic materials. Someone chose this location deliberately. Lightweight touring splits the difference between racing and loaded expedition. You carry enough to be self-sufficient but not so much that hills become suffering. The reward is covering ground quickly while still having what you need. The frame proportions are aggressive: lower front end, longer top tube, the geometry of someone who wants to cover miles efficiently. Military precision, touring ambition. Ready for the Sands. 🏜️

title: Nice #commuterbike build by Alex.
body: That forest green marbled finish on the lugs? Proper commitment to making something different. Alex built this commuter to handle London's unpredictable weather and potholed streets. The flat bar setup keeps things practical for daily riding, while the Hunt wheels with tubeless-ready Schwalbe G-One tyres mean punctures are mostly a thing of the past. What catches the eye immediately is the lug treatment. That dark green with the textured, almost camouflage-like finish creates serious visual interest against the natural bamboo tubes. It's a technique that takes patience — building up layers of resin with pigment, then sanding back to reveal depth. The carbon fork keeps the front end light and responsive, important when you're filtering through traffic or hopping curbs. And those platform pedals suggest this bike sees real daily use, not just weekend show-offs. There's something honest about a commuter build. No pretence about racing or adventure touring — just a bike that needs to get someone to work reliably, comfortably, and in style. The phone mount on the stem says it all: this is a working bike. The backdrop of that wooden fence and brick paving could be any London garden. Which is rather the point. A bamboo bike doesn't need to be exotic or precious. It can just be your bike. The one you ride every day. 🚲

title: New #cyclocross build by @the_shop_and_postoffice. Some nice customisations and very cool #laufforks
body: British winter riding captured in a single frame. Wet road, stone walls, mist rolling in, and a bamboo bike ready to tackle whatever the Dales throw at it. This cyclocross build by The Shop and Postoffice pairs some seriously thoughtful kit choices with frame-building skill. The Lauf suspension fork up front — that distinctive leaf-spring design — soaks up the rough stuff without adding complexity or weight. Perfect for the limestone tracks and farm roads of northern England. That saddle though. The teal and pink colourway looks like an Italian flag interpretation, adding a flash of Mediterranean colour to an otherwise moody scene. It's the kind of detail that makes a build personal rather than just functional. R500 wheels and chunky tyres suggest this bike lives for mixed terrain. Road to bridleway to muddy field crossing — the kind of riding that makes cyclocross bikes so versatile for British conditions. The natural bamboo finish keeps things subtle. No flashy lug colours here, just clean black joints that let the frame material speak for itself. Against those weathered stone walls, it looks like it belongs. Some bikes are built for sunny Instagram moments. This one clearly gets ridden in the rain, the cold, the grey. And that's rather the point of bamboo — it's not precious. It's tough. 🌧️

title: From the Videos to the Heathland — @tidzenga's Bamboo Gravel Build
body: The caption says it all: "Reading the stories and watching videos in which cyclists were riding..." And then @tidzenga went and built one themselves. What ended up in their hands is this — a clean gravel bike photographed against classic British heathland. Sandy soil, silver birch, open sky. The kind of terrain that rewards a light, responsive frame with proper off-road rubber. The build is done right. Natural bamboo tubes running from the lugged head tube down through the main triangle, with a 1x drivetrain keeping things simple — single chainring up front with a Shimano derailleur at the rear, the red body catching the light against the dark chain. DT Swiss wheels are laced up with Tufo Training Dry gravel tyres — a sensible choice for mixed-surface riding where you want performance without being precious. Look at the black carbon lugs at the head tube junction: neat, precisely fitted, the bamboo tubes cut clean and bonded in tight. The whole front end is confident and well-proportioned. A bottle cage on the down tube, one bidon ready for the ride. To the left of the frame, what looks like the edge of a wooden board is visible — possibly the BBC jig nearby, or just a piece of timber. Either way it's a nice reminder that this bike was literally assembled in pieces not long ago and is now out in a field looking like it's always existed. That's what gets people. The transformation from component parts to finished machine. From kit to a bike you're genuinely excited to ride. @tidzenga read the stories. Watched the videos. Then made it happen. That's the pattern. That's how most BBC builds start. Proper gravel energy. 🎋

title: Gravel lugged build fitted with #campagnolo #ekar.
body: Campagnolo Ekar and a bamboo frame. Italian precision meets sustainable craft, photographed against one of London's most iconic sporting venues. That's the Lee Valley VeloPark in the background — Zaha Hadid's swooping velodrome from the 2012 Olympics. And in the foreground, a gravel bike that proves bamboo builds can carry the finest components without breaking a sweat. The colour scheme here is bold. Teal lugs against natural bamboo is a combination we see fairly often, but that bright yellow fork changes everything. It's a risk — yellow can go wrong quickly — but here it works. The gum wall tyres tie the warm tones together, creating a cohesive palette that feels vintage-modern. Campagnolo's Ekar groupset was designed specifically for gravel racing. Thirteen speeds, a single chainring, and that distinctive Italian mechanical precision. It's not a cheap choice, but it's a statement: this bamboo frame is worthy of the best. The bars are wrapped in what looks like a matching pattern to the lugs — attention to detail that elevates the whole build. Same with the saddle choice, keeping things dark to let the frame and fork do the talking. Photographing a bike against the velodrome is cheating slightly. That building makes anything look good. But then again, this bike doesn't need the help. It would turn heads in any car park. 🏟️

title: Bamboo touring bike built by Doug. .
body: Racing green lugs, high-gloss finish, and proper touring geometry. Doug built a bike that looks ready to cross a continent. The setting here is pure contemporary London — corten steel panels, blue engineering brick, that distinctively 2010s urban architecture. Against it, a bamboo touring bike that bridges traditional craft and modern materials. Those Meilenstein wheels are a premium choice for touring. German engineering, ceramic bearings, designed to spin smoothly for tens of thousands of kilometres. Combined with disc brakes, Doug's equipped for any condition — alpine descents, wet coastal roads, whatever a touring route throws at you. The green lug treatment is beautifully executed. That deep racing green has depth, catching light differently as the bike moves. It's a colour that ages well, looking better after a few thousand miles of road grime and weather than the day it was finished. The leather saddle is a classic touring choice. Brooks or similar — something that moulds to the rider over time, becoming more comfortable with every mile. The drop bars give multiple hand positions for long days in the saddle. There's a specific confidence in building a touring bike from bamboo. You're trusting your frame to handle loaded panniers, rough roads, and remote locations far from any bike shop. That trust is earned — bamboo's natural vibration damping makes it genuinely more comfortable over distance than metal alternatives. Doug clearly understood that. 🗺️

title: Carbon bamboo build by Shane. “Rides like dream. Very comfy!”
body: When Shane says the frame rides like a dream, believe it. This carbon bamboo build proves you can have it all: the comfort of natural fibre and the stiffness of composite. The personal touches here tell the real story. 'Me Ol' Bamboo' engraved on the top tube. 'Bamboo Bicycle Club' on the down tube. 'Turner 79er' on the seat tube. This isn't just a bike — it's got a name and a birthday. Hunt wheels front and rear provide the go-fast factor. These aren't cheap wheels, and pairing them with the home-built frame shows confidence in what Shane created during the workshop. The carbon fork and black components keep everything sleek and purposeful. Carbon bamboo builds use bamboo tubes for the main triangle with carbon fibre reinforcement at the joints. You get the vibration-damping comfort of natural material with added stiffness where the forces concentrate. Best of both worlds. That garden setting — wicker furniture, greenhouse glimpsed in the background, neat lawn — is pure suburban England. The bike fits right in. Practical enough for a weekend ride to the coffee shop, fast enough to hold your own on a club run. The 79er designation suggests wheel size experimentation. These kinds of decisions are what make home builds interesting. You're not limited to what a manufacturer decided was best for 'most riders.' You build what's best for you. 🏡

title: Over the years we've designed frames specifically for touring. For people crossing continents, the b
body: This is what touring looks like when you're not messing about. Full Vaude panniers front and rear, handlebar bag, saddlebag, and a bamboo frame designed to carry it all. We've spent years refining touring geometry. For people crossing continents — and we've had quite a few — the bike needs to handle heavy loads without becoming twitchy or exhausting. Longer chainstays for stability. Lower bottom bracket for confidence when loaded. Relaxed head angle for predictable steering. That 'LIMITLESS' text on the frame isn't marketing — it's aspiration. When you're building for expedition use, you're imagining where this bike might end up. Patagonian gravel. Mongolian steppe. German cycle paths. The frame needs to handle all of it. The kit choices here are serious. Vaude makes some of the best waterproof touring bags available. That Specialized helmet has seen miles. The flat bars give an upright position for comfort on long days. Fat tyres soak up rough roads. Bamboo works brilliantly for touring because the natural vibration damping reduces fatigue over distance. When you're riding eight hours a day, every day, for weeks, that comfort advantage adds up. Your hands, your back, your shoulders — they'll thank you. The wet pavement and urban background suggest this photo was taken mid-tour, probably on a rest day. Smart. Even expedition bikes need occasional breaks. 🌍

title: Nice 29er kit build by Matt
body: Utah red rock and a bamboo 29er. Some bikes were born for specific landscapes, and Matt's build looks absolutely at home on this canyon rim. The warm tones of the bamboo tubes practically disappear into the sandstone surroundings. That brown leather saddle picks up the earth colours perfectly — intentional or happy accident, it works. The whole bike feels like it belongs here. This is proper mountain bike territory. Those canyon walls in the background are no joke — we're talking serious technical riding in some of the world's most dramatic scenery. Moab, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef — any of these could be the backdrop. The 29er wheel size makes sense for this terrain. Roll over obstacles easier, maintain momentum through rough sections, cover ground efficiently on the long approaches these desert rides demand. The suspension fork handles the technical bits. Building a mountain bike from bamboo still surprises people, but the natural material handles trail abuse remarkably well. Bamboo has been used for scaffolding on Hong Kong skyscrapers for decades — it's tougher than it looks. The flex characteristics actually help on rough terrain, smoothing impacts before they reach the rider. That view though. Sometimes the best thing about a bike is where it takes you. This frame clearly gets ridden properly, not just displayed. The dust on the tyres doesn't lie. 🏜️

title: Packing up Dave frame all finished at a 2 day workshop, before boxing snapped a quick shot. Finished
body: Workshop floor parts layout — that moment when the frame is finished and the build can finally begin. Dave's got plans. This is a belt drive single speed setup, and the component choices tell the story. Gates CDX belt system — that black carbon belt and the matching chainring at the bottom of the frame. Virtually silent, maintenance-free, clean. No greasy chain to worry about. Those bullhorn bars on the left will give multiple hand positions without the complexity of drops. The tooled leather saddle at the top is proper craftsmanship — some kind of engraved design that'll only look better with age. Brooks or similar. The orange grips are a statement. They'll pop against the black lugs and natural bamboo once everything's assembled. Small colour choices like this transform a build from functional to personal. The hub shell on the right suggests attention to wheel building details. Someone here isn't just bolting parts together — they're thinking about every component choice. There's something pure about a single speed, especially belt-driven. No derailleurs to adjust. No cables to replace. Just clean lines and honest mechanics. The frame Dave built during the workshop deserves that simplicity. The concrete floor and industrial feel of this photo is workshop reality. Before the glamour shots against scenic backdrops, there's this: components spread out, plans taking shape, anticipation building. 🔧

title: Simple single speed build by Sam. Lugs finished in orange! #bamboobike #fixedgear #fixie #fixedlifes
body: Orange lugs and a fixed gear drivetrain. Sam went bold, and it absolutely works. This detail shot focuses on what matters: the rear triangle where builder skill really shows. Those seat stays and chainstays meet the bottom bracket and seat tube with clean joints, properly wrapped and finished. The bright orange catches light beautifully against the weathered brick. The matching orange chainring bolt is the kind of detail that separates a thoughtful build from a parts-bin special. Someone spent time coordinating every element. Even the track-style crankset complements the colour scheme. Fixed gear riding has its devotees for good reason. The direct connection between pedal and wheel — no freewheel to coast on — makes you feel every contour of the road. Bamboo's natural compliance softens that connection just enough to be comfortable without losing the feedback that fixie riders crave. Single speed simplicity means this bike will outlast complex geared setups. Nothing to adjust, nothing to break, nothing to replace except wear items. A properly maintained fixie can last decades with minimal attention. The brick wall background feels very London backstreet. Old meets new — Victorian infrastructure and contemporary sustainable craft. There's poetry in that, even if Sam was just looking for somewhere to lean the bike for a photo. 🧡

title: Cyclocross build by Rob.
body: Riverside and long grass — the kind of terrain cyclocross was made for. Rob's build looks perfectly at home here. Those earthy brown lugs blend with the muddy banks and winter vegetation. It's not a flashy colour choice, but it works. The natural bamboo tubes pick up the golden tones of the dead grass, creating a frame that almost camouflages into its environment. Cyclocross bikes need to handle everything: wet fields, muddy paths, road transitions, shouldering over obstacles. The drop bars give multiple hand positions for different terrain. The wheels with their subtle red accents on the decals add just enough visual interest without shouting. That saddle bag suggests this bike sees regular use beyond race days. Spare tube, multi-tool, maybe a snack for longer rides. Practical additions that separate a bike that gets ridden from one that sits in a garage. The water behind, still and reflecting sky, could be a canal towpath or river trail anywhere in Britain. These paths are cyclocross territory — too rough for pure road bikes, too tame for mountain bikes, perfect for something versatile. Building a cyclocross frame from bamboo makes particular sense. The natural vibration damping helps on rough ground. The material's resilience handles the occasional crash or clumsy dismount. And when you're covered in mud anyway, the organic aesthetic feels right. 🌿

title: Aurelien in Nantes, France enjoying the lovely weather, 19 degrees for February!
body: Nineteen degrees in February. Aurelien picked the right day for a ride along the Loire. That smile says everything about what a bamboo bike brings to the experience. This isn't training, it isn't commuting, it isn't exercise ticked off a to-do list. It's simply enjoying being on a bike, in beautiful surroundings, on an unexpectedly warm winter day. The setting is pure western France — reed beds, calm water, that distinctive low-angle winter light that makes everything golden. Nantes sits at the confluence of the Loire and the Erdre, surrounded by this kind of waterside cycling terrain. The bike itself is understated. Natural bamboo, clean lines, drop bars wrapped in what looks like white tape. No flashy components or attention-seeking colours. It fits the scene rather than dominating it. Our French builders have always had a particular sensibility. There's something about combining traditional craft with the cycling culture that runs so deep in France. From Tour stages to village vélo clubs, bikes mean something here. The puffy jacket and trainers say this is casual riding, not a training session. The kind of ride where you stop to take photos, maybe find a café, let the route unfold rather than following a plan. That's what 19 degrees in February calls for. ☀️

title: Happy new year, we are back in the workshop. New build by Andrew a #roadbike built at home.
body: New year, new build. Andrew kicked off the riding season with a proper road bike built at home from our kit. The setting screams Australia — eucalyptus trees, dry grass turning gold, that particular quality of antipodean light. Somewhere around Melbourne or Adelaide, perhaps, where the cycling scene is strong and the roads are made for long rides. Shimano 105 on the drivetrain is the smart choice for a road build. Reliable, serviceable anywhere in the world, and performs way above its price point. The groupset has been the workhorse of club cyclists for decades. The frame itself shows clean execution. Those brown lugs have a speckled, almost cork-like texture that pairs well with the golden bamboo tubes. The proportions look right — proper road geometry with a comfortable but efficient position. Building a road bike at home requires precision. The demands are higher than a casual cruiser: everything needs to be aligned, the contact points need to be exactly right, the frame needs to handle speed and distance. Andrew clearly got it right. That post leaning in the background looks like a local park or trail head — a starting point for rides into the Australian countryside. Happy new year indeed. 🇦🇺

title: For out traditional kits and workshop builds we use a combination of materials to create a frame. Ba
body: This is where the magic happens. The head tube junction — where top tube, down tube, and steerer all meet — is the most complex joint on any bicycle frame. Our traditional kits combine bamboo tubes with flax fibre composite lugs. The natural linen fibres, set in bio-resin, create a material that's strong, workable, and environmentally sound. You can see the weave pattern in the finished lug, that distinctive herringbone texture. The graphic on the down tube shows someone getting creative. Bold black brushstroke-style lettering against the natural bamboo — a personal touch that transforms a functional frame into something individual. That Crossover fork at the bottom of the frame is designed for versatility. The logo visible on the steerer tube indicates a component choice that can handle road, light gravel, and everything between. Workshop photos like this matter because they show the reality of frame building. Not every surface is perfectly smooth. Some tool marks remain. The lugs have character from the hand-layup process. This isn't factory production — it's craft. The white backdrop suggests a proper documentation shot, probably taken just before final assembly. A moment to appreciate the frame itself before wheels and components transform it into a rideable bike. 🔍

title: Two tone colours in a bicycle head tube, build by Fabio .
body: Two-tone head tube in pink and green. Fabio went for it, and the result is spectacular. This kind of colour split takes planning and patience. Masking off one half, applying the first colour, waiting for cure, then reversing the process for the second side. Get the tape line wrong and you've got a mess. Get it right and you've got this: clean division, bold statement. The pink and green combination could easily go wrong — too much, too loud, too 80s aerobics instructor. But against the natural bamboo peeking out at the top, it works. The colours feel fresh rather than garish. That gold headset spacer is a lovely detail. It picks up the bamboo tones while adding another layer of visual interest to an already striking junction. Someone thought about every element here. Macro shots like this reveal details you'd never notice on a passing bike. The smooth transition where paint meets bamboo. The precise circle of the headset bearings. The way light catches the glossy finish differently on each colour. Bicycle head tubes see a lot of stress — all the steering forces pass through here. They also get a lot of attention. When someone admires your bike, this junction is often where their eyes land first. Making it distinctive makes sense. Making it this distinctive takes confidence. 💗💚

title: Each of our frames is hand-finished by each of our first-time frame builders.  Once the flax fibre i
body: Hands on bamboo. This is what frame building actually looks like. Once the flax fibre lugs are wrapped and cured, the finishing begins. Here, someone is hand-sanding a junction to smooth the transitions between lug and tube. The grey surface is either primer or a base coat, ready for final colour. This step takes patience. You're removing material to create clean lines, but remove too much and you compromise the joint. The skill is knowing when to stop, feeling through the sandpaper when the surface is right. The blurred hands suggest movement — this isn't a posed shot but a capture of actual work in progress. The workshop setting, out of focus in the background, is where all our frames come to life. First-time builders often find this stage surprisingly satisfying. There's something meditative about hand-finishing. After the technical precision of aligning tubes and wrapping fibres, smoothing surfaces is almost relaxing. The visible bamboo nodes at top and bottom of frame remind you what's underneath. Natural material, shaped by hand, becoming something rideable. Every frame that leaves a workshop carries the marks of whoever finished it — invisible to most eyes, but present in every surface. This is the part that machines can't replicate. The human touch that makes each frame individual. 🖐️

title: NEW BUILD BY FRANK - The bike is outstanding, amazing, and surprising. Went out with a big smile and
body: Outstanding, amazing, and surprising. Frank's words, not ours — but we couldn't agree more. That location is unmistakably British heritage. The stone monument with its carved coat of arms, Georgian buildings behind wrought iron railings, flagstone pavement — this could be Bath, Oxford, or any of the historic cities where ancient architecture meets daily cycling. The bike earns its spot in the frame. Golden bamboo tubes catch the winter sun. Black lugs and fork provide contrast. Those gum wall tyres add warmth that echoes the honey-coloured stone. Even the pink water bottle feels considered. 'Bamboo Bicycle Club' is clearly visible on the down tube. Some builders keep things subtle; Frank wanted the provenance on display. Fair enough — when you've built something this good, you might as well sign it. The flat bar setup suggests versatility. Commuter-friendly for navigating historic streets, but with enough gearing range for longer rides into the surrounding countryside. Practical choices for a bike that clearly gets used. Going out with a big smile is the point. We can teach the technical skills, provide the materials, guide the process — but that feeling when you first ride something you built yourself? That's between you and the road. Frank found it. 😄

title: New build by Ted using are pre-lugged kit.
body: Dry stone walls and summer grass. Ted built his bike from our pre-lugged kit and immediately took it somewhere beautiful. That bright green bar tape is a statement. Against the natural bamboo, the weathered stone, the golden field behind — it pops. Some might call it loud. We call it confident. Pre-lugged kits are our most accessible option for home builders. The structural work is done: lugs are pre-formed, tubes are pre-cut, geometry is set. What remains is the satisfaction of assembly and finishing without the intimidation of starting from raw materials. The frame shows clean execution. Bronze-toned lugs complement the bamboo tubes. The proportions look right for gravel or light touring — relaxed geometry for comfort on long rides. Yorkshire? Derbyshire? Somewhere in the Dales or Peak District, probably. These walls have stood for centuries, built by hand from stones cleared from the fields. There's something fitting about parking a handmade frame against handmade stonework. The late afternoon light catches the bamboo beautifully. Builders often take their new frames to meaningful places for first photos. The choice of location says as much about the rider as the bike itself. Ted clearly values landscape. 🌾

title: Robin, hitting the hill upto Epping Forest on his bamboo #touringbike .
body: Robin, hitting the hill up to Epping Forest on his bamboo touring bike. That wave to camera captures the joy perfectly. Epping Forest is a cyclist's institution in northeast London. Ancient woodland, managed by the City of London Corporation since 1878, and home to some properly challenging hills. The sign in frame confirms the location — no mistaking that distinctive green and orange branding. That red jersey stands out against the autumn colours. The backpack suggests this is a practical ride rather than pure sport — maybe a commute through the forest, or an errand combined with training. The kind of riding that touring bikes excel at. The bike itself shows touring sensibility: upright position, mudguards ready for British weather, lights mounted for darker evenings. Built to go places and get things done, not just chase Strava segments. The brick building behind is typical Essex vernacular. These roads were made for cycling before they were made for cars — narrow, winding, connecting villages that predate the internal combustion engine. Action shots capture what static photos miss: the bike doing its job, the rider in motion, the context of where these frames actually get used. Robin clearly uses his. That wave suggests he knows he's living well. 👋

title: Gravel build by Jason. Gravel lugged kit with grx finishing pack.
body: Bamboo against bamboo. Jason's gravel build, photographed against a reed fence that mirrors the frame material. Intentional or lucky coincidence, it works. This is one of our lugged gravel kits, finished with Shimano's GRX groupset. GRX was designed specifically for gravel riding — brake lever ergonomics for drops, clutch derailleur for rough terrain, gear ratios optimised for mixed surfaces. Premium choice. Those Vision wheels are ready for serious distance. The carbon fork keeps the front end light and responsive. Black lugs keep things understated, letting the natural bamboo be the visual statement. The dappled light creates beautiful patterns across the frame. Late afternoon sun filtering through leaves — the kind of light that photographers chase and builders hope for when documenting their work. The concrete beneath and wooden decking suggest a garden or courtyard setting. After a ride, or before? The chain and cassette look clean, so possibly this is a documentation shot before first dirt. Gravel bikes have exploded because they answer the question of 'what if I didn't have to choose?' Road and trail, fast and comfortable, race-ready and adventure-capable. A bamboo gravel bike takes that further — what if your frame was as interesting as the places you'll ride it? 🌿

title: New single speed build by George. Featuring our road bike kit and single speed kit.
body: Grey skies, muddy bank, winter reservoir. George's single speed looks perfectly at home in this moody British scene. Those burgundy speckled lugs give the frame character. The textured finish catches light differently across each surface, creating depth that flat paint can't match. Against the golden bamboo and overcast water, it's a warm accent in a cold landscape. Single speed plus road kit equals simplicity squared. No derailleur, no cable mess, no decisions about which gear to use. Just you, the bike, and whatever gradient the road throws at you. George committed to the purity. The Weinmann wheels are a practical choice — reliable, rebuildable, proven over decades of road use. The drop bars give proper hand positions for serious riding, even without the complexity of gears. That suburban backdrop across the water is classic outer London reservoir country. These spots are cyclist favourites — flat-ish loops around the water, rarely far from a café, and views that change with the seasons and weather. The bike stands in mud but looks unfazed. A winter rider's machine doesn't need to be precious. It needs to work when conditions are grim and the temptation to stay home is strong. George clearly rides through everything. 🌧️

title: Built by Kim, using thick-walled Tonkin Bamboo which allows the lugs to be integrated into the frame
body: Kim built something different. Thick-walled Tonkin bamboo allows the lugs to integrate into the frame, creating this stealthy all-black aesthetic with just glimpses of natural material. The effect is striking. From a distance, this could be a carbon superbike. Only up close do you notice the bamboo sections at the seat tube and the organic grain hidden within the black exterior. The 'Kim Simmons' text on the top tube and 'HANDMADE' badge claim ownership of the craft. This approach requires thicker-walled bamboo than our standard builds. The extra wall thickness provides enough material to shape the lug transitions smoothly, almost invisibly. The result is more sculptural than functional, but that's rather the point for a build like this. The brick wall backdrop is pure London backstreet. The pavement kerb, the tarmac, the slight angle of the shot — it could be any of a thousand spots in the capital. The bike fits the urban context perfectly. Road geometry, proper groupset, deep-section wheels. Kim didn't compromise on performance to achieve the aesthetic. This is a bike built to ride, not just to photograph. The confidence to make it look like this comes from knowing it handles like it should. 🖤

title: Great way to transport a bamboo gravel kit!
body: A bamboo cargo bike delivering a bamboo gravel kit. Sometimes the universe aligns. This is bamboo-on-bamboo transportation at its finest. The cargo frame, with its extended bamboo front section, hauls a kit box strapped down with cargo netting. 'Bamboo Bicycle Club' visible on the packaging makes the content clear. Someone's gravel adventures are about to begin. The cargo bike itself is a piece of work. That long bamboo front triangle creates the load platform, held together with the same lug-and-tube construction as our regular frames. It's proof that the technique scales — from racing bikes to utility workhorses. The European cobblestone setting adds character. Could be Berlin, Amsterdam, or any city where cargo bikes have replaced cars for sensible transport. The zebra crossing and urban density in the background confirm the urban context. There's something satisfying about a product delivering itself. Traditional couriers use vans. Dedicated builders use bamboo. The kit inside that box will become someone's new ride, and when they finish building it, perhaps they'll have ideas about what bamboo can carry too. Full circle, in the most literal way possible. 📦

title: Built by Lee as part of a weekend workshop.
body: Weekend workshop, and Lee went all-in on colour. Hot pink lugs, lime green bar tape, and absolutely zero regret. This is what happens when someone decides their bike should be unmistakable. Not subtle, not blending in, not apologising. Just confident, bright, visible from a hundred metres away. The combination shouldn't work, but it does. The pink saturates every junction — head tube, seat cluster, bottom bracket, dropouts. The lime green on the bars picks up the accent, creating a cohesive loudness. Against the weathered wooden gate and cobblestones, it practically glows. Weekend workshops compress the build timeline. Two days, start to finish, with guidance every step. Lee made all the decisions — geometry, components, and obviously colours — then executed them in 48 hours. That padlock on the gate suggests this photo was taken right outside the workshop, first ride imminent. The black-and-green saddle continues the colour theme. Even small choices matter when you're building something this intentional. Nothing here happened by accident. Building a bike you can't miss is its own kind of courage. Lee has it. 💗💚

title: Gravel lugged kit in build!
body: Gravel lugged kit in progress. This is the moment when frame becomes real. Our pre-lugged system uses pre-formed joints in black — you can see the seat tube junction here, where chainstays, seat stays, and seat tube all meet. The bamboo tubes slot in, get bonded and reinforced, and suddenly you have a gravel frame. The workshop setting tells the story. Tools on pegboards, power equipment on benches, blue-taped jigs holding alignment. This isn't a factory floor — it's where individual frames are built, one at a time, by people learning the craft. That junction in the foreground is critical for rear wheel clearance and drivetrain alignment. Get it wrong and nothing else matters. The pre-formed lug takes some of the guesswork out, but the skill is in the preparation and bonding. For home builders, this is the most rewarding phase. The planning is done. The tubes are cut. Now you're actually assembling something that will become rideable. The materials in your hands will carry you over gravel, through woods, across continents if you want. That potential is what makes workshop photos exciting. Every finished bike started here, held in a jig, waiting to become. 🔧

title: Our gravel lugged frame is ready for pre-order. We have a first batch landing in early May. Develope
body: Gravel lugged frame, ready for pre-order. The result of development work that started years before this announcement. Designing a pre-lugged system for gravel meant solving specific problems. Wider tyre clearance. Disc brake mounts. Geometry that handles rough terrain with confidence. You can see the result here: black pre-formed lugs meeting golden bamboo tubes in a frame ready for adventure. The ghosted components around the frame show what it becomes. Drop bars for multiple hand positions. Wide tyres for mixed surfaces. Disc brakes for confident stopping in any weather. A complete gravel machine waiting to happen. Pre-lugged kits make frame building more accessible. The complex structural work is done — angles are set, tube sockets are formed, threaded inserts are installed. What remains is preparation, bonding, and finishing. Still satisfying, but with less room for error. That first batch landing in early May represented months of testing, refining, testing again. We don't release products until they're right. The wait is intentional. For anyone who's thought about building a gravel bike but worried about the complexity — this is the answer. The engineering is handled. The adventure is yours to define. 🚴

title: Gravel lugged frame with cameo finish. Any finish can be applied to the bamboo, painted, stained or
body: Camouflage finish on bamboo. Any finish can be applied — painted, stained, or something entirely unexpected like this. The camo pattern plays with the natural bamboo colour. Dark green and olive shapes break up the golden tubes, creating a military-inspired aesthetic that's both functional and distinctive. Good luck blending into the woods though — that Hunt wheelset gives you away. Those 4Season Gravel Xwide wheels from Hunt are built for year-round abuse. Tubeless-ready, wide enough for comfort on rough surfaces, narrow enough for efficiency on tarmac. The GRX groupset completes the gravel-ready specification. The roller shutter backdrop is pure urban grit. Metal, concrete, drainage grates — the contrast with the organic frame material is intentional. Bamboo bikes don't need pastoral settings to look good. They work in cities too. Staining or painting bamboo requires preparation. The natural surface needs sealing first, then the finish can be applied in layers. The camo effect here probably involved masking between colours — time-consuming but worth it for something this individual. The 'Bamboo Bicycle Club' text on the seat tube is a small detail in this busy frame, but it's there. Every frame we help create carries that connection to the workshop where it started. Even when it's hiding in plain sight. 🌲

title: Jon on his bamboo gravel bike. Built using flax and bamboo #eppingforest
body: Jon in Epping Forest, riding the gravel he built for this exact purpose. Orange jersey, lime green helmet, bamboo frame — impossible to miss on the trail. This is proper gravel riding. Birch trees lining a packed earth path, winter conditions stripping the canopy, that particular quality of light you only get in ancient woodland. Epping Forest is cyclist territory, especially for anyone who wants mixed surfaces close to London. The flax and bamboo construction shows in the frame's profile. Natural materials handling the demands of off-road riding without complaint. Jon's body position — relaxed, smiling, clearly enjoying himself — suggests the bike handles exactly as intended. That smile matters more than any specification sheet. This is what building your own bike leads to: moments in forests, on paths, in places that make you glad you're riding. The technical details enable the experience, but the experience is the point. Building a gravel bike from bamboo makes particular sense. The natural vibration damping smooths the rough stuff. The material's resilience handles impacts that would stress other frames. And when you're covered in trail dust, the organic aesthetic feels right. Jon clearly gets it. The forest is waiting, and he brought the right bike. 🌳

title: Lovely road bike built by Phil as a home build #roadbike.
body: Golden hour, winter hedgerow, and a road bike that catches every ray of fading light. Phil built this at home, and the finishing choices show real thought. Those olive-toned lugs complement the natural bamboo rather than fighting it. The Brooks saddle and brown bar tape bring warmth. The reflective wheel rims — catching the low sun — add sparkle without flashiness. This is classic British countryside cycling. The hedgerow is dormant, the fields beyond are green even in winter, and the light is doing that thing it does when the sun gets low and everything turns amber. Perfect conditions for a ride, and perfect conditions for a photo. The frame itself shows clean execution. Home builds require learning as you go, but Phil clearly got everything right. The proportions look correct, the joints look solid, and the overall aesthetic is cohesive. There's something about winter riding that feels more deliberate than summer miles. You have to want to be out there. The cold, the short days, the mud — none of it stops proper cyclists. Phil's clearly one of them. Building a road bike from bamboo takes confidence. The performance demands are high. Phil trusted the materials, trusted the process, and ended up with something worth photographing in perfect light. 🌅

title: Bit of #bikepacking using our road carbon kit. Thanks for the photo from Jeremy in France.
body: Bikepacking on a bamboo road carbon kit, somewhere on the French Atlantic coast. Jeremy sent this photo, and it stopped us in our tracks. That beach could be Brittany, could be the Vendée, could be anywhere along that stunning western coastline. Rocky outcrops framing golden sand, families playing in the shallows, surf rolling in. And in the foreground, a loaded bamboo bike taking a well-deserved rest. The setup is serious bikepacking. Frame bag filling the main triangle. Handlebar roll with red and orange accents. Green saddle pack on a Vaude setup. Water bottles, GPS mount, everything needed for self-sufficient travel. This isn't credit card touring — this is carrying your world on two wheels. Building a bike and then riding it across a country is the full expression of what we offer. The workshop is just the beginning. The real story is written on roads like this, with views like this, in moments of pause between days of pedalling. Jeremy chose our road carbon kit for the performance it delivers under load. Stiff enough for efficient climbing, compliant enough for comfort over distance. The bamboo handles the vibration; the rider handles the adventure. This is what it's all about. Build. Ride. See the world. Merci, Jeremy. 🏖️

title: Busy teaching a workshop in Falun, Sweden. @cykelkoketfalun . #bamboobike #maker #handmade #sundayle
body: Workshop day in Falun, Sweden. Multiple frames in jigs, builders focused on their work, and that particular energy of people learning something new together. Cykelköket Falun — the Bike Kitchen — hosts workshops that bring frame building to Scandinavia. The setup here shows our portable teaching approach: jigs on tables, tools within reach, frames taking shape under careful hands. You can see the concentration. The builder in the foreground, cap on, apron tied, is working on a junction that requires precision. Behind him, another frame at the same stage. The banner on the wall shows finished bikes — a reminder of where all this careful work leads. Swedish makers bring a particular sensibility to craft. There's something in the culture that values doing things properly, taking time, getting details right. It translates well to frame building. The room itself tells a story. Tools on pegboards. Finished frame hanging in the window. Roll of protective paper. Industrial floor worn by years of use. This is a working space, not a showroom. Teaching workshops in other countries extends what we do beyond London. The skills transfer. The frames go home with their builders. The network grows, one careful junction at a time. 🇸🇪

title: One thing we’re really missing at the moment is the freedom to travel. Here’s a throw back photo
body: The freedom to travel. This throwback photo captures exactly what we've been missing — and what bamboo bikes were made for. That turquoise glacial lake, those Andean peaks, the loaded touring setup. This is expedition territory. Somewhere in Chile or Argentina, high altitude, remote, spectacular. The kind of place you can only reach by pedalling there yourself. The bike is properly loaded. Rear panniers in burgundy and purple. Front panniers in bright orange and yellow. Stuff sacks strapped to the rack. Everything needed for self-sufficient travel in places where the next shop might be days away. Teal lugs match the impossible colour of that water. Coincidence or planning? Either way, the frame looks at home in this landscape. Natural material against natural wonder. Touring at altitude demands reliable equipment. The thin air makes climbing harder. The temperature swings test materials. The isolation means you fix problems yourself or you don't fix them at all. A bamboo frame built for this purpose handles it all. This is why we do what we do. Not just building frames, but enabling journeys. The workshop is where it starts; photos like this are where it leads. Whenever travel opens up again, the bikes will be ready. 🏔️

title: All finished #bamboobike. Perfect for #sportive and light #bicycle touring. #bamboobicycleclub #road
body: Finished and ready for sportives, light touring, or whatever the road offers. This bamboo road bike shows what clean execution looks like. The aesthetic here is stealth with accents. Black frame, black fork, black components — but those exposed bamboo sections at seat tube and down tube break the monotony with organic warmth. It's a subtle reveal rather than a shout. The brick wall backdrop is classic British urban. Could be any town, any street, any moment between rides. The bike fits the context without trying to dominate it. Sportive-ready means the geometry needs to balance speed with comfort. Long days in the saddle require a position you can sustain. The proportions here suggest someone thought carefully about how they ride and what they need. Light touring capability adds versatility. Rack mounts for when you need to carry more. Tyre clearance for when the road gets rough. The foundation for adventures that start as day rides and grow into something more. The 'MERIT' branding on the frame is barely visible — understated, like the rest of the build. Some bikes demand attention. This one earns it through quality rather than flash. 🚴

title: @wilrides with his finished #bamboo #mtb. Um not sure what the panda costume is for... if a panda at
body: We're not entirely sure why @wilrides is wearing a panda costume, but we're absolutely here for it. The bamboo MTB is serious kit though. Maxxis tyres for proper grip. Suspension fork for trail abuse. Geometry that says this bike has seen dirt, rocks, roots, and probably a few things pandas shouldn't attempt. The frame itself shows trail-ready proportions. Short chainstays for agility. Sloping top tube for standover clearance when things go wrong. The golden bamboo tubes contrast nicely with the dark components and, well, the black and white panda suit. There's something wonderfully absurd about the juxtaposition. Technical mountain bike engineering meets full-body animal costume meets concrete block wall. Peak internet? Peak bamboo community? Both? Mountain biking on bamboo still surprises people, but the material handles trail demands brilliantly. Natural vibration damping smooths the rough stuff. The frame's resilience absorbs impacts that would stress other materials. And apparently, it works fine in costume. We love our community. People who build bikes and then do whatever they want with them — including, apparently, dressing as endangered species for the photo. Respect, Will. 🐼

title: 🤜Awesome! 🤛 build 🚴‍♀️ by Mark, finshed with Sram Rival #huntwheels and condor forks.
body: Mark's build came together with serious components. SRAM Rival groupset, Hunt wheels, Condor fork. This is a gravel bike that means business. The black lugs against golden bamboo is our most popular colour combination for good reason. Clean, professional, timeless. The contrast works from any angle, in any light. SRAM Rival sits in the sweet spot of performance and value. Reliable shifting, good brake feel, weight that doesn't break the bank. Paired with Hunt's wheelsets — known for their value proposition — this is a thoughtful spec for someone who rides hard without chasing marginal gains. The Condor fork is a smart choice from a British brand that understands what riders here need. Clearance for bigger tyres. Disc brake mounts properly placed. The geometry to handle mixed terrain without compromising road manners. That white rendered wall and gravel surface suggest a suburban setting. The bike looks ready to escape — to find trails, gravel tracks, quiet roads that lead somewhere interesting. The saddle bag hints at self-sufficiency. Tube, tools, snacks — whatever Mark needs to keep rolling when the ride extends beyond the original plan. Proper cyclists always carry enough to get home. 🤜🤛

title: Build by Dan at a weekend workshop.
