title: BBC at Luxembourg Museum: Bamboo in Exhibition
tags: case-study, cultural-institution, design, education, exhibition, museum, sustainability
body: The Museum That Put a Bamboo Kit on Display In November 2023, a Bamboo Bicycle Club home build kit was placed on display at the Grand Palais in Paris as part of a Luxembourg Museum exhibition. James Marr was invited to write an essay for the exhibition manual — exploring bamboo bicycle building as a statement about craft, agency, and sustainability in a consumer-driven world. When a major European cultural institution asks you to explain what you do, you know you are doing something worth explaining. The Challenge The challenge that drove James Marr to found Bamboo Bicycle Club in 2012 — and the challenge he articulated for the Luxembourg Museum — is both personal and cultural. In today's mass-produced world, most people have no meaningful relationship with the objects they use. A bicycle is purchased, ridden, and discarded. The design decisions, the material choices, the manufacturing processes that produced it are invisible. Most people have no idea how a bicycle works, let alone how one is made. BBC's entire model is a response to that disconnection. The programme is not primarily about bamboo — though the material is extraordinary. It is about restoring the human relationship with making: the idea that you should be able to modify, create, and improve the objects you own, and that this agency matters both personally and societally. The Solution The Luxembourg Museum exhibition — at the Grand Palais, one of Paris's most significant cultural venues — placed BBC's home build kit in a display context that framed bamboo bicycle building as a cultural practice, not just a manufacturing process. James Marr's essay for the exhibition manual articulated the philosophy explicitly: "As Founder of Bamboo Bicycle Club I have always challenged this, as I believe we should all be able to modify, create and improve everything we own, giving us agency over both a products function and aesthetic. As humans we have engaged in the act of making for thousands of years, and I strongly believe in the importance of physically touching, crafting and tweaking a design and its materials, until you have a unique finished product." The essay also addressed bamboo's material properties — its negative carbon footprint (absorbing 30% more CO₂ than traditional timber), its over 1,500 species, its global cultivability, its tensile strength and vibration-dampening characteristics — and connected BBC's educational mission to its Africa programme (Kenya and Ethiopia), its European workshop hubs, and its university research partnerships. The Outcomes The Grand Palais exhibition places BBC alongside the cultural institutions that define what matters in European design. The Luxembourg Museum's decision to feature BBC's home build kit — and to commission an essay from James Marr for the exhibition catalogue — is curatorial validation: an institution that studies and interprets design culture chose BBC as a representative of something significant. For schools, the Luxembourg Museum connection reframes what BBC's programme represents in the cultural landscape. This is not a vocational training programme or a STEM enrichment add-on. It is a practice that European cultural institutions recognise as a meaningful response to one of modernity's most persistent challenges: the disconnection between people and the objects they use. When a student builds a bamboo bicycle frame in a school D&T workshop, they are doing something that the Grand Palais thought worth displaying. That is not hyperbole. It is the curation decision of one of Europe's most significant cultural venues. Design, Culture, and the Curriculum For D&T teachers, art teachers, and heads of creative curriculum, BBC's Grand Palais connection opens a discussion about the relationship between design, culture, and making that goes beyond standard curriculum content. title: Aston Martin Engineer's Path Led Back to BBC
tags: careers, case-study, dt, education, engineering, ks5, secondary, university
body: The Colleague Who Wouldn't Stop Talking About Their Bike Somewhere in Aston Martin's engineering offices, a conversation happened. An engineer mentioned — probably not for the first time — that they had built a bamboo bicycle frame at university. Their colleague listened. And then their colleague found their way to Bamboo Bicycle Club. This is how lasting D&T education works: not through the qualification certificate, but through the conversation years later, when someone describes what they made and why it mattered. The Challenge The challenge for D&T teachers making the case for hands-on manufacturing education is the time horizon. The Ofsted inspection is this term. The university application is next year. The argument that a student's woodwork project or electronics build will still be resonating with them at 28 — in an engineering office at a performance car manufacturer — requires a faith in long-term educational value that is difficult to substantiate in a school context. BBC's case for school partnerships is partly about immediate curriculum alignment, OCN accreditation, and Ofsted-relevant outcomes. But it is also about the longer argument: that making something real, with real materials, in real time, creates a category of knowledge and memory that conventional instruction does not. The Aston Martin engineer is that argument, in a single anecdote. The Solution The engineer at Aston Martin came to BBC in March 2020. The route was indirect — a colleague's university bamboo bike project, mentioned in passing, led to curiosity, which led to BBC. But the fact that the journey was indirect makes it more interesting, not less: this is organic, word-of-mouth endorsement from within one of the UK's most technically demanding automotive engineering environments. BBC's post from March 2020 records the participant's account: "When I was working at Aston Martin and came across a colleague who had done a bamboo bike project at Uni..." — and then BBC. The journey from university D&T project to professional engineering career to BBC is documented in a single sentence, across what was likely several years. Aston Martin engineers work at the intersection of materials science, structural engineering, and performance optimisation. They are not easily impressed. When one of them chooses to spend four days building a bamboo bicycle frame, it is because the process offers something genuinely substantive — engineering depth, material challenge, and a hands-on experience that reconnects to the curiosity that led them into engineering in the first place. The Outcomes For careers advisors and D&T teachers, the Aston Martin case study is the proof point for the long game. The colleague's university bamboo project was still being talked about in professional engineering circles years after it was completed. It was specific enough to be memorable — not a generic group project, but a bamboo bicycle frame — and technical enough to be relevant to a professional automotive engineer's interests. BBC has now supported builds by engineers, designers, and technical professionals from a range of organisations. The professional-level credibility of the process — the same techniques that built a UCL research vehicle and were demonstrated at the UK Bamboo Summit — means that BBC's school and university programmes produce outcomes that have genuine currency in professional engineering contexts. For schools: the student who builds a bamboo frame in your D&T room this year may be the engineer who tells a colleague about it at 28. That is not a trivial educational outcome. It is the kind of formative experience that shapes how people think about materials, manufacturing, and their own technical capability — long after the school bell has rung. title: King's College London: Bamboo Staff Workshop
tags: case-study, education, higher-education, russell-group, stem, teacher-training, university
body: The Professor Who Picked Up a Saw At King's College London in March 2020, a group of teaching staff gathered in a workshop space. They were not there to observe a demonstration. They were there to build a bamboo bicycle frame — as participants, not observers — before deciding whether the programme belonged in their university's curriculum. The academics went first. The students would come later, if the staff decided it was worth it. The Challenge King's College London is a founding Russell Group member, consistently ranked among the global top 40 universities. Its standards for curriculum content are correspondingly high. Any programme proposed for integration into a KCL module must withstand academic scrutiny: is the subject matter substantive? Does the process generate learning that maps to university-level outcomes? Can the teaching staff deliver it with confidence? BBC's bamboo building programme presented KCL with a specific evaluation challenge. It is experiential, practical, and tactile — qualities that do not always translate easily into university curriculum frameworks designed for lecture-based or laboratory-based learning. The question was whether building a bamboo composite bicycle frame, as a learning activity, generated sufficient depth and rigour to justify curriculum time at a research-intensive institution. The Solution BBC ran a practice workshop with King's College London teaching staff in March 2020. The staff — academics and technical instructors — participated as learners, working through the full BBC building process: bamboo tube preparation, frame geometry layout, flax-and-natural-resin joinery, curing and finishing. An academic audience brings different questions to the process than a school student or a corporate team-building participant. They ask about failure modes — how does the joint fail under load, and what does that tell you about the material? They ask about the mechanics of fibre reinforcement — why flax, and how does the weave direction affect tensile strength? They ask about carbon accounting — what is the embodied carbon of the resin, and how does it affect the frame's overall lifecycle footprint? These are precisely the questions that make BBC's programme genuinely rigorous at university level. BBC's post from March 2020 records the outcome: "We've been working with King College London to look at introducing bike building into the university. Here is an interesting build built during a practice workshop with teaching personnel." The Outcomes The KCL practice workshop model — staff as learners before students — is a transferable standard. It is also available to any school or college that wants to evaluate BBC's programme rigorously. A D&T teacher who has built a bamboo joint understands the process at a different level than one who has only read about it. BBC actively encourages staff CPD sessions as a precursor to student programmes. The KCL partnership, developing actively in early 2020 before the pandemic interrupted education sector relationships globally, adds a Russell Group institution to BBC's university engagement record. The relationship was not concluded — it was paused. The programme's fit with KCL's materials science, engineering, and sustainability curricula remains as strong as it was in 2020. For schools that want to model the KCL approach — staff workshop first, then student programme — BBC can design and deliver a half-day or full-day CPD session for D&T departments before committing to a student programme. Contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org . The Staff CPD Model for Schools BBC's staff CPD sessions follow the KCL model: teaching staff experience the programme as participants before they deliver it. This approach builds genuine material confidence, not just theoretical knowledge. title: UCL Commissions BBC: Bamboo Electric Cargo Bike
tags: cargo-bike, case-study, education, engineering, higher-education, stem, ucl, university
body: A Top-Ten University, a Research Brief, and Bamboo University College London is one of the ten best universities in the world. In October 2020, UCL needed an electric cargo bike — one capable of carrying 100 kilograms, powered by a front hub motor, and built entirely from bamboo composite. No commercial vehicle met the specification. UCL commissioned Bamboo Bicycle Club to build one. The fact that a global top-ten research institution, with access to advanced engineering expertise, chose BBC for this commission is the most concentrated form of technical validation BBC has received. The Challenge UCL's research interest was specific: could bamboo composite construction meet the structural requirements of a functional electric cargo vehicle? Existing e-cargo bikes use aluminium and steel — materials with significant embodied carbon, energy-intensive production, and poor end-of-life profiles. If bamboo could perform at cargo specification, it would represent a significant advance in sustainable transport engineering. The engineering requirements were demanding. A 100kg payload frame must handle static loads far in excess of a standard bicycle, plus the dynamic forces generated by road surfaces, cornering, and motor-assisted braking. Integrating an electric front hub requires careful torque analysis and frame geometry decisions. The result must be a functional vehicle, not a demonstration prototype. The Solution BBC applied its established bamboo composite engineering methodology to the UCL specification: bamboo tube selection and preparation, geometric frame design for the cargo configuration, flax-and-natural-resin joinery at all structural nodes, and iterative testing at each build stage. The structural decisions drew on BBC's experience building frames tested at university laboratory facilities — including load testing of bamboo-flax composite joints that informed the joinery specifications for high-load applications. The cargo configuration required non-standard geometry and reinforced connection points to distribute the 100kg payload across the frame safely. The electric front hub integration — connecting a motor drivetrain to a bamboo composite frame — required careful consideration of torque distribution, mounting point design, and frame flex under powered acceleration. BBC completed the build and delivered the vehicle to UCL in October 2020. The Outcomes The UCL cargo bike commission answers, in the most direct way possible, the question schools sometimes hesitate to ask: is this programme serious engineering? UCL — a university whose materials science and engineering departments operate at global frontier level — said yes, clearly enough to commission a vehicle. For A-level and degree-level students in engineering, materials science, or sustainable transport, the UCL cargo bike situates the techniques learned in a BBC school workshop within professional research practice. The flax-and-resin joinery a student practises in a school D&T room is the technique that built a UCL research vehicle. The scaling is different; the knowledge is continuous. BBC's university network — UCL, Coventry University, King's College London, LSBU (£70,000 active partnership), University of Manchester — reflects a consistent pattern: research institutions engaging with BBC because the practical bamboo engineering knowledge BBC holds is not available elsewhere in the UK. That knowledge base is what BBC brings to school programmes. Engineering Pathways Through BBC BBC's school and university programmes are designed to be continuous — students who build in a school workshop can progress to university research collaborations, design projects, and engineering roles that engage with bamboo composite materials at a professional level. For A-level students heading toward engineering degrees, BBC provides an early, substantive encounter with applied composite engineering. Contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org .

title: Coventry University: BBC at UK Bamboo Summit
tags: bamboo-summit, case-study, education, higher-education, stem, sustainability, university
body: When Bamboo Experts Needed Someone to Run the Workshop The UK Bamboo Summit at Coventry University in September 2024 brought together the most knowledgeable bamboo researchers and practitioners in Britain — architects, engineers, academics, and designers who have spent careers working with this material. When the organisers needed someone to lead the hands-on workshop component of the event, they chose Bamboo Bicycle Club. In a room of specialists, BBC ran the practical session. That choice is significant. The Challenge Academic sustainability conferences face a structural problem: they are attended by people who already understand the theory and rarely get to test the practice. The UK Bamboo Summit was designed to be different — to bring the research community into direct contact with the material itself, not just with papers about it. But running a live, hands-on bamboo building workshop for an audience of specialists requires a level of technical authority that most providers cannot meet. The facilitator needs to be credible to engineers, architects, and academics simultaneously. BBC, with over 4,000 builds completed across 36+ countries since its founding in 2012, is the UK's most experienced bamboo frame-building organisation. That track record — and the depth of practical knowledge it represents — made BBC the natural choice for the Summit's workshop leadership. The Solution BBC led the hands-on workshop session at the UK Bamboo Summit, guiding delegates through core bamboo building techniques: tube preparation, grain structure analysis, flax-and-natural-resin joinery, and the structural principles that govern bamboo composite frame design. The delegates represented some of the UK and international bamboo sector's most significant organisations: Brilliant Bamboo UK, Atelier One, Imagine Bamboo, World Bamboo, and Terragrn, alongside Coventry University academic staff and students. James Marr, BBC's founder, also gave a presentation covering BBC's thirteen-year track record, its educational programmes, and the case for bamboo in the next generation of sustainable manufacturing education. The Summit itself — the first national UK gathering of its kind — positioned bamboo as a serious structural and manufacturing material, not a novelty. BBC's role as the workshop facilitator placed it at the centre of that positioning. The Outcomes BBC's involvement in the UK Bamboo Summit provides a form of peer validation that is difficult to manufacture. This was not a school enrichment visit or a corporate away-day. It was a national academic summit, with international delegates, assessing the material's future. BBC was invited to lead the practical session because its expertise is recognised by the sector's academic leadership. For universities and schools evaluating BBC's programme, the Coventry Summit sits alongside BBC's broader university engagement: UCL (100kg electric cargo bike commission), King's College London (teaching staff practice workshop), London South Bank University (active partnership, £70,000 equipment investment), and the University of Manchester (ongoing research collaboration). This is a programme with genuine academic standing. The OCN Level 2 in Sustainable Manufacturing — the accreditation BBC holds for its educational programmes — maps directly onto the curriculum interests of universities working in sustainable design, engineering, and materials science. The Summit's academic audience recognised in BBC's programme a qualification framework that connects secondary and further education with higher education research. University Partnership Opportunities BBC works with universities on workshop facilitation, curriculum integration, research collaboration, and staff CPD. For design, engineering, materials science, and sustainability programmes, BBC can co-design sessions that connect the bamboo building process to specific learning outcomes. Contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org .

title: Blackhorse Lane Open Weekend: Bamboo Building
tags: case-study, community, design, education, making, public-engagement, sustainability
body: The Workshop Open to Everyone In September 2024, a weekend of design, craft, and making spread across Blackhorse Lane and the Addison Road area of east London. Makers opened their studios. Designers shared their practice. Craftspeople demonstrated their work to anyone who walked through the door. Bamboo Bicycle Club was among them. For a school considering a BBC workshop, the Blackhorse Lane weekend is worth understanding. It is BBC in its most open, accessible form: not a closed school session with a fixed cohort, but a public demonstration of what the programme looks like when anyone can walk in and pick up a piece of bamboo. The Challenge Public engagement events for technical craft practices face a consistent tension: the work is complex enough to be interesting, but accessible enough that a curious passer-by can participate in some meaningful way in a short visit. Welding or CNC machining cannot be demonstrated safely or accessibly to a general public in an open-door setting. Bamboo building can. BBC's participation in the Blackhorse Lane Open Weekend tested exactly this: can the fundamentals of bamboo bicycle building — the material properties, the joining techniques, the design thinking — be communicated and experienced by people with no prior knowledge, in an informal community setting, within the time constraints of a festival visit? The Solution BBC presented hands-on Introduction to Building with Bamboo workshops and demonstrations across the Blackhorse Lane Open Weekend in September 2024. Participants — members of the public ranging across ages and backgrounds — engaged with bamboo as a material: handling the tubes, understanding the grain structure, trying the basic shaping and joinery techniques. The format at Blackhorse Lane was necessarily condensed compared to a full school workshop, but it demonstrated the programme's accessibility range. Bamboo bicycle building does not require prior engineering knowledge or specialist tools. It requires curiosity, patience, and a willingness to work carefully with a material that behaves differently from timber or metal. BBC's Instagram reel from the event captured the energy: "What a weekend!! Many thanks to all those who participated in our 'Introduction to Building with Bamboo' workshops and demonstrations." The response — public participation, positive feedback, and ongoing interest — confirmed that the programme's appeal extends well beyond the structured school or university context. The Outcomes For schools, the Blackhorse Lane Open Weekend demonstrates something specific: BBC's programme is calibrated for genuine public accessibility, not just expert audiences. The same organisation that delivered workshops to automotive engineers at GM in Zurich, and was invited to lead the practical session at the UK Bamboo Summit at Coventry University, also runs open-door community sessions where anyone who wants to try bamboo building can. That range — from research-grade engineering commissions for UCL to open weekend demonstrations in Leyton — is not a contradiction. It reflects the fundamental nature of the material and the process. Bamboo composite building has a floor accessible to beginners and a ceiling that challenges professionals. The Blackhorse Lane weekend put that range on public display. For schools running enrichment weeks, community engagement events, or D&T open days, BBC's public event experience means the programme can be adapted for a range of formats: half-day sessions, single-period introductions, parent events, or open-door demonstrations. The core technique remains the same; the session structure is flexible. Bringing BBC to Your Community BBC works with schools, community organisations, and public institutions on events ranging from full multi-day build programmes to single-session introductory workshops. title: Regina School Canada: BBC Bamboo Bike Support
tags: case-study, dt, education, international, secondary, self-delivery, stem
body: 5,000 Miles Away, Still Building Regina is the capital of Saskatchewan, Canada. It sits on the flat Canadian prairies, roughly 5,000 miles from BBC's workshop in Leyton, east London. In February 2020, a school in Regina was building bamboo bicycles — guided by BBC from the other side of the world, with no BBC facilitator in the room, in a country where bamboo bicycle building has no established tradition. They made it work. The Challenge Regina School faced the same challenge that confronts any educational institution trying to introduce BBC's programme in a location where BBC has no physical presence: how do you access the technical knowledge, the material guidance, and the curriculum support that makes the programme work, when the people who have that knowledge are 5,000 miles away? This is not a unique challenge. Schools across the UK regularly run programmes from external providers with limited on-site support. But building a bamboo composite bicycle frame involves a specific set of techniques — tube preparation, geometric layout, flax-and-resin joinery, curing schedules — that require clear, detailed guidance, especially for first-time builders. Getting it wrong at any stage affects the structural integrity of the finished frame. The Solution BBC provided remote consultation and technical support for Regina School's bamboo bicycle project. The school sourced materials, set up their workspace, and followed BBC's guidance on the building process — with BBC answering questions through their blog Q&A format and direct correspondence. BBC's Facebook post from February 2020 records the outcome: "We've been helping Regina School in Canada building bamboo bikes. Learn more? Read some questions and answers on our Blog." The reference to a published Q&A suggests BBC documented the support process explicitly — creating a resource that other international schools could use to run the programme in their own context. The programme likely connected to multiple curriculum areas: Design and Technology (or the Canadian equivalent), Physics (materials and structures), and Environmental Science (bamboo as a sustainable material). The remote support model demonstrated that BBC's knowledge base — accumulated over more than a decade and 4,000+ builds across 36+ countries — is transferable without a physical BBC presence. The Outcomes The Regina School project confirms what the Munich franchise visit and The Oratory School's permanent workshop both demonstrate from different angles: BBC's methodology is genuinely portable. It works in Germany, in Canada, in the Netherlands, in France, and in Kenya — because the core knowledge is clear, teachable, and not dependent on a specific practitioner being present. For UK schools evaluating the self-delivery model, Regina is the most demanding test case available. A Canadian school, on a different continent, with no on-site BBC support, in a completely different educational system, built bamboo bicycles by following BBC's guidance. UK schools working with BBC's self-delivery package — which includes in-person training, dedicated tooling, curriculum materials, and ongoing support — are in a substantially stronger position than Regina was, and Regina managed it. BBC's 36+ country reach is built on cases like this: communities and educational institutions around the world that recognised the programme's value and found a way to run it, regardless of geography. Each one adds to a body of evidence that the model works at distance as well as in person. How Other Schools Can Access Remote Support For schools considering BBC's programme in areas where BBC cannot deliver on-site, remote consultation is available. BBC has supported projects across North America, Africa, and Asia alongside its European workshop network. For UK schools, on-site delivery and self-delivery training are the primary options. Contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org to discuss which model suits your context.

title: BBC Munich: Franchise Delivers School Workshop
tags: case-study, dt, education, franchise, international, secondary, self-delivery
body: The Practitioner Who Went to School One morning in March 2020, Des — the practitioner who runs Bamboo Bicycle Club's München workshop — loaded some bamboo bicycle frames into his car and drove to a local school. He was not accompanied by anyone from BBC's London headquarters. No facilitator flew over from the UK. Des simply went, showed the bikes, talked about the building process, and demonstrated what bamboo composite engineering looks like in practice. It worked. BBC shared the visit because it was worth sharing — and because it illustrated something important about how the BBC model actually functions at scale. The Challenge One of the most common questions schools ask when evaluating BBC's programme is this: what happens when BBC can't be here? It is a reasonable concern. If the programme depends entirely on BBC's London team being present for every session, it is always an external provider — never an embedded capability. Schools want programmes they can own, not just visit. The broader challenge for BBC as an organisation is the same problem in reverse: how do you bring high-quality bamboo bicycle education to schools in Munich, or Amsterdam, or Toulouse, or Regina — cities and communities where BBC has no permanent staff presence? The answer cannot be to fly facilitators everywhere for every school visit. The answer has to be a model where trained local practitioners can deliver the programme independently, in their own language, in their own community context. The Solution Des runs Bamboo Bicycle Club München — BBC's Munich franchise hub. He is not a BBC employee. He trained with BBC, adopted the methodology, and now operates a permanent workshop in Munich that has grown to over 4,600 Instagram followers and 206 posts of continuous activity. In March 2020, he took the next step: he visited a local school. He brought bamboo bikes. He talked about how they are built, what the material is, why it matters, and what students could do with that knowledge. He did it without a curriculum pack designed for the German school system, without a BBC facilitator present, and without the safety net of an established school relationship. It went well enough that BBC wanted to document and share it. The visit represented the full self-delivery model in operation: a trained practitioner, embedded in their local community, engaging with schools on their own initiative and representing the BBC programme credibly without any central support required. The Outcomes The Munich school visit establishes a specific and important proof point for UK schools considering the self-delivery model. In a school system BBC had no existing relationship with. And it was good enough to share. BBC München has continued to grow since 2020. Its Instagram presence (4,600+ followers, 200+ posts) reflects a community of active builders in one of Europe's most technically sophisticated cities. That community exists because Des — a trained BBC practitioner — went out and built it. The school visit was part of that community-building; it was also proof of the methodology's portability. For UK schools: if the self-delivery model works in Munich, in German, without support, it will work in your D&T department. The training and tooling BBC provides to UK schools is more comprehensive than anything Des had access to in 2020. The Munich school visit is what that looks like in practice — scaled to a school setting, supported from the start, and growing over time. Contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org .

title: Stoke-on-Trent College: Bamboo Build Workshop

body: Students and Artists, Side by Side In March 2025, a further education student at Stoke-on-Trent College found themselves at a workbench next to a professional artist. Between them: a length of bamboo, some hand tools, and a set of instructions for a joinery technique neither had used before. By the end of the session, both had built something they had never built before. Both had surprised themselves. That collision — craft, education, and community in the same room — is what Bamboo Bicycle Club and Brilliant Bamboo CIC were after when they designed the joint workshop for Stoke-on-Trent College. The Challenge Further education colleges carry a specific curriculum burden. Their students are diverse — in age, background, and educational history — and their programmes must deliver practical skills, employability relevance, and genuine engagement simultaneously. Sustainability is no longer optional in FE curriculum design: from September 2025, the Department for Education requires all educational institutions to have active Climate Action Plans, and FE colleges are expected to embed sustainable practice into their delivery. The challenge is making that feel real. Lecture-based sustainability units teach the facts but rarely leave a lasting impression. Students who have cut, shaped, and joined a natural composite material — who have felt how bamboo behaves under hand tools, how the resin sets, how a structural joint holds — understand sustainable manufacturing in a way that slides cannot deliver. The challenge was finding a programme that could carry that weight across a mixed-background FE cohort. The Solution BBC partnered with Brilliant Bamboo CIC — a Community Interest Company focused on expanding bamboo education in the UK — to deliver a cross-sector workshop at Stoke-on-Trent College in March 2025. The session brought together college students and a local community artist, working alongside each other on the same techniques. Participants engaged with bamboo as an engineering material: its grain structure, tensile strength, workability under hand tools, and the flax-and-resin joinery process that connects tubes into structural forms. The cross-sector format was deliberate: mixing FE students with a practising artist changed the dynamic of the room. Students who might have hesitated in a purely academic setting were energised by the presence of a creative professional working through the same challenges. Curriculum links covered Creative Arts (material exploration, craft tradition), D&T (material properties, joinery, structural thinking), Sustainability (bamboo as a renewable material, carbon sequestration), and Employability (practical skills, precision work, following technical specifications). The Outcomes BBC's post from the session captured the intent in its hashtags: #HandsOnLearning #SustainableMaking . These are not aspirational tags. They describe what actually happened: a room of people with different backgrounds, all making something real, all engaging with a sustainable material through direct physical experience. The Brilliant Bamboo partnership also signals something significant for colleges considering longer-term collaboration. BBC is not a standalone enrichment provider — it sits within a growing UK bamboo education ecosystem that includes academic institutions (Coventry University, UCL, King's College London), charity partners (Brilliant Bamboo CIC), and international networks across 36+ countries. body: The Workshop That Stayed When James Marr from Bamboo Bicycle Club first walked through the D&T corridor at The Oratory School in Reading, the school had a decision to make. They could book a day visit — fun, memorable, and gone by Friday. Or they could do something they had never seen another UK secondary school do: keep BBC permanently. They chose permanence. In February 2020, The Oratory School launched a dedicated, in-school bamboo bicycle workshop — the first of its kind in a UK secondary school. The jigs, tools, and materials stayed. The knowledge became part of the school. The Challenge The Oratory School is an HMC independent boarding and day school for boys aged 11–18, founded in 1859 in Woodcote, Oxfordshire. Like many schools at this level, it had excellent D&T facilities and capable students — but enrichment that genuinely challenged advanced learners was harder to find. One-off workshops are exciting. What D&T departments actually need is a programme that can be delivered year after year, creating real curriculum depth rather than a single memorable afternoon. The school was also responding to the broader shift in the D&T curriculum toward sustainability and materials literacy. Students need to engage with real materials, real manufacturing constraints, and real design problems — not just CAD simulations. Bamboo composite engineering offered something that standard resistant materials units could not: a genuinely novel material, with engineering properties that challenged assumptions. The Solution BBC worked with The Oratory School to establish a dedicated in-school workshop space, providing frame jigs, hand tools, and an initial materials training package. The school provided the room; BBC provided the programme infrastructure. The launch event — Saturday 29 February 2020, 13:30–17:00 — was open to students and parents together. An unusual format for a school technical programme, and a deliberate one: it signalled from the start that bamboo bike building is a social, collaborative activity, not a solitary project. Families building together created a community moment around the school's new capability. The curriculum integration covers KS3 and KS4 D&T (materials selection, manufacturing processes, structural joinery), Physics (forces, stress, material properties), Chemistry (composite materials, resin chemistry), and Geography (bamboo cultivation, carbon sequestration, global supply chains). Students working with BBC's flax-and-natural-resin joinery technique engage directly with composite engineering principles — the same fundamentals used in aerospace and automotive manufacturing. The Oratory's decision to house BBC's equipment on a long-term basis is itself the evidence of programme quality. Bamboo Bicycle Club, founded in 2012, has now supported over 4,000 builds across 36+ countries. The Oratory School represents a milestone: the first UK secondary school to transition from visitor engagement to institutional partnership. That transition — from a single workshop to an embedded programme — is precisely the model BBC is now offering to other schools. For Ofsted purposes, the programme contributes to the personal development and enrichment strand: students are acquiring skills outside the standard curriculum, developing independence, resilience, and technical confidence through a genuine manufacturing challenge. For D&T departments, it provides a recurring, high-quality practical unit with clear curriculum links, OCN Level 2 pathway access, and a finished product — a bamboo bicycle frame — that demonstrates real engineering capability. title: UCL Commissions Bamboo Electric Cargo Bike from BBC
tags: cargo-bike, case-study, education, engineering, higher-education, stem, university
body: A University Needed Something That Didn't Exist. They Called BBC. In October 2020, University College London commissioned Bamboo Bicycle Club to build an electric cargo bike. Not a standard bicycle. A cargo vehicle, fitted with an electric front hub motor, engineered to carry payloads of up to 100 kilograms. In bamboo. UCL consistently ranks in the global top ten universities. When it needed a bamboo electric cargo bike that could carry 100kg, it went to BBC. The Challenge: Engineering a Vehicle That Doesn't Exist Electric cargo bikes are a growing category in sustainable urban transport. But existing commercial e-cargo bikes are built almost entirely from aluminium and steel — materials with significant embodied carbon and substantial environmental footprint. UCL's research interest was whether bamboo composite construction could meet the structural requirements of an electric cargo vehicle. Not a theoretical question. An empirical one: build it, test it, find out. The specification was demanding: Electric front hub motor integration — requiring torque analysis and frame stress distribution calculations 100kg payload capacity — significantly beyond standard bicycle frame engineering requirements Bamboo composite construction throughout Functional vehicle — operational, not a static prototype No off-the-shelf vehicle met these specifications. BBC built one. The Solution: Applied Bamboo Composite Engineering BBC's approach drew on the same fundamental techniques used in every BBC frame build — bamboo tube preparation, flax-and-natural-resin composite joinery, iterative geometric design — scaled and adapted for a cargo vehicle specification. The structural requirements for a 100kg cargo frame are substantially higher than for a standard road or mountain bike frame. The join geometry, tube dimensions, and resin layering schedule all needed to account for significantly higher static and dynamic loads. BBC's experience with university-tested structural joints — flax-and-resin bamboo connections tested under load at university laboratory facilities — informed the engineering decisions. The completed vehicle was delivered to UCL in October 2020. Outcomes The UCL commission establishes BBC's engineering credentials at the most demanding level available. A global top-ten university chose BBC to build a vehicle that required composite engineering judgement, structural design capability, and bamboo material expertise in combination. For schools evaluating BBC's programme, the UCL commission answers a question that sometimes goes unasked: is this real engineering? The techniques students use in a BBC school workshop — preparing bamboo tubes, wrapping flax fibre composites, applying and curing natural resin — are the same techniques used to build a vehicle commissioned by UCL for research purposes. The application scales. The knowledge is the same. UCL joins BBC's university partner network: Coventry University, King's College London, London South Bank University (£70,000 active partnership), and the University of Manchester. BBC's Engineering Capability: What Schools Can Expect BBC's school programmes draw on the same technical knowledge base that produced the UCL cargo bike. Students working with BBC do not encounter simplified versions of the process — they engage with the actual material, the actual techniques, and the actual challenges, adapted for their level and context. To discuss engineering partnerships or curriculum collaboration, contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org .

title: King's College London: Bamboo Building for Teaching Staff
tags: case-study, education, higher-education, russell-group, stem, teacher-training, university
body: The Academics Built First King's College London is one of the UK's leading research universities — a founding member of the Russell Group and consistently ranked in the global top 40. In March 2020, King's was exploring whether to introduce bamboo bicycle building into its curriculum. Before any student was invited to participate, the teaching staff built one themselves. That decision — run a practice workshop with academic staff as the learners before making any curriculum commitment — reflects the rigour of serious educational due diligence. You cannot evaluate a programme from the outside. You have to be in the room, working with the material, to know what it demands of participants and what it returns. The Challenge: Evaluating a New Programme for University Curriculum Universities face a specific challenge when considering novel practical programmes. The question is never simply: is this interesting? The question is: does this work educationally, can our staff deliver it, does it map to our learning outcomes, and is the material knowledge deep enough to withstand academic scrutiny? The practice workshop with teaching personnel was the evaluation mechanism. If the process was interesting to teach — if the material questions it raised were genuinely complex — then the programme had a place in the university curriculum. The Solution: Teaching Staff as Learners First BBC ran a practice workshop at King's College London in March 2020, with teaching staff as the participants. The workshop covered bamboo tube preparation, geometric frame design, flax-and-resin joinery, and the curing and finishing process. Teaching staff at a research university would naturally bring a different set of questions to the process than a school student: about failure modes, about the mechanics of flax fibre reinforcement, about joint geometry and structural performance, about the carbon accounting of bamboo versus industrial composites. Those questions are what make a BBC workshop rigorous. The partnership was developing actively in early 2020. BBC's post confirms the ongoing relationship: "We've been working with King College London to look at introducing bike building into the university." Past continuous. Active. Ongoing — until the pandemic interrupted what had been a live conversation. Outcomes The King's College London practice workshop establishes several important precedents for schools and universities evaluating BBC's programme. First, it confirms that BBC's approach to academic partnership begins with the educators, not the students. The practice workshop model — teach the teachers before you teach the students — is available to any school or university that wants to evaluate the programme rigorously before committing. Second, it places BBC within the Russell Group's orbit as a serious partner. King's College London does not run practice workshops with organisations whose programmes do not meet academic standards. Third, it adds KCL to BBC's growing university network: UCL, Coventry University, LSBU (£70,000 active partnership), and the University of Manchester. How Universities Can Evaluate BBC's Programme BBC actively encourages the King's College model: a practice workshop with academic or technical staff before any student cohort is committed. BBC can also co-design curriculum content, mapping the bamboo building process to specific learning outcomes and module structures. BBC holds OCN Level 2 accreditation in Sustainable Manufacturing. To discuss a university partnership, contact james@bamboobicycleclub.org .

title: Coventry University: BBC at UK Bamboo Summit 2024

The gap between research and practice — between knowing bamboo has a negative carbon footprint and knowing how to work with it — is where most sustainability education breaks down. BBC was the natural choice. With over 4,000 builds completed across 36+ countries since 2012, BBC has more practical bamboo frame-building experience than any other organisation in the UK. body: In 2016, BBC partnered with UCL to design and build a bamboo cargo bike for an African farmer. The brief: create a load-carrying bicycle from bamboo that could serve smallholder agricultural needs — robust, locally repairable, and manufacturable from locally available materials. The project brought together BBC's practical frame-building expertise and UCL's engineering design methodology — an early example of design-for-development work that has since become central to BBC's impact narrative. The cargo bike specification required BBC to think beyond the recreational cycling market: load distribution, dirt road durability, component replacement in the field, and manufacturing constraints without power tools. The UCL African Farmer Cargo Bike seeded a productive long-term relationship, leading to three further documented collaborations: two Masters electric vehicle projects (2018 and 2020) and ongoing informal engagement. A builder in New Zealand, Japan, or Germany can learn to fit a tapered headset by watching a Hackney founder explain it in real time. BBC's knowledge has always been global — Workshop Wednesdays made that explicit. Key Facts Format: Live YouTube education series Year: 2021 Topics: Headsets, dropouts, metal inserts, frame finishing Access: Free, archived "Join us live to learn how to fit a tapered headset to your bike. 🍻" — Bamboo Bicycle Club, Workshop Wednesdays, 2021

title: Balance Bike Tutorial Series: Free Digital Education
tags: balance bike, digital, education, free, tutorial, YouTube
summary: YouTube Education | Global | 2024–2025 In November 2024, BBC launched a structured tutorial video series on YouTube for bamboo balance bike construction — making professional frame-building education freely accessible to anyone, anywhere i...
body: In November 2024, BBC launched a structured tutorial video series on YouTube for bamboo balance bike construction — making professional frame-building education freely accessible to anyone, anywhere in the world. The series covers every stage of the balance bike build: selecting and preparing bamboo, setting up the jig, cutting and fitting tubes, preparing joints, applying bio-resin, and finishing the frame. Free digital education is a conscious choice. BBC believes that knowledge of how to build a bicycle from bamboo should be democratised — anyone who wants to learn should be able to. The YouTube series is the most scalable expression of that belief. The tutorials followed BBC's Workshop Wednesdays series (2021), which covered headsets, dropouts, metal inserts, and frame finishing. Together they represent a significant body of free, high-quality bicycle engineering education. Key Facts Platform: YouTube (@BamboobicycleclubOrg) Launched: November 2024 Content: Step-by-step bamboo balance bike construction Access: Free, global "New balance bike tutorials on our YouTube channel — along with lots of other tutorials." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, November 2024

title: Falun, Sweden: Teaching a Bike Cooperative
summary: International Community Education | Falun, Sweden | June 2018 In June 2018, James Marr travelled to Falun, Sweden, to teach a local bicycle cooperative how to build bamboo bikes — no formal institutional partnership, just a direct invitation from a community of ...
body: In June 2018, James Marr travelled to Falun, Sweden, to teach a local bicycle cooperative how to build bamboo bikes — no formal institutional partnership, just a direct invitation from a community of builders who wanted to learn. The Falun session demonstrates that BBC's education model is not dependent on institutional infrastructure: a workshop, a willing group, and the right materials are enough. Community bicycle cooperatives provide affordable maintenance, build cycling confidence, and serve as hubs for advocacy. Teaching one to build bamboo frames extends that model with a new product they can offer their community. Falun was one of several international teaching moments alongside Kenya (2017), The Hague (2017), and later international work — demonstrating the global appetite for bamboo bike building education. Key Facts Location: Falun, Sweden Date: June 2018 Host: Local bicycle cooperative Taught by: James Marr, Founder "Great group and some real enthusiasm for bike building!" — James Marr, June 2018

title: Kenya: Teaching Communities to Build Their Own Bikes
tags: Africa, community, education, international, Kenya, skills transfer
summary: International Education Programme | Kenya | 2017–2019 BBC took its education model to Kenya — teaching local communities to build bamboo bicycles from locally available materials. In 2017, BBC's Munich team was documented as being 'currently in Kenya.' B...
body: BBC took its education model to Kenya — teaching local communities to build bamboo bicycles from locally available materials. In 2017, BBC's Munich team was documented as being 'currently in Kenya.' By 2019, a full video had been produced: 'Making bicycles simple — teaching people in Kenya to build bikes.' The Kenya programme addresses a fundamental access problem. In many parts of East Africa, bicycles are essential transport but import costs and lack of repair infrastructure make conventional bikes fragile assets. BBC's approach was not to deliver bikes but to transfer knowledge. Participants learned to select bamboo, prepare it, construct frames, fit components, and maintain the finished bicycle — creating lasting capacity rather than dependency. Kenya is part of BBC's wider Africa education work, which has included Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Ghana — translating BBC's core mission into a global development context. Key Facts Location: Kenya (wider East Africa programme) Years: 2017–2019 Model: Skills transfer, not bike donation Related: Munich workshop team; Africa programme "Making bicycles simple — teaching people in Kenya to build bikes." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, 2019

title: UCL Masters Programme: Electric Bamboo Bike Engineering
tags: education, electric bike, engineering, Masters, UCL, university
summary: University Partnership | University College London | 2018–2020 For two years running, Bamboo Bicycle Club partnered with UCL's Department of Mechanical Engineering to provide the live design brief for a Masters-level electric vehicle project....
body: For two years running, Bamboo Bicycle Club partnered with UCL's Department of Mechanical Engineering to provide the live design brief for a Masters-level electric vehicle project. In 2018, students produced a bamboo e-bike with a fully integrated rear electric motor hub and battery system. In 2020, the project extended to a 100kg-capacity cargo bike with an electric front hub drive. Running a live Masters programme brief means students do genuine engineering work with real constraints. The bamboo frame provides an unusually complex design challenge: a non-standard, variable-section material requiring manual joining techniques incompatible with conventional manufacturing assumptions. BBC's involvement with UCL confirmed that bamboo bicycle construction is a legitimate subject for advanced engineering research — not just a craft activity. Key Facts Institution: University College London Department: Mechanical Engineering Years: 2018, 2020 Projects: Electric bamboo bike; 100kg cargo bike Level: Masters degree "We run a master program at UCL. This year's project was an electric bike." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, 2018

title: Reeds School: End-of-Term Bamboo Racing
tags: education, hands-on learning, racing, school, Surrey
summary: Independent School Programme | Surrey | 2019 In 2019, students at Reeds School in Surrey built four bamboo bicycles as part of a BBC school programme — then raced them at the end of term....
body: In 2019, students at Reeds School in Surrey built four bamboo bicycles as part of a BBC school programme — then raced them at the end of term. BBC brought tools, jigs, and bamboo materials to the school's workshop. Students worked through the build process over multiple sessions, with the end-of-term race as their goal — proof of work that a bike built well is a bike that races well. The combination of technical making and competitive end-goal is powerful. Students learn to care about precision because an imprecise bike rides badly. They learn to finish what they start because there is a race waiting. Reeds was one of several schools engaged during BBC's active schools programme period, alongside programmes in the Netherlands and international enquiries. Key Facts Institution: Reeds School, Surrey Year: 2019 Output: 4 bamboo bicycles built and raced End goal: End-of-term bamboo bike race "End of term bamboo racing, Reeds School. Four bamboo bikes built by students racing!" — Bamboo Bicycle Club, 2019

title: The Hague School Project: Seven Bikes in a Classroom
tags: design technology, education, international, Netherlands, school
summary: International Schools Programme | Netherlands | December 2017 In December 2017, pupils at a school in The Hague, Netherlands built seven bamboo bicycles using BBC's educational starter kit — proving the concept internationally....
body: In December 2017, pupils at a school in The Hague, Netherlands built seven bamboo bicycles using BBC's educational starter kit — proving the concept internationally. BBC's educational kit is specifically designed for school-based delivery: self-contained, tool-minimal, and structured around a clear instructional sequence that teachers can follow without specialist knowledge. Seven bikes in a classroom is no small achievement. Each requires precise measurement, careful bamboo selection, accurate cutting, patient joint preparation, and methodical assembly — developing spatial reasoning, precision craftsmanship, and confidence. The Hague project remains one of the earliest examples of international school delivery and proved that BBC's educational model works across languages and cultures. Key Facts Location: The Hague, Netherlands Year: December 2017 Output: 7 bamboo bicycles built by students Delivery model: Self-contained educational starter kit "Pupils at a school in The Hague building 7 bamboo bikes using our educational starter kit." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, December 2017

title: Southbank UTC: Six Students Build Six Bikes
tags: design technology, education, school, Southbank, students, UTC
summary: School Education Partnership | London | 2016 In 2016, students at Southbank University Technical College built six bamboo bicycles under the guidance of Bamboo Bicycle Club — then rode them. It is one of the earliest and most complete examples o...
body: In 2016, students at Southbank University Technical College built six bamboo bicycles under the guidance of Bamboo Bicycle Club — then rode them. It is one of the earliest and most complete examples of BBC delivering a structured schools programme. BBC delivered jig components directly to the school, equipping the workshop to run the build programme in-house. Students worked through the full frame-building process: measuring, cutting, mitring, joining, and finishing. Six complete bikes were produced. Southbank UTC is specifically designed to combine academic education with technical and vocational learning. Bamboo bicycle building covers materials science, design technology, product design, engineering principles, and sustainable manufacturing — all in one practical activity. The success of the programme demonstrated that BBC's methodology could be delivered within a school setting without a professional workshop instructor on site at all times. Key Facts Institution: Southbank University Technical College Year: 2016 Output: 6 bamboo bicycles built by students Curriculum links: Design Technology, Product Design, Engineering "Students out on their bamboo bikes — good to see the bikes all together." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, 2016

title: London Design Festival: Introduction to Bamboo Workshop
tags: design, education, London Design Festival, sustainability, workshop
summary: Design Education | London | August 2024 In August 2024, Bamboo Bicycle Club participated in the London Design Festival — the annual event that has defined London's global status as a design capital since 2003....
body: In August 2024, Bamboo Bicycle Club participated in the London Design Festival — the annual event that has defined London's global status as a design capital since 2003. BBC ran its Introduction to Bamboo Workshop as part of the festival, offering design professionals, students, and the public a chance to work with bamboo, understand its material properties, and build their first bamboo structure. Participants discovered bamboo's remarkable properties firsthand: tensile strength of 28,000 newtons vs 23,000 for steel, natural anti-bacterial properties, a carbon-sequestering growth cycle, and workability with simple hand tools. The London Design Festival appearance was part of BBC's strategy to build credibility within the design and creative industries — positioning bamboo as a serious material for contemporary sustainable design. Key Facts Event: London Design Festival Date: August 2024 BBC offering: Introduction to Bamboo Workshop Audience: Global design professionals, students, public "Our involvement in London Design Festival reflects our commitment to innovation and sustainability." — Bamboo Bicycle Club

title: UK Bamboo Summit: Keynote and Workshop at Coventry University
tags: bamboo summit, Coventry, education, keynote, university
summary: Higher Education | Coventry University | September 2024 In September 2024, Bamboo Bicycle Club was invited to keynote and lead a hands-on workshop at the UK Bamboo Summit at Coventry University — bringing together researchers, engineers, architects, and cr...
body: In September 2024, Bamboo Bicycle Club was invited to keynote and lead a hands-on workshop at the UK Bamboo Summit at Coventry University — bringing together researchers, engineers, architects, and craft practitioners from across the world. BBC's session combined a presentation on bamboo bicycle construction with a practical workshop where delegates built their first bamboo joint. Attendees came from Brilliant Bamboo UK, Atelier One, Imagine Bamboo, World Bamboo, and Terragrn. For BBC, the summit represented recognition from the academic and professional bamboo community that 12 years of hands-on building knowledge has scientific and educational validity. The summit confirmed BBC's position at the intersection of craft education and material innovation — giving it credibility across both the maker community and the sustainability research world. Key Facts Event: UK Bamboo Summit Host: Coventry University Date: September 2024 BBC role: Keynote speaker and workshop leader "What an insightful and promising event. So pleased to be part of the future vision for building with bamboo." — James Marr, Bamboo Bicycle Club

title: Stoke-on-Trent College: Craft, Community and Bamboo
tags: Brilliant Bamboo, college, education, further education, Stoke
summary: Further Education Partnership | Stoke-on-Trent | March 2025 In March 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club partnered with Brilliant Bamboo UK to deliver an introductory workshop for students at Stoke-on-Trent College alongside local artists and community makers....
body: In March 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club partnered with Brilliant Bamboo UK to deliver an introductory workshop for students at Stoke-on-Trent College alongside local artists and community makers. The session brought together further education students — many of whom had never built anything with their hands before — with experienced makers and craft practitioners. Working side by side, they explored bamboo as a structural material: its tensile strength, workability, and potential as a sustainable alternative to steel. The workshop was deliberately collaborative. Students and local artists worked at the same benches, with no hierarchy between formal learners and community participants — central to both Brilliant Bamboo UK's model and BBC's approach to skills education. Participants left with hands-on experience of precision cutting and joining and — perhaps more importantly — a felt sense that making something difficult is within their reach. Key Facts Partner: Brilliant Bamboo UK Institution: Stoke-on-Trent College Format: Introductory workshop, mixed FE students and community Date: March 2025 "Creativity, craftsmanship, and community — all in one workshop." — Bamboo Bicycle Club, March 2025

title: Build to Bond: Fathers Building Balance Bikes for Their Children
tags: balance bike, Build to Bond, family, prison, rehabilitation
summary: Prison Rehabilitation Programme | HMP Lowdham Grange | 2025 Inside HMP Lowdham Grange, incarcerated fathers are building bamboo balance bikes — not for themselves, but for their children on the outside. That's the whole point of Build to Bond....
body: Inside HMP Lowdham Grange, incarcerated fathers are building bamboo balance bikes — not for themselves, but for their children on the outside. That's the whole point of Build to Bond. The programme takes the technical skills from the six-week OCN bamboo frame-building course and redirects them towards a single, deeply personal object: a hand-crafted balance bike, built by a father, sized for his child, finished with care. When the bike is complete, it leaves the prison and finds its way home. The research case for family-centred rehabilitation is well established. Prisoners who maintain strong family contact during custody are significantly less likely to reoffend. Build to Bond operationalises that research — it turns abstract family connection into something physical that a child can ride. Build to Bond received a full feature in the Financial Times in September 2025 and a public endorsement from James Timpson, the UK Prisons Minister, who cited it as an example of the kind of innovative rehabilitation work that makes communities safer. Key Facts Programme type: Family reunification through craft Output: Bamboo balance bikes, gifted to participants' children Government endorsement: James Timpson, UK Prisons Minister National media: Financial Times, September 2025 "Innovative projects, such as Build to Bond, support rehabilitation and help people leave prison as better citizens, boosting the economy and keeping our streets safe." — James Timpson, UK Prisons Minister

title: OCN Level 2: Bamboo Bicycle Building at HMP Lowdham Grange
summary: Prison Education | Nottinghamshire | 2025 In March 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club launched a structured vocational education programme inside HMP Lowdham Grange — a Category B male training prison in Nottinghamshire. The six-week course is fully a...
body: In March 2025, Bamboo Bicycle Club launched a structured vocational education programme inside HMP Lowdham Grange — a Category B male training prison in Nottinghamshire. The six-week course is fully accredited to OCN Level 2 in Sustainable Manufacturing, the first of its kind in any UK prison. Each cohort of twelve carefully selected inmates attends 18 hours of hands-on sessions per week. The curriculum covers bamboo frame construction, precision cutting, mitre joining, bio-resin application, bicycle mechanics, and quality control. A peer-learning model runs alongside formal instruction: trusted inmates assist staff in delivering the training, building leadership skills as well as craft skills. What sets this programme apart is its material philosophy. At the end of each six-week cohort, frames are deconstructed. Lugs and connections are cleaned and reused for the next group. Bamboo offcuts are composted. Nothing is wasted. The course teaches circular manufacturing not as theory but as daily practice. The programme arrived at a critical time. HMP Lowdham Grange underwent a management takeover by HMPPS in December 2023. BBC's workshop was commissioned as part of a broader rehabilitation reset — purposeful, skills-based activity designed to address behavioural challenges through focus and craft. Key Facts Programme length: 6 weeks, 18 hours/week Cohort size: 12 inmates Accreditation: OCN Level 2, Sustainable Manufacturing Workshop size: 2,000 sq ft dedicated facility "Training prisoners in the building of frames and mechanics of bikes so they can build themselves a brighter future." — James Marr, Founder, Bamboo Bicycle Club

title: Bamboo Bicycle Club Partners with Southbank University: A New Hub for Sustainable Bike Building
summary: Bamboo Bicycle Club has partnered with Southbank University to establish a dedicated workshop space on campus, promoting sustainable design and hands-on learning. This new hub will support students and staff in building their own bamboo bicycles, providing tools, materials, and expert guidance. The
body: We’re excited to announce a groundbreaking educational partnership between Bamboo Bicycle Club and Southbank University. This collaboration marks a significant step forward in promoting sustainable design and hands-on learning within the university community. As part of this partnership, we’re establishing a dedicated space within Southbank University’s campus, specifically designed to support students and staff in building their own bamboo bicycles. This space will be equipped with all the tools, materials, and expertise needed to guide participants through the entire process—from concept to completion. Our goal is to empower students and faculty to explore the possibilities of sustainable transport while gaining practical skills in design and manufacturing. Bamboo Bicycle Club has always been passionate about education and innovation. By partnering with Southbank University, we aim to create a vibrant learning environment where creativity and sustainability intersect. The new workshop will not only serve as a hands-on lab but also as a platform for collaborative projects, research, and experimentation. Whether you’re an engineering student looking to apply your knowledge, a design student eager to explore sustainable materials, or simply someone passionate about bicycles, this space will offer invaluable resources and support. We believe that by working together, we can inspire a new generation of innovators who are committed to sustainability and craftsmanship. This partnership also reflects our commitment to fostering connections between industry and academia. By integrating real-world projects into the educational experience, we hope to bridge the gap between theory and practice, providing students with the skills and confidence they need to succeed in their future careers. Stay tuned for more updates on this exciting initiative. We can’t wait to see the incredible creations that will come out of this collaboration!

title: The University of Texas at San Antonio Launches Bamboo Bicycle Club
summary: Bamboo Bicycle Club launches in Texas with student starting to build using our lugged frame kit
body: The University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) as the campus welcomes a groundbreaking new initiative: the Bamboo Bicycle Club. Spearheaded by engineering enthusiast Elliot Howard, this club aims to blend sustainability, innovation, and hands-on learning by building two bamboo lugged frame kits. Elliot Howard, a passionate advocate for eco-friendly engineering solutions, saw an opportunity to introduce a unique project that combines creativity and environmental consciousness. The Bamboo Bicycle Club will challenge students to design and construct bicycles using sustainable bamboo materials, offering a hands-on experience that complements their academic studies. Members of the club will work collaboratively to build two custom bamboo bikes from scratch. This process will not only enhance their understanding of design and engineering principles but also promote teamwork and problem-solving skills. The use of bamboo, a rapidly renewable resource, underscores the club's commitment to sustainability and eco-friendly practices. The project culminates in an exciting showcase where students will present their completed bicycles, demonstrating their craftsmanship and innovative designs. This initiative not only provides practical skills but also fosters a sense of community and shared purpose among participants. The Bamboo Bicycle Club at UTSA, with Elliot Howard at the helm, promises to be an inspiring journey of learning, creativity, and sustainability. Keep an eye out for the amazing bamboo bikes set to roll out on campus soon!

title: Empowering Rwanda Through Bamboo: The Bamboo Bicycle Club's Sustainable Vision in Partnership with Urumuri
summary: At the Bamboo Bicycle Club, our mission extends beyond crafting unique bicycles. We're committed to driving sustainable development, empowering local communities, and advocating for eco-friendly transportation. Our latest initiative in Rwanda, in partnership with Urumuri's "Ride for the Future" prog
body: At the Bamboo Bicycle Club, our mission extends beyond crafting unique bicycles. We're committed to driving sustainable development, empowering local communities, and advocating for eco-friendly transportation. Our latest initiative in Rwanda, in partnership with Urumuri's "Ride for the Future" program, exemplifies this commitment by combining resourcefulness with resilience to foster a green revolution on two wheels. Cultivating Skills and Sustainability Our project's heart lies in transferring skills and knowledge to local artisans in Rwanda. By introducing them to the art of bamboo bicycle construction, we are not just sharing techniques; we are planting the seeds of self-reliance and environmental stewardship. Bamboo is a sustainable material that offers a significant reduction in environmental impact compared to traditional metal frames, making it an ideal resource for eco-conscious manufacturing. Tools of Change: Inserts and Jigs The backbone of our training involves equipping Rwandan builders with specialized tools like custom-made inserts and jigs. These instruments are crucial for maintaining precision and facilitating the assembly process, allowing builders of all skill levels to produce durable and reliable bicycles. By providing these tools, we ensure a foundation for sustainable practices that can be replicated and adapted locally. Phases of Development: From Basics to Specialized Bicycles Our engagement unfolds in phases, beginning with the production of standard bicycles that cater to daily commuting needs. This foundational phase is crucial for solidifying skills and production capabilities. Progressing to cargo bikes, we aim to address the logistical needs of local businesses, helping them enhance their operations sustainably. Advancing to Testing and Market Entry In collaboration with Urumuri's "Ride for the Future," are planing to establish a frame testing facility in Rwanda. This step is vital for ensuring the safety and reliability of the bicycles and acts as a bridge to the market entry. This facility will not only set quality benchmarks but also facilitate the entry of these eco-friendly bamboo bikes into local and international markets. https://urumuri.ch/ride-for-the-future/
